1. Limb (a) inquires whether loans and advances made on the basis of security have been properly secured and whether their terms are prejudicial to the interests of the company or its members.
2. Limb (c) requires an inquiry into securities sold below cost in every company, including investment and banking companies.
3. Limb (d) concerns whether personal expenses have been charged to the revenue account.
4. Limb (f) applies where the books state that shares were allotted for cash and asks whether cash was actually received.
options: 1 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
questions.explanation: Statement 2 is not correct: limb (c) applies only where the company is not an investment company or a banking company, so asserting that it applies to every company including investment and banking companies is false. Statement 3 is not correct: limb (d) concerns loans and advances shown as deposits, whereas personal expenses charged to revenue fall under limb (e), so this pairing is wrong. Statements 1 and 4 accurately reproduce limbs (a) and (f). Because the question asks for the statements that are NOT correct, the answer is 2 and 3 only; options that flag statement 1 or statement 4 wrongly mark a correct statement as incorrect.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A banking company's auditor does not have to inquire under section 143(1)(c) into whether shares and debentures were sold below their purchase price.
Reason (R): Section 143(1)(c) applies only where the company is not an investment company and not a banking company.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is correct but R is not correct.
A is not correct but R is correct.
questions.explanation: Limb (c) of section 143(1) is expressly conditioned by the words "where the company, not being an investment company or a banking company", so the inquiry into shares, debentures and other securities sold below purchase price simply does not operate for a banking company. The assertion (that the banking company's auditor need not inquire under limb (c)) follows directly and correctly from this condition, which is exactly what the reason states. No separate justification is required because the exclusion is built into the opening words of the limb. Hence both are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.question: An auditor finds that a company made a secured loan but the security taken is wholly inadequate, and the terms of the loan are such that they disadvantage the shareholders. Under which limb of section 143(1), and to what extent, is this an inquiry?
options: Limb (a), but only as to whether the security is adequate, not as to prejudice to shareholders.
Limb (b), because an inadequate loan is a book-entry transaction.
Limb (c), because the loan is an asset of the company.
Limb (a), covering both whether loans made on the basis of security have been properly secured and whether the terms are prejudicial to the interests of the company or its members.
questions.explanation: Limb (a) has two components: whether loans and advances made on the basis of security have been properly secured, and whether the terms on which they are made are prejudicial to the interests of the company or its members. These facts engage both - inadequate security goes to the first component and disadvantage to the shareholders (the members) goes to the second - which is why the wider option is most appropriate and the narrow option that excludes prejudice to members is incomplete. Limb (b) concerns transactions represented merely by book entries and limb (c) concerns securities sold below cost, neither of which describes a loan made by the company.

questions.question:
Case Study. Venus Apparels Pvt Ltd is a private company. For FY 2024-25 its turnover (as per the financial statements) was ₹42 crore and its aggregate borrowings from banks and financial institutions never exceeded ₹18 crore at any time during the year. Its auditor, CMA Prakash, is completing his report under section 143(3).
The following statements are made:
1. Venus is not required to have its internal financial controls reported under section 143(3)(i) because it satisfies both threshold conditions.
2. Venus would lose the exemption if, at any time during the year, its borrowings exceeded ₹25 crore.
3. The exemption is available only because Venus is a public company.
4. For the carve-out to apply, Venus's turnover must be less than ₹50 crore and its aggregate borrowings less than ₹25 crore.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 3 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Section 143(3)(i) does not apply to a private company whose turnover is less than ₹50 crore and whose aggregate borrowings are less than ₹25 crore at any time during the year; Venus, at ₹42 crore turnover and ₹18 crore borrowings, satisfies both, so statements 1 and 4 are correct. Statement 2 correctly reads the words "at any time during the year", meaning a temporary breach of ₹25 crore borrowings defeats the carve-out. Statement 3 is wrong because the exemption flows from the financial thresholds (and from one-person-company status), not from being a public company - a public company would not get this carve-out. Any option admitting statement 3 is rejected.

questions.question: Venus Apparels Pvt Ltd is a private company whose turnover for FY 2024-25 is ₹42 crore. For most of the year its borrowings from banks were ₹15 crore, but in August 2024 it temporarily drew a working-capital limit taking aggregate borrowings to ₹27 crore for about two weeks before repaying them. The auditor must decide whether to report on internal financial controls under section 143(3)(i). How does the carve-out apply?
options: The carve-out applies because borrowings were below ₹25 crore for the majority of the year.
The carve-out does not apply because the ₹25 crore test is measured at any time during the year and it was breached.
The carve-out applies because the breach was temporary and the borrowing was repaid.
The carve-out is irrelevant because private companies never report under 143(3)(i).
questions.explanation: The section 143(3)(i) carve-out for a private company requires that aggregate borrowings be less than ₹25 crore at any time during the year; a breach, even for only two weeks, defeats the exemption because the test is an "at any time during the year" test, not an average or year-end test. Venus touched ₹27 crore, so the condition fails and the auditor must report on the adequacy and operating effectiveness of internal financial controls with reference to the financial statements. Options relying on the breach being temporary, on the majority of the year, or on a general private-company exemption all misread the timing condition.

questions.question: Venus Apparels Pvt Ltd is a private company with aggregate borrowings of ₹10 crore from banks throughout FY 2024-25, but its turnover for the year was ₹55 crore. The auditor considers whether the section 143(3)(i) carve-out applies. What is the correct position?
options: It does not apply because both turnover below ₹50 crore AND borrowings below ₹25 crore must be satisfied, and the turnover condition fails.
It applies because borrowings are comfortably below ₹25 crore.
It applies because turnover is the less important of the two conditions.
It does not apply only if the company is a public company.
questions.explanation: The carve-out is expressed as "turnover less than ₹50 crores plus aggregate borrowings less than ₹25 crores", which requires both conditions to be satisfied together; meeting only the borrowings test is not enough. Venus's ₹55 crore turnover exceeds the ₹50 crore ceiling, so the exemption is lost and reporting under 143(3)(i) is required. Treating the borrowings condition as sufficient, or the turnover condition as the less important of the two, misreads this cumulative test, and a public/private distinction is not the reason the carve-out fails on these facts. The decisive fact is that the two thresholds are cumulative.

questions.question: Aadhya Components Pvt Ltd is a private company that is a subsidiary of a listed public company. For FY 2024-25 its turnover is ₹40 crore and its aggregate borrowings from banks were ₹15 crore at all times during the year. The auditor argues that the section 143(3)(i) carve-out cannot apply because Aadhya is a subsidiary of a public company. Judged against the carve-out as stated for section 143(3)(i), is this argument correct?
options: Correct - being a subsidiary of a public company always defeats the 143(3)(i) carve-out.
Correct - the carve-out is available only to one person companies.
Not correct - the 143(3)(i) carve-out for a private company turns on the two financial thresholds (turnover below ₹50 crore and borrowings below ₹25 crore), not on subsidiary status.
Not correct - the carve-out is available to every private company regardless of any threshold.
questions.explanation: As stated for section 143(3)(i), the private-company carve-out is defined by the two financial conditions - turnover less than ₹50 crore and aggregate borrowings less than ₹25 crore at any time during the year - alongside the separate coverage of one person companies. Aadhya satisfies both conditions, so the duty to report on internal financial controls does not apply, and the auditor's reliance on subsidiary status is misplaced because the 143(3)(i) carve-out is not conditioned on the company being independent of a public company. The view that subsidiary status always defeats the carve-out imports a test the clause does not contain; the view that only one person companies qualify ignores the private-company limb; and the view that every private company qualifies regardless of threshold ignores the financial conditions. The decisive point is the wording of the 143(3)(i) carve-out.

questions.question:
Match the following limbs of section 143(3) with the matters the auditor's report must state.
Column I:
P. Limb (a)
Q. Limb (c)
R. Limb (d)
S. Limb (g)
Column II:
1. Whether the report on the accounts of a branch office audited by another person has been sent to the auditor and the manner in which he dealt with it.
2. Whether the auditor has obtained all information and explanations necessary for the purposes of the audit, and if not, the details and their effect on the financial statements.
3. Whether any director is disqualified from being appointed as a director under section 164(2).
4. Whether the company's balance sheet and profit and loss account are in agreement with the books of account and returns.
questions.explanation: Limb (a) is about whether all information and explanations necessary for the audit were obtained, and where not, the details and their effect on the financial statements, so P pairs with 2. Limb (c) concerns the branch audit report prepared by another person and how the auditor dealt with it, so Q pairs with 1. Limb (d) requires the balance sheet and profit and loss account to be in agreement with the books and returns, so R pairs with 4. Limb (g) requires a statement on whether any director is disqualified under section 164(2), so S pairs with 3; the other options swap these reporting duties.

questions.question:
The auditor's report under section 143(3) must also include the auditor's views and comments on certain "other matters". Consider the following:
1. Whether the company has disclosed the impact of pending litigations on its financial position in the financial statements.
2. Whether the company has made provision for material foreseeable loss, if any, arising from contracts including derivative contracts.
3. Whether there has been any delay in transferring amounts required to be transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund.
4. Whether the company has defaulted in repayment of loans to a bank during the year.
5. Whether the dividend declared or paid during the year complies with section 123.
Which of the above are among the "other matters" required to be commented on under section 143(3)?
options: 1, 2, 3 and 5 only
2, 3, 4 and 5 only
1, 3 and 5 only
questions.explanation: Section 143(3) lists as "other matters" the disclosure of the impact of pending litigations, provision for material foreseeable loss on contracts, delay in transferring amounts to the Investor Education and Protection Fund, compliance of dividend with section 123, and use of accounting software with an audit-trail feature. Statements 1, 2, 3 and 5 fall within this list. Statement 4, default in repayment of loans to banks, is not one of these section 143(3) other matters (it belongs to a different reporting framework), so options including it are wrong. The decisive skill is identifying the prescribed "other matters" and excluding an item that superficially resembles a reporting duty but is not in this clause.

questions.question:
Case Study. Coastal Textiles Ltd for FY 2024-25: (i) the accounting software used to maintain its books has a feature of recording an audit trail, but the feature was switched off for four months during the year; (ii) the company paid a dividend without complying with the conditions of section 123; (iii) a sum required to be transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund was transferred 40 days after the due date; (iv) the company has a pending litigation whose possible financial effect was not quantified or disclosed in the notes to the accounts. The auditor is framing the "other matters" part of his section 143(3) report.
The following statements are made:
1. The switched-off audit-trail feature must be commented on under the accounting-software "other matter".
2. Non-compliance of the dividend with section 123 must be commented on.
3. The delay in transferring amounts to the Investor Education and Protection Fund must be commented on.
4. The undisclosed impact of pending litigation is outside the "other matters" and need not be commented on.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: The section 143(3) "other matters" expressly include whether the accounting software with an audit-trail feature was operated throughout the year (it was switched off for four months, so statement 1 is correct), whether dividend complies with section 123 (statement 2 correct), and whether there has been delay in transferring amounts to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (statement 3 correct). Disclosure of the impact of pending litigations is itself one of the "other matters", so the failure to disclose it in fact engages that item, and statement 4, which says it need not be commented on, is wrong. Options admitting statement 4 are rejected. The decisive fact is that all listed items, including pending litigation, are "other matters".

questions.question: A company has a branch office at Indore whose accounts were audited by a different chartered accountant. The Indore auditor has not yet sent his report to the company's principal auditor before the principal auditor signs off. Under section 143(3), what is the principal auditor's duty regarding this branch report?
options: He must re-audit the Indore branch himself before signing.
He need not say anything, because branch audits by other auditors are outside section 143(3).
He must state whether the report on the branch accounts audited by the other person has been sent to him and the manner in which he has dealt with it in preparing his report.
He must qualify the opinion solely because the branch was audited by someone else.
questions.explanation: Limb (c) of section 143(3) requires the auditor's report to state whether the report on the accounts of a branch office audited by another person has been sent to him and the manner in which he has dealt with it in preparing his report. Here, since the Indore report was not received, the principal auditor's report must reflect that fact and how he dealt with it. He is not obliged to re-audit the branch himself, he cannot remain silent as though branch reports by other auditors were outside section 143(3), and the mere fact that a branch was audited by another person does not by itself force a qualification. The decisive provision is the transparency requirement in limb (c).

questions.question:
Consider section 143(3)(b). Which of the following statements are correct?
1. It requires a statement on whether proper books of account have been kept by the company.
2. It requires a statement on whether proper returns adequate for the audit have been received from branches not visited by the auditor.
3. The returns limb covers returns from all branches, including those the auditor personally visited.
4. It concerns the reconciliation of the balance sheet with the profit and loss account.
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Limb (b) combines two statements: whether proper books of account have been kept by the company, and whether proper returns adequate for the purposes of the audit have been received from branches not visited by the auditor, so statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong because the returns limb is directed specifically to branches not visited by the auditor, not to every branch. Statement 4 is wrong because agreement of the balance sheet and profit and loss account with the books is dealt with by limb (d), not limb (b). Hence only 1 and 2 are correct; the options that pull in returns from visited branches, or the balance-sheet reconciliation, misattribute the limbs.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about section 143(3). Which are NOT correct?
1. Limb (a) requires the auditor, where information and explanations were not obtained, to give details and the effect on the financial statements.
2. Limb (f) requires observations or comments on financial transactions or matters which have any adverse effect on the functioning of the company.
3. Limb (e) requires a statement on whether the financial statements comply with the requirements of any law, not accounting standards.
4. Limb (i) on internal financial controls applies to every company without exception.
options: 3 and 4 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statement 3 is not correct: limb (e) requires the auditor to state whether the financial statements comply with the accounting standards, so recharacterising it as a compliance-with-law-and-not-accounting-standards statement misstates the limb. Statement 4 is not correct: limb (i) is subject to the carve-out for one person companies and qualifying private companies (turnover below ₹50 crore and borrowings below ₹25 crore at any time during the year), so it does not apply to every company without exception. Statements 1 and 2 accurately reproduce limbs (a) and (f). Because the question asks for the statements that are NOT correct, the answer is 3 and 4 only; the options including 1 or 2 wrongly flag a correct statement.

questions.question: M/s Sharma & Co audit Nagpur Steels Ltd for FY 2024-25. The company gave a loan of ₹1 crore to another company and, in its books, wrongly presented that loan as a deposit accepted by it; on inquiry the auditor finds the presentation to be incorrect and the answer to the inquiry is adverse. The company also accepted genuine public deposits during the year, but everything about those deposits was perfectly regular, yielding no adverse answer. Considering section 143(1), which option best describes the auditor's reporting duty?
options: He must report both the mis-shown loan and the regular genuine deposits under limb (d).
He must report neither, as deposits are outside section 143(1).
He must report only the mis-shown loan under limb (d), because 143(1) reporting is required only where the answer is in the adverse; the fully regular deposits need not be reported.
He must report the genuine deposits under section 143(3)(f).
questions.explanation: Limb (d) of section 143(1) inquires whether loans and advances made by the company have been shown as deposits; here a genuine loan was wrongly shown as a deposit, so the answer is adverse and must be reported. The Note to section 143(1) means the auditor reports only when the answer is adverse, so the entirely regular genuine deposits, where the inquiry yields no adverse answer, are not reported. Reporting the regular deposits as well, or refusing to report anything on the premise that deposits are outside section 143(1), are both wrong, and the mis-shown loan is not a section 143(3)(f) matter. The decisive reasoning combines the limb-(d) inquiry with the adverse-only reporting condition.

questions.question: Case Study. During the FY 2024-25 audit of Konkan Pharma Ltd, the auditor is satisfied, on the basis of the company's records, that one of its directors stands disqualified from being appointed as a director under section 164(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, yet continues to hold office. Under which limb of section 143(3) must the auditor deal with this, and what must he state?
options: Limb (h), a qualification relating to maintenance of accounts.
Limb (f), an adverse-effect observation on the functioning of the company.
Limb (b), whether proper books of account have been kept.
Limb (g), whether any director is disqualified from being appointed as a director under section 164(2).
questions.explanation: Section 143(3)(g) specifically requires the auditor's report to state whether any director is disqualified from being appointed as a director under section 164(2); since the facts establish such a disqualification, this limb is engaged and the auditor must state it. This is not a maintenance-of-accounts qualification under limb (h), nor a generic adverse-effect observation under limb (f), nor a books-of-account statement under limb (b), each of which addresses different subject matter even though the facts superficially touch compliance. The decisive hook is the express cross-reference to section 164(2) in limb (g).

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A qualification or adverse remark relating to the maintenance of the company's books of account is reported under section 143(3)(h).
Reason (R): Section 143(3)(h) requires the auditor's report to state any qualification, reservation or adverse remark relating to the maintenance of accounts.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is correct but R is not correct.
A is not correct but R is correct.
questions.explanation: Limb (h) of section 143(3) requires the auditor's report to state any qualification, reservation or adverse remark relating to the maintenance of accounts, which is exactly what the reason sets out. The assertion - that such a remark is reported under limb (h) - follows directly from that wording, so the reason correctly explains the assertion. The candidate must not confuse this with limb (b), which asks affirmatively whether proper books of account have been kept; limb (h) is the home for any qualification or adverse remark about their maintenance. Both statements are correct and R explains A.

questions.question:
An auditor is examining the following matters. Match each to whether it is a duty to INQUIRE under section 143(1) or a duty to REPORT under section 143(3).
P. Whether loans and advances made by the company have been shown as deposits.
Q. Whether the balance sheet and profit and loss account are in agreement with the books and returns.
R. Whether personal expenses have been charged to the revenue account.
S. Whether proper returns adequate for the audit have been received from branches not visited.
options: P and Q under 143(1); R and S under 143(3)
P and R under 143(1); Q and S under 143(3)
All four under 143(1)
P and S under 143(1); Q and R under 143(3)
questions.explanation: Showing loans as deposits (limb (d)) and charging personal expenses to revenue (limb (e)) are matters the auditor inquires into under section 143(1); agreement of the balance sheet and profit and loss account with the books and returns (limb (d) of 143(3)) and receipt of adequate returns from branches not visited (limb (b) of 143(3)) are affirmative statements required in the report under section 143(3). This pairing - P and R to 143(1), Q and S to 143(3) - is the only correct mapping. The classic error is to treat every finding as a report duty or every duty as an inquiry, which the other options commit. The decisive skill is separating the 143(1) inquiry list from the 143(3) reporting list.

questions.question:
Case Study. During the FY 2024-25 audit of Mysore Alloys Ltd (neither an investment nor a banking company), the auditor finds the answers to the following inquiries to be in the adverse: (i) a loan made on the basis of security was not properly secured; (ii) a transaction represented merely by book entries was prejudicial to the company; (iii) shares held as an asset were sold below their purchase price; (iv) a loan was shown as a deposit. The auditor must now decide how to deal with these in his report.
Which of the following actions should the auditor take?
options: Report only (i) and (iii), as book entries and deposits are not 143(1) matters.
Report only under section 143(3)(f), since all reporting goes through that limb.
Report none, because section 143(1) never requires reporting.
Report all four, since each is a matter within section 143(1) on which the answer has been found in the adverse.
questions.explanation: Each finding maps to a limb of section 143(1): improperly secured loans to limb (a), prejudicial book-entry transactions to limb (b), securities sold below cost by a non-investment, non-banking company to limb (c), and loans shown as deposits to limb (d); because the answer to each inquiry is in the adverse, the Note requires the auditor to report them. Excluding book entries and deposits would be wrong because they are limbs (b) and (d) respectively, and channelling everything through section 143(3)(f) would be wrong because that limb concerns matters adversely affecting the functioning of the company rather than these inquiries. Reporting nothing would misread the Note, which suspends reporting only for favourable answers. The decisive condition is the "only if adverse" trigger, satisfied here for all four.

questions.question: A company's books state that shares of ₹50 lakh were allotted for cash. The auditor verifies that the full ₹50 lakh cash was in fact received in the bank on the allotment date and the balance sheet correctly records it. What does section 143(1) require the auditor to do?
options: Report it under limb (f) because any share allotment must be reported.
Report it under limb (c) as a securities transaction.
Report nothing under limb (f), since cash was actually received and the position stated is correct, regular and not misleading - the answer is not in the adverse.
Report it under section 143(3)(h) as a reservation on maintenance of accounts.
questions.explanation: Limb (f) inquires, where the books state that shares were allotted for cash, whether cash was actually received and, if not, whether the stated position is correct, regular and not misleading. Here cash was fully received and the balance sheet correctly records the allotment, so the answer is favourable and the Note to section 143(1), which requires reporting only where the answer is adverse, means nothing is reported. Treating limb (f) as a positive-confirmation duty that compels reporting of every allotment is wrong; limb (c) concerns securities sold below purchase price, not an allotment, and limb (h) concerns qualifications on the maintenance of accounts, none arising here. The decisive fact is the absence of an adverse answer.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the two reporting provisions.
1. Section 143(1) prescribes a duty to inquire into specified matters, whereas section 143(3) prescribes a duty to report specified matters in the auditor's report.
2. The auditor must make the 143(1) inquiries but need not report them unless the answer is adverse.
3. Section 143(3)(i)'s requirement to report on internal financial controls applies to all companies including one person companies.
4. Non-compliance with an accounting standard is dealt with under section 143(1) as a book-entry inquiry.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statement 1 correctly distinguishes the exhaustive inquiry list in section 143(1) from the affirmative reporting duties in section 143(3), and statement 2 correctly captures the "only if adverse" Note to section 143(1). Statement 3 is wrong because the 143(3)(i) carve-out expressly excludes one person companies and qualifying private companies, so the duty does not apply to all companies. Statement 4 is wrong because accounting-standard non-compliance is a section 143(3)(e) reporting duty, not a 143(1) book-entry inquiry - limb (b) of 143(1) deals with transactions represented merely by book entries. Hence only 1 and 2 are correct; any option admitting 3 or 4 misstates the provisions.

questions.category: Section 143(3) - Residual Limb (j) and Other Matters
questions.question:
Case Study. While finalising the section 143(3) report of Trichur Ceramics Ltd, an articled clerk proposes how four matters should be placed within the statutory structure of the clause:
Statement A: covering such other matters as may be prescribed.
Statement B: whether the dividend paid during the year complies with section 123.
Statement C: whether the balance sheet and profit and loss account are in agreement with the books and returns.
Statement D: whether the accounting software used to maintain the books had a feature of recording an audit trail which was operated throughout the year.
The clerk's placements are: (i) A falls under the residual limb (j); (ii) both B and D fall under the residual limb (j); (iii) C falls under limb (d); (iv) B is one of the separately enumerated "other matters".
Which of the clerk's placements are correct?
options: Only (i), (ii) and (iii)
Only (ii), (iii) and (iv)
Only (i), (iii) and (iv)
All of (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv)
questions.explanation: Section 143(3) closes its list of specific reporting statements with limb (j), a residual entry requiring the report to deal with such other matters as may be prescribed, so placement (i) is correct, and the agreement of the balance sheet and profit and loss account with the books and returns is limb (d), so placement (iii) is correct. Dividend compliance with section 123 (B) and the audit-trail accounting software (D) are two of the five separately listed "other matters" on which the report must carry the auditor's views - additional to limbs (a)-(j) - which makes placement (iv) correct and placement (ii), which mis-files both as limb (j), wrong. The decisive distinction is between the residual limb (j), the specific limb (d) and the enumerated "other matters"; conflating the "other matters" with the residual limb is the error to avoid.

questions.question:
Bharat Steels Ltd., a listed company, is audited by Vandana & Co., Chartered Accountants, for FY 2024-25; Vandana & Co. is also the cost auditor of the company. On 5 August 2025, during finalisation of the accounts, Vandana obtains information from a supplier that the Finance Director and a warehouse manager of Bharat Steels had, over several months, raised bills for stores never delivered and had the payments routed to a firm owned by a relative of the Finance Director; the amount so computed is ₹4.65 crore. Vandana forms the view that an offence of fraud has been committed in the company by its officers and employees. On 7 August 2025 she writes to the Audit Committee setting out the matter and requesting its reply within 45 days. The Audit Committee's reply reaches her on 22 August 2025. During the same audit she also notices that a cashier has fabricated reimbursement claims totalling ₹18 lakh and that an office clerk has been drawing salary against a fictitious employee, amounting to ₹9 lakh.

Taking the dates in the case as given, by which date and to whom must the ₹4.65 crore fraud matter be reported, and what must accompany the auditor's report?
options: To the Central Government by 7 August 2025, that is, within 2 days of her knowledge of the fraud, the report being confined to the facts as she has recorded them
To the Board of Directors by 6 September 2025, together with the internal audit notes bearing on the ₹4.65 crore matter
To the Central Government by 6 September 2025, together with the reply received from the Audit Committee on 22 August 2025
To the Central Government by 21 September 2025, being 45 days from the date of her letter to the Audit Committee, along with the reply if then received
questions.explanation: Section 143(12) requires an auditor who has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving ₹1 crore or above has been committed in the company by its officers or employees to report the matter to the Board or Audit Committee within 2 days of his knowledge seeking their reply within 45 days, and then to forward his report and the reply of the Board or Audit Committee to the Central Government within 15 days from receipt of such reply. The reply here was received on 22 August 2025, so the 15-day clock runs from that date and the filing with the Central Government falls due by 6 September 2025, carrying both the auditor's report and the Audit Committee's reply. The decisive fact is that the 2-day period governs only the first step addressed to the Board or Audit Committee, which is why a report to the Central Government by 7 August 2025 is wrong. The 45 days is the period sought for the Board's or Committee's reply and not a deadline for the auditor's own filing, so 21 September 2025 is not the operative date; and the ultimate addressee for a fraud of this size is the Central Government, not the Board.

questions.question:
Bharat Steels Ltd., a listed company, is audited by Vandana & Co., Chartered Accountants, for FY 2024-25; Vandana & Co. is also the cost auditor of the company. On 5 August 2025, during finalisation of the accounts, Vandana obtains information from a supplier that the Finance Director and a warehouse manager of Bharat Steels had, over several months, raised bills for stores never delivered and had the payments routed to a firm owned by a relative of the Finance Director; the amount so computed is ₹4.65 crore. Vandana forms the view that an offence of fraud has been committed in the company by its officers and employees. On 7 August 2025 she writes to the Audit Committee setting out the matter and requesting its reply within 45 days. The Audit Committee's reply reaches her on 22 August 2025. During the same audit she also notices that a cashier has fabricated reimbursement claims totalling ₹18 lakh and that an office clerk has been drawing salary against a fictitious employee, amounting to ₹9 lakh.

With reference to the ₹18 lakh and ₹9 lakh matters described in the case, which of the following correctly states Vandana & Co.'s reporting obligation?
options: Both matters go to the Central Government in Form ADT-4, since every fraud noticed in the course of audit is reportable to the Government whatever its amount

Each matter is to be reported by her to the Audit Committee or Board within 2 days of her knowledge of it, specifying the nature of fraud with description, the amount involved and the parties involved, and the company shall disclose the details of such frauds in its Board report
No report is required on either matter, because amounts below ₹1 crore are for the management to settle and fall outside the fraud-reporting requirements
Both matters must be reported to the Audit Committee only after the reply on the ₹4.65 crore matter is received, since they relate to the same period and the same staff
questions.explanation: The reporting to the Central Government under section 143(12) is conditioned on an offence of fraud involving ₹1 crore or above, and the two-stage chain of 2 days, 45 days and 15 days together with Form ADT-4 is attached to that route alone. For a fraud involving less than ₹1 crore the auditor shall report the matter to the Audit Committee or Board within 2 days of his knowledge of the fraud, specifying the nature of fraud with description, the amount involved and the parties involved, and it is the company which shall disclose details about such frauds in the Board report. The decisive facts are the amounts, ₹18 lakh and ₹9 lakh, each below ₹1 crore, so the sub-threshold route applies, the details going to the Audit Committee or Board within 2 days and then into the Board report by the company, which is the course stated as right here. The position that every fraud noticed in the course of audit is reportable to the Government in Form ADT-4 whatever its amount wrongly extends the Central Government route to sub-threshold frauds. The position that amounts below ₹1 crore are for the management to settle and fall outside the fraud-reporting requirements wrongly treats a smaller fraud as not reportable at all. And the position that both matters must go to the Audit Committee only after the reply on the ₹4.65 crore matter is received invents a dependency on the Board's reply that the provision does not create.

questions.question:
Bharat Steels Ltd., a listed company, is audited by Vandana & Co., Chartered Accountants, for FY 2024-25; Vandana & Co. is also the cost auditor of the company. On 5 August 2025, during finalisation of the accounts, Vandana obtains information from a supplier that the Finance Director and a warehouse manager of Bharat Steels had, over several months, raised bills for stores never delivered and had the payments routed to a firm owned by a relative of the Finance Director; the amount so computed is ₹4.65 crore. Vandana forms the view that an offence of fraud has been committed in the company by its officers and employees. On 7 August 2025 she writes to the Audit Committee setting out the matter and requesting its reply within 45 days. The Audit Committee's reply reaches her on 22 August 2025. During the same audit she also notices that a cashier has fabricated reimbursement claims totalling ₹18 lakh and that an office clerk has been drawing salary against a fictitious employee, amounting to ₹9 lakh.

Which of the following correctly sequences the steps Vandana & Co. must complete in respect of the ₹4.65 crore fraud?
options: Report to the Central Government within 2 days of knowledge -> then report to the Board or Audit Committee within 45 days -> then forward the reply to the Central Government within 15 days

Seek the Board's or Audit Committee's reply within 15 days -> report to the Board or Audit Committee within 2 days of the balance sheet date -> file with the Central Government within 45 days of knowledge
Report to the Board or Audit Committee within 45 days of knowledge -> wait for their reply -> forward the report to the Central Government within 2 days of receipt of the reply

Report to the Board or Audit Committee within 2 days of knowledge seeking their reply within 45 days -> on receipt of the reply, forward his report and the reply to the Central Government within 15 days of receipt -> send that report in a sealed cover to the Secretary, MCA in Form ADT-4
Report to the Audit Committee and disclose the matter in the Board report -> thereafter file Form ADT-4 with the Central Government within 45 days of knowledge
questions.explanation: The chain laid down for a fraud of ₹1 crore or above is strictly ordered: the auditor reports to the Board or Audit Committee within 2 days of his knowledge and seeks their reply within 45 days; on receipt of that reply he forwards his report and the reply to the Central Government within 15 days from receipt; and that report is sent in a sealed cover to the Secretary, MCA in Form ADT-4. Each competing chain mis-allocates at least one day-count to the wrong step. The chain that begins with a report to the Central Government within 2 days of knowledge makes the Central Government the first addressee, and the chain that reports to the Board within 45 days of knowledge puts 45 days on the auditor's own report and 2 days on the filing with the Central Government. The chain that reports to the Board within 2 days of the balance sheet date runs the period from the balance sheet date instead of from the auditor's knowledge. The 15 days runs from receipt of the reply and not from the date of the auditor's letter or from the balance sheet date, which is the decisive point. The chain that discloses the matter in the Board report and files Form ADT-4 within 45 days of knowledge also errs by pushing the matter into the Board report, that being the disclosure route prescribed for frauds involving less than ₹1 crore.

questions.question:
Bharat Steels Ltd., a listed company, is audited by Vandana & Co., Chartered Accountants, for FY 2024-25; Vandana & Co. is also the cost auditor of the company. On 5 August 2025, during finalisation of the accounts, Vandana obtains information from a supplier that the Finance Director and a warehouse manager of Bharat Steels had, over several months, raised bills for stores never delivered and had the payments routed to a firm owned by a relative of the Finance Director; the amount so computed is ₹4.65 crore. Vandana forms the view that an offence of fraud has been committed in the company by its officers and employees. On 7 August 2025 she writes to the Audit Committee setting out the matter and requesting its reply within 45 days. The Audit Committee's reply reaches her on 22 August 2025. During the same audit she also notices that a cashier has fabricated reimbursement claims totalling ₹18 lakh and that an office clerk has been drawing salary against a fictitious employee, amounting to ₹9 lakh.

Assume instead that the Audit Committee sends no reply and none reaches Vandana by 21 September 2025. What is her obligation with respect to the Central Government?
options: She must wait until the Audit Committee replies, because the duty to forward the report is expressed only with reference to receipt of a reply
She must forward her report to the Central Government along with a note that she has not received any reply
She must treat the matter as closed, the reporting chain being completed once the Board or Audit Committee is informed within 2 days
She must forward her report to the Central Government but omit all reference to her letter to the Audit Committee, the 45-day reply period still being open
questions.explanation: The provision specifically meets this situation: in case the auditor fails to get any reply, he shall forward his report to the Central Government along with a note that he has not received any reply. The absence of a reply therefore does not suspend or extinguish the duty to report; it merely changes what accompanies the report, the auditor's own report going forward together with his note of non-receipt instead of the Board's or Committee's reply. The decisive fact is that the auditor had already discharged the first step by writing to the Audit Committee within 2 days of his knowledge and seeking a reply within 45 days, and on 21 September 2025 that 45-day period stands expired without a reply. Waiting indefinitely, treating the matter as closed, or filing while suppressing the fact that a reply was sought, each fail to give effect to the express requirement that the report be forwarded with a note of non-receipt.

questions.category: Section 143(12) - Manner and Form of Report
questions.question:
Bharat Steels Ltd., a listed company, is audited by Vandana & Co., Chartered Accountants, for FY 2024-25; Vandana & Co. is also the cost auditor of the company. On 5 August 2025, during finalisation of the accounts, Vandana obtains information from a supplier that the Finance Director and a warehouse manager of Bharat Steels had, over several months, raised bills for stores never delivered and had the payments routed to a firm owned by a relative of the Finance Director; the amount so computed is ₹4.65 crore. Vandana forms the view that an offence of fraud has been committed in the company by its officers and employees. On 7 August 2025 she writes to the Audit Committee setting out the matter and requesting its reply within 45 days. The Audit Committee's reply reaches her on 22 August 2025. During the same audit she also notices that a cashier has fabricated reimbursement claims totalling ₹18 lakh and that an office clerk has been drawing salary against a fictitious employee, amounting to ₹9 lakh.

Which of the following actions should Vandana & Co. take while actually dispatching the report on the ₹4.65 crore fraud?
Actions:
1. Address the report in a sealed cover to the Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs.
2. Send it by Registered Post with Acknowledgement Due, or by Speed Post followed by e-mail.
3. Issue it on the letter-head of the auditor containing the postal address, e-mail address and mobile number, and sign it with the auditor's seal and Membership Number.
4. Present the report in Form ADT-4.
5. Forward only a summary of the fraud to the Central Government and retain the Audit Committee's reply in the audit working papers.
options: 1, 2 and 5 only
2, 3 and 5 only
1, 2, 3 and 4 only
1, 3, 4 and 5 only
3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: The prescribed manner and content are cumulative: the report shall be sent to the Secretary, MCA in a sealed cover by Registered Post with Acknowledgement Due or by Speed Post followed by e-mail; it shall be on the letter-head of the auditor containing his postal address, e-mail address and mobile number and shall be signed by the auditor with his seal and Membership Number; and the report shall be in Form ADT-4. Actions 1 to 4 reproduce exactly these requirements, so the correct combination is 1, 2, 3 and 4. Action 5 fails because the auditor is required to forward his report and the reply of the Board or Audit Committee, so a bare summary with the reply kept in the working papers does not discharge the duty. That Vandana & Co. also holds the cost audit is beside the point here, since the statutory auditor's own duty is unaffected, though the fraud-reporting provisions do extend to a cost auditor as well.

questions.question:
Bharat Steels Ltd., a listed company, is audited by Vandana & Co., Chartered Accountants, for FY 2024-25; Vandana & Co. is also the cost auditor of the company. On 5 August 2025, during finalisation of the accounts, Vandana obtains information from a supplier that the Finance Director and a warehouse manager of Bharat Steels had, over several months, raised bills for stores never delivered and had the payments routed to a firm owned by a relative of the Finance Director; the amount so computed is ₹4.65 crore. Vandana forms the view that an offence of fraud has been committed in the company by its officers and employees. On 7 August 2025 she writes to the Audit Committee setting out the matter and requesting its reply within 45 days. The Audit Committee's reply reaches her on 22 August 2025. During the same audit she also notices that a cashier has fabricated reimbursement claims totalling ₹18 lakh and that an office clerk has been drawing salary against a fictitious employee, amounting to ₹9 lakh.

If Vandana & Co. fails to comply with section 143(12) in respect of the ₹4.65 crore fraud, what is the consequence?
options: A penalty of ₹1 lac, that being the amount prescribed for every company to which the fraud-reporting provisions apply
A penalty of ₹5 lacs, because Bharat Steels Ltd. is a listed company
A penalty of ₹5 lacs only if a court ultimately holds that an offence of fraud was committed, and ₹1 lac in any other case
No monetary penalty, the only consequence being that the audit report has to be modified
questions.explanation: In case of non-compliance with section 143(12) the auditor shall be liable to a penalty of ₹5 lacs in the case of a listed company and ₹1 lac in the case of any other company. Bharat Steels Ltd. is stated to be a listed company, so the higher figure of ₹5 lacs is the exposure of Vandana & Co. if the report to the Central Government is not made, which is the conclusion drawn as right here. The rate is graded by the class of the company audited and not by the quantum of the fraud, so the size of the ₹4.65 crore fraud does not by itself fix the penalty. It is likewise why the reading that ₹1 lac is the amount prescribed for every company to which the fraud-reporting provisions apply does not hold, the figure for a listed company being the higher one. The condition that a penalty of ₹5 lacs arises only if a court ultimately holds that an offence of fraud was committed, and ₹1 lac in any other case, has no basis in the provision. The penalty is a liability of the auditor for non-compliance and is not substituted by any modification of the audit report, so the suggestion that there is no monetary penalty and the only consequence is that the audit report has to be modified is wrong.

questions.question:
Bharat Steels Ltd., a listed company, is audited by Vandana & Co., Chartered Accountants, for FY 2024-25; Vandana & Co. is also the cost auditor of the company. On 5 August 2025, during finalisation of the accounts, Vandana obtains information from a supplier that the Finance Director and a warehouse manager of Bharat Steels had, over several months, raised bills for stores never delivered and had the payments routed to a firm owned by a relative of the Finance Director; the amount so computed is ₹4.65 crore. Vandana forms the view that an offence of fraud has been committed in the company by its officers and employees. On 7 August 2025 she writes to the Audit Committee setting out the matter and requesting its reply within 45 days. The Audit Committee's reply reaches her on 22 August 2025. During the same audit she also notices that a cashier has fabricated reimbursement claims totalling ₹18 lakh and that an office clerk has been drawing salary against a fictitious employee, amounting to ₹9 lakh.

Assume instead that the Audit Committee's reply reaches Vandana only on 5 October 2025, well beyond the 45 days she had sought. On these facts, what is her obligation towards the Central Government?
options: The report should have gone to the Central Government by 6 September 2025, so the later reply is of no consequence and no filing is now required
Because the reply came after the period sought, she must disregard it and forward her report with a note that no reply was received
She must forward her report together with the reply to the Central Government within 15 days from 5 October 2025, the clock running from receipt of the reply
She must return the reply to the Audit Committee and seek a fresh reply within the original 15 days
questions.explanation: The second step is expressed as a duty to forward the auditor's report and the reply of the Board or Audit Committee to the Central Government within 15 days from receipt of such reply, so the trigger for the 15-day period is the fact of receipt and not the expiry of the 45 days sought. A reply that actually arrives on 5 October 2025 has been received, and the filing therefore falls due within 15 days of that date, that is by 20 October 2025, which is the course stated as right here. The view that, the reply having come after the period sought, she must disregard it and forward her report with a note that no reply was received is wrong because the provision's allowance for forwarding the report with a note applies only where the auditor fails to get any reply at all, not where a reply arrives late. The position that the report should already have gone to the Central Government by 6 September 2025 so that the later reply is of no consequence and no filing is now required is wrong because 6 September 2025 is 15 days from the reply of 22 August 2025 on the unmodified facts; the assumption has moved receipt to 5 October 2025, and the 15 days run from the reply actually received. The proposal to return the reply to the Audit Committee and seek a fresh reply within the original 15 days invents a procedure that the provision does not contemplate.

questions.question:
Niroshan Pharma Ltd. is an unlisted public company. Ms. Rhea is its secretarial auditor. On 3 March 2026, in the course of her work, she finds that the Company Secretary and an accounts clerk have falsified statutory records and siphoned ₹1 crore exactly from the company's current account into entities controlled by the Company Secretary. She has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving that amount has been committed in the company by its officers or employees. On 4 March 2026 she reports the matter to the Board, seeking its reply within 45 days, and the Board's reply reaches her on 25 March 2026. She separately discovers that the purchase manager has received personal kickbacks of ₹70 lakh from a vendor.

A director tells Ms. Rhea that section 143(12) cannot apply because the amount is not more than ₹1 crore and because she is only the secretarial auditor. Which of the following states the correct position and timetable?
options: The provision does not reach a secretarial auditor, whose remit is confined to compliance with the Act and the rules made thereunder, so the matter must be handed to the statutory auditor, who alone can file in Form ADT-4

The provision applies only where the fraud exceeds ₹1 crore, so this matter and the ₹70 lakh kickback are for the Audit Committee or Board alone and the company will disclose both in its Board report without any filing outside it

The provision does apply, since the threshold is ₹1 crore or above and the fraud-reporting provisions also apply to a secretarial auditor; her report to the Board was within time and her report together with the Board's reply must now go to the Central Government within 15 days of receipt of that reply
The provision applies, but her report had to reach the Central Government within 2 days of 3 March 2026, the Board's reply being irrelevant to the filing and the 45 days mattering only to the Board
questions.explanation: The Central Government route is triggered where the fraud involves ₹1 crore or above, so a fraud of exactly ₹1 crore is inside the threshold and the reading that the provision applies only where the fraud exceeds ₹1 crore, sending both this matter and the ₹70 lakh kickback to the Audit Committee or Board alone with disclosure only in the Board report, is wrong; the ₹70 lakh kickback stands on a different footing as a fraud below ₹1 crore while the ₹1 crore matter does not. The provisions regarding fraud reporting also apply to a cost auditor and a secretarial auditor, so Ms. Rhea is not merely a witness to the statutory auditor's duty and the matter need not be handed to that auditor as the one who alone can file in Form ADT-4; she holds the duty herself, and the position stating this is right. Her report to the Board within 2 days of her knowledge on 3 March 2026 was met by the report of 4 March 2026, and that report together with the Board's reply must go to the Central Government within 15 days of receipt of the reply, that is by 9 April 2026. The view that her report had to reach the Central Government within 2 days of 3 March 2026, the Board's reply being irrelevant to the filing and the 45 days mattering only to the Board, wrongly applies the 2-day period to the filing with the Central Government and ignores that the filing runs from receipt of the reply.

questions.question:
Niroshan Pharma Ltd. is an unlisted public company. Ms. Rhea is its secretarial auditor. On 3 March 2026, in the course of her work, she finds that the Company Secretary and an accounts clerk have falsified statutory records and siphoned ₹1 crore exactly from the company's current account into entities controlled by the Company Secretary. She has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving that amount has been committed in the company by its officers or employees. On 4 March 2026 she reports the matter to the Board, seeking its reply within 45 days, and the Board's reply reaches her on 25 March 2026. She separately discovers that the purchase manager has received personal kickbacks of ₹70 lakh from a vendor.

Ms. Rhea does not forward any report to the Central Government, taking the view that the Board's reply has disposed of the matter and that in any event she is only a secretarial auditor. What is the consequence?
options: No monetary consequence, since a secretarial auditor is outside the fraud-reporting provisions
A penalty of ₹5 lacs, that being the rate prescribed for every company to which the fraud-reporting provisions apply
A penalty of ₹5 lacs, because failure by a secretarial auditor is always penalised at the listed-company rate
A penalty of ₹1 lac, since Niroshan Pharma Ltd. is not a listed company
questions.explanation: Non-compliance with section 143(12) makes the auditor liable to a penalty of ₹5 lacs in the case of a listed company and ₹1 lac in the case of any other company, and the fraud-reporting provisions apply equally to a secretarial auditor. Niroshan Pharma Ltd. is an unlisted public company, so it is a company other than a listed company and the ₹1 lac figure applies to Ms. Rhea's failure to report. The decisive fact is the listing status of the audited company, not the profession in which the reporting duty arose and not the amount of the fraud, so both suggestions of ₹5 lacs are wrong on the rate. The view that the Board's reply disposed of the matter is also wrong, because it is the auditor who must forward his report and the Board's reply to the Central Government within 15 days of receipt of that reply.

questions.question:
Niroshan Pharma Ltd. is an unlisted public company. Ms. Rhea is its secretarial auditor. On 3 March 2026, in the course of her work, she finds that the Company Secretary and an accounts clerk have falsified statutory records and siphoned ₹1 crore exactly from the company's current account into entities controlled by the Company Secretary. She has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving that amount has been committed in the company by its officers or employees. On 4 March 2026 she reports the matter to the Board, seeking its reply within 45 days, and the Board's reply reaches her on 25 March 2026. She separately discovers that the purchase manager has received personal kickbacks of ₹70 lakh from a vendor.

How should the ₹70 lakh kickback be dealt with under the fraud-reporting requirements?
options: Reported to the Central Government in Form ADT-4 within 15 days of the Board's reply, since it arises from the same period and involves a person employed by the company just as the ₹1 crore matter does

Reported by her to the Audit Committee or Board within 2 days of her knowledge of it, specifying the nature of fraud with description, the amount involved and the parties involved, and the company shall disclose the details in the Board report
Reported to the Audit Committee or Board within 45 days of her knowledge, the 45 days being the period applied to all fraud reporting
Left to management to dispose of, because a kickback received by a single employee below ₹1 crore is a service matter which the auditor merely records in his working papers
questions.explanation: A fraud involving less than ₹1 crore takes the shorter route: the auditor shall report the matter to the Audit Committee or Board within 2 days of his knowledge of the fraud, specifying the nature of fraud with description, the amount involved and the parties involved, and the company shall disclose details about such frauds in the Board report. The ₹70 lakh kickback is below the ₹1 crore threshold, so neither the ADT-4 filing nor the 15-day forwarding to the Central Government is attracted, however closely connected in time with the larger siphoning or however much it involves a person employed by the company; reporting to the Audit Committee or Board within 2 days of her knowledge, with the company then disclosing the details in the Board report, is the right course. The period that binds the auditor is 2 days from his knowledge, so the view that the 45 days is the period applied to all fraud reporting misplaces that 45 days, which belongs to the other route as the period within which the reply is sought. And the suggestion that a kickback below ₹1 crore is a service matter to be left to management and merely recorded in the working papers is wrong because sub-threshold frauds are expressly made reportable, only to a different forum.

questions.question:
Niroshan Pharma Ltd. is an unlisted public company. Ms. Rhea is its secretarial auditor. On 3 March 2026, in the course of her work, she finds that the Company Secretary and an accounts clerk have falsified statutory records and siphoned ₹1 crore exactly from the company's current account into entities controlled by the Company Secretary. She has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving that amount has been committed in the company by its officers or employees. On 4 March 2026 she reports the matter to the Board, seeking its reply within 45 days, and the Board's reply reaches her on 25 March 2026. She separately discovers that the purchase manager has received personal kickbacks of ₹70 lakh from a vendor.

In the above situation, which of the following statements are correct?
1. The fraud-reporting provisions extend to Ms. Rhea as a secretarial auditor.
2. A fraud of exactly ₹1 crore is within the reporting to the Central Government, the threshold being ₹1 crore or above.
3. Her report to the Board was within time, having been made on 4 March 2026, that is within 2 days of her knowledge on 3 March 2026.
4. The report to the Central Government had to be dispatched within 15 days of 4 March 2026.
options: 1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 each reproduce the express requirements: the provisions regarding fraud reporting also apply to a cost auditor and a secretarial auditor; the Central Government route attaches to an offence of fraud involving ₹1 crore or above, so a figure of exactly ₹1 crore is inside it; and the first report must reach the Board or Audit Committee within 2 days of the auditor's knowledge of the fraud. Statement 4 is wrong on the starting point of the 15-day period, which runs from receipt of the Board's or Audit Committee's reply, here 25 March 2026, and not from the date of the auditor's own letter to the Board. The decisive distinction is between the 2-day clock measured from knowledge and the 15-day clock measured from receipt of the reply. Consequently only the combination of statements 1, 2 and 3 is correct.

questions.question:
Meridian Agrotech Ltd. is an unlisted public company. Mr. Kunal is its statutory auditor. On 12 January 2026, while finalising the accounts for FY 2024-25, he obtains bank statements showing that two employees of the purchase department, including the purchase head, received credits of ₹42 lakh during the year from three supplier firms, and that purchase bills of ₹3.8 crore raised by those firms relate to goods never received. He has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving ₹3.8 crore has been committed in the company by its officers or employees. The Board has ordered an internal inquiry which is still in progress, and no court or investigating agency has recorded any conclusion on the matter. Mr. Kunal is completing his audit report.

A partner of Mr. Kunal's firm argues that as the internal inquiry is unfinished and no authority has held that a fraud occurred, section 143(12) is not attracted. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
options: The partner is right, because the auditor's duty arises only once the internal inquiry concludes that an offence of fraud occurred, and until then there is no determinate matter which he may put before the Board or Audit Committee

The partner is wrong: the trigger is that the auditor has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving ₹1 crore or above has been committed in the company by its officers or employees, and neither the conclusion of an internal inquiry nor a finding by a court is a condition of the report

The partner is wrong, because any fraud of which the auditor obtains knowledge in the course of audit compels a report to the Central Government in the same manner, whether or not officers or employees of the company are involved in it
The partner is right on the law, but the auditor must still report to the Central Government within 2 days of the date of his audit report, knowledge being relevant only when the report is signed
questions.explanation: The statute fixes the auditor's own state of satisfaction as the trigger, namely that he has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving ₹1 crore or above has been committed in the company by its officers or employees; it does not condition the duty on the outcome of a departmental or management inquiry or on any adjudication, so the position that the duty arises only once the internal inquiry concludes that an offence of fraud occurred, there being no determinate matter to put before the Board or Audit Committee until then, is wrong. Mr. Kunal has already formed that view on bank evidence of ₹42 lakh in employee credits against ₹3.8 crore of bills for goods not received, so the reporting chain begins on his knowledge and not later, and neither the conclusion of an internal inquiry nor a finding by a court is a condition of the report. The position that any fraud of which the auditor obtains knowledge compels a report to the Central Government in the same manner states the rule too broadly, because the Central Government route is confined to frauds of ₹1 crore or above and to the framing of the trigger, and smaller frauds go to the Audit Committee or Board. The view that the auditor must report within 2 days of the date of his audit report, knowledge being relevant only when the report is signed, confuses the 2-day period, which runs from the auditor's knowledge of the fraud, with the date of the audit report.

questions.question:
Meridian Agrotech Ltd. is an unlisted public company. Mr. Kunal is its statutory auditor. On 12 January 2026, while finalising the accounts for FY 2024-25, he obtains bank statements showing that two employees of the purchase department, including the purchase head, received credits of ₹42 lakh during the year from three supplier firms, and that purchase bills of ₹3.8 crore raised by those firms relate to goods never received. He has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving ₹3.8 crore has been committed in the company by its officers or employees. The Board has ordered an internal inquiry which is still in progress, and no court or investigating agency has recorded any conclusion on the matter. Mr. Kunal is completing his audit report.

Applying the fraud-reporting provisions to the above facts, what is the first step Mr. Kunal must take and by when?
options: Report the matter to the Board or Audit Committee on or before 14 January 2026, seeking their reply within 45 days
File the report directly with the Central Government in Form ADT-4 on or before 14 January 2026
Report the matter to the Board or Audit Committee within 15 days of 12 January 2026, seeking their reply within 2 days
Report the matter to the Board or Audit Committee within 45 days of 12 January 2026, the reply period being the dominant clock
questions.explanation: Even though the ultimate report is addressed to the Central Government, the first step in the chain is that the auditor shall report the matter to the Board or Audit Committee within 2 days of his knowledge of the fraud, seeking their reply within 45 days. Mr. Kunal's knowledge is dated 12 January 2026, so this first report must be made on or before 14 January 2026, and only after the Board's or Committee's reply, or its absence, does the report move to the Central Government. Skipping the Board or Audit Committee is wrong because the Central Government filing is expressed as the auditor forwarding his report along with that reply, within 15 days of receipt. The 15-day and 45-day periods are attached respectively to the forwarding stage and to the reply sought, so neither can be read as the period for the auditor's first report.

questions.question:
Meridian Agrotech Ltd. is an unlisted public company. Mr. Kunal is its statutory auditor. On 12 January 2026, while finalising the accounts for FY 2024-25, he finds that three supplier firms and their owners alone have engineered bogus purchase bills of ₹3.8 crore relating to goods never received, and that no officer and no employee of Meridian Agrotech Ltd. is in any manner implicated in the arrangement. He has reason to believe that an offence of fraud of that amount has been committed by these outside parties, and the loss is well above ₹1 crore. The Board has ordered an internal inquiry which is still in progress.

On the express terms of the fraud-reporting requirement from which this question is framed, what follows?
options: The report to the Central Government remains mandatory, because a fraud on the company involving more than ₹1 crore is reportable in the same manner whoever the perpetrator may be, the pending internal inquiry being beside the point
The auditor must report to the Board or Audit Committee only after the internal inquiry ends, the 2-day period being suspended by the inquiry

The reporting chain to the Central Government is not attracted on its own terms, since the trigger is framed as an offence of fraud involving ₹1 crore or above committed in the company by its officers or employees, and here no officer or employee is implicated
The requirement applies only where such a fraud crosses ₹5 crores, frauds by persons outside the company being on a different footing and needing no report by the auditor
questions.explanation: The requirement as framed has three cumulative elements: reason to believe of an offence of fraud, an amount involving ₹1 crore or above, and its commission in the company by its officers or employees. Here the money element is satisfied and Mr. Kunal's satisfaction is assumed, but the perpetrator element as expressed in the provision is absent, since the arrangement is attributed solely to outsiders, so the specified chain of 2 days, 45 days and 15 days in Form ADT-4 is not attracted on its own terms, which is the conclusion stated as right here. This question is confined to that trigger and decides nothing about any other reporting duty of the auditor elsewhere in the chapter. The position that the report to the Central Government remains mandatory because a fraud on the company involving more than ₹1 crore is reportable whoever the perpetrator may be omits the officer-or-employee condition. The suggestion that the requirement applies only where such a fraud crosses ₹5 crores invents a ₹5 crore figure the provision does not contain. And the view that the auditor must report only after the internal inquiry ends, the 2-day period being suspended by the inquiry, wrongly supposes that an internal inquiry can suspend a period that runs from the auditor's knowledge.

questions.category: Section 143(12) - Manner and Form of Report
questions.question:
Match the following with reference to the duty to report frauds of ₹1 crore or above.
Column I
(a) Addressee of the report forwarded under section 143(12)
(b) First posting of the matter by the auditor to the Board or Audit Committee
(c) Period within which the reply of the Board or Audit Committee is sought
(d) Period for forwarding the report and reply after receipt of the reply
(e) Form in which the report is made
Column II
(1) 2 days from the auditor's knowledge of the fraud
(2) Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs
(3) Form ADT-4
(4) 45 days
(5) 15 days from receipt of the reply
questions.explanation: The manner and timetable prescribed are that the auditor reports to the Board or Audit Committee within 2 days of his knowledge seeking their reply within 45 days, forwards his report and that reply to the Central Government within 15 days from receipt of the reply, and that the report is sent in Form ADT-4 to the Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs in a sealed cover. The correct pairing is therefore (a)-(2), (b)-(1), (c)-(4), (d)-(5), (e)-(3). The common confusions which the distractors exploit are interchanging the 2-day and 45-day periods, treating Form ADT-4 as the addressee's designation, and reading the 15 days as the period for the reply rather than for the forwarding. Note that 45 days is the period within which the auditor seeks the reply, and not a period within which he must himself file anything.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the auditor's duty to report frauds:
1. Where the auditor has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving ₹1 crore or above has been committed in the company by its officers or employees, he shall report the matter to the Central Government in the manner and time prescribed.
2. Where the fraud involves less than ₹1 crore, the auditor shall report the matter to the Audit Committee or Board within 2 days of his knowledge of the fraud, specifying the nature of fraud with description, the amount involved and the parties involved.
3. In the case of frauds involving less than ₹1 crore, the company shall disclose details about such frauds in the Board report.
4. Where the fraud involves less than ₹1 crore, the auditor must nevertheless forward his report to the Central Government if the Board does not reply within 45 days.
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 reproduce the two distinct routes correctly: a fraud of ₹1 crore or above committed in the company by its officers or employees goes forward to the Central Government through the Board or Audit Committee, while a smaller fraud is reported to the Audit Committee or Board within 2 days of the auditor's knowledge specifying the nature of fraud with description, the amount involved and the parties involved, with the company disclosing details of such frauds in the Board report. Statement 4 is wrong because the 45-day reply period and the consequence of no reply belong only to the ₹1 crore or above route; a sub-₹1 crore fraud does not migrate to the Central Government merely because the Board or Audit Committee stays silent. The decisive distinction is the threshold, which fixes the forum and the timetable. Sub-threshold frauds are disposed of by the report to the Audit Committee or Board and the company's Board-report disclosure.

questions.category: Section 143(12) - Manner and Form of Report
questions.question:
Which of the following statements are NOT correct with reference to the report to be sent to the Central Government on a fraud of ₹1 crore or above?
Statement 1. The report may be sent by Registered Post with Acknowledgement Due, or by Speed Post followed by e-mail, in a sealed cover addressed to the Secretary, MCA.
Statement 2. The report may be sent by e-mail alone, provided a copy of the sealed cover is retained in the audit file.
Statement 3. The report may be sent by Speed Post alone without any e-mail, the postal dispatch being complete in itself.
Statement 4. The report must be on the letter-head of the auditor containing his postal address, e-mail address and mobile number, and be signed by him with his seal and Membership Number.
options: 1 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
questions.explanation: The manner prescribed admits exactly two channels, namely Registered Post with Acknowledgement Due, or Speed Post followed by e-mail, the cover being sealed and addressed to the Secretary, MCA. Statement 2 is not correct because e-mail is contemplated only as a follow-up to Speed Post and never as a substitute for physical dispatch, and statement 3 is not correct because the Speed Post route carries the further requirement that it be followed by e-mail, so postal dispatch alone is not complete. Statements 1 and 4 are correct, the latter giving the letter-head content of postal address, e-mail address and mobile number together with signature under seal and Membership Number, and the report being in Form ADT-4. The point tested is the conjunctive character of the Speed Post and e-mail channel, a frequent source of error.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The auditor's report of a company to which CARO 2020 applies must also include a statement on the matters specified in CARO 2020.
Reason (R): CARO 2020 has been issued by the Central Government, after consultation with the National Financial Reporting Authority, in exercise of the power to specify other matters on which the auditor's report shall include a statement.
options: Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
A is not correct but R is correct
questions.explanation: Section 143(11) is the duty to report on any other matter specified by the Central Government, and the source records that the Central Government, after consultation with the National Financial Reporting Authority, has issued CARO 2020, so the auditor's report shall also include a statement on the matters specified in CARO 2020. Reason (R) supplies precisely the reason why the statement must appear in the auditor's report, namely that the Central Government has specified these matters under this enabling power, and so R explains A. A view that CARO is issued by the National Financial Reporting Authority itself, or that it is an industry pronouncement with no statutory linkage, misstates the arrangement recorded here. The inclusion is not an optional addition to the report but the discharge of the duty under section 143(11).

questions.question:
Consider the following statements with reference to section 143(11):
1. It is the National Financial Reporting Authority which has issued CARO 2020.
2. The Central Government has issued CARO 2020 after consultation with the National Financial Reporting Authority.
3. The auditor's report shall also include a statement on the matters specified in CARO 2020.
4. Section 143(11) is the provision from which the auditor's duty to report a fraud of ₹1 crore or above to the Central Government arises.
options: 1 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
questions.explanation: The provision records that the Central Government, after consultation with the National Financial Reporting Authority, has issued CARO (Companies Auditor's Report Order) 2020, and that the auditor's report shall also include a statement on the matters specified in CARO 2020; the Authority is the body consulted and not the issuer, so statement 1 is wrong. Statement 4 wrongly relocates fraud reporting, since the duty to report an offence of fraud involving ₹1 crore or above to the Central Government, and the sub-threshold report to the Audit Committee or Board, arise under section 143(12) and not under section 143(11). The decisive distinction is between the general power to specify other reporting matters, which produces CARO 2020, and the special fraud-reporting duty with its 2-day, 45-day and 15-day chain in Form ADT-4. Only statements 2 and 3 are correct.

questions.question: Mr. Alok is the cost auditor of Kanak Ceramics Ltd.
