In the course of his cost audit he finds that the plant manager and two store keepers have been issuing raw material to an outside processor without any records, the value involved being ₹2.4 crore, and he has reason to believe that an offence of fraud to that extent has been committed in the company by its officers or employees. The statutory auditor, to whom Alok mentions this, tells him that fraud reporting is the statutory auditor's work alone and that Alok need do nothing. Who is correct?
options: The statutory auditor is right, the fraud-reporting duty being addressed only to the statutory auditor appointed under the Act
Mr. Alok need not report, because a cost auditor's work is confined to cost records and cannot yield reason to believe that fraud occurred
Mr. Alok must first obtain the written concurrence of the statutory auditor before any report can be made
Mr. Alok is right, because the provisions regarding fraud reporting also apply to a cost auditor, and equally to a secretarial auditor, so on these facts the duty is his own
questions.explanation: The fraud-reporting provisions are expressly made applicable also to a cost auditor and to a secretarial auditor, so the duty is not reserved to the statutory auditor appointed under the Act; the position that Mr. Alok is right because these provisions also reach a cost auditor and equally a secretarial auditor, so that on these facts the duty is his own, is the right view. On Alok's facts the elements of the trigger are present, namely reason to believe of an offence of fraud involving ₹1 crore or above, here ₹2.4 crore, committed in the company by its officers or employees, being the plant manager and store keepers, so he must set in motion the report to the Board or Audit Committee within 2 days of his knowledge seeking their reply within 45 days. The view that Mr. Alok need not report because a cost auditor's work is confined to cost records and cannot yield reason to believe that fraud occurred confuses the subject-matter of a cost audit with the standard of belief, which turns on whether the auditor has reason to believe and not on the audit from which the information came. There is no provision requiring the written concurrence of the statutory auditor before any report can be made, and the reading that the fraud-reporting duty is addressed only to the statutory auditor simply misstates the extension of the provisions.

questions.question: Ms. Seema audits a company for FY 2024-25. The fraud she eventually reports was committed during the year under audit. On 2 July 2025 a trade magazine published allegations about it. On 18 August 2025, examining corroborating records, she obtains reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving ₹1.6 crore has been committed in the company by its officers or employees. The Board approved the accounts on 30 September 2025. From which of these events does the 2-day period for reporting the matter to the Board or Audit Committee run?
options: The date on which the fraud was committed, the fraud having occurred within FY 2024-25
2 July 2025, the date on which the allegations first appeared in the trade magazine
18 August 2025, the date of her knowledge of the fraud, so that the report to the Board or Audit Committee was due on or before 20 August 2025
30 September 2025, the date the Board approved the accounts, her knowledge being complete only then
questions.explanation: The statutory clock is expressed as 2 days of the auditor's knowledge of the fraud, and the requirement is triggered when he has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving ₹1 crore or above has been committed in the company by its officers or employees. Ms. Seema acquired that reason to believe on 18 August 2025, so the first report was due on or before 20 August 2025. The date of commission of the fraud and the date of press allegations are extrinsic to her knowledge, and the approval of the accounts is not the reference point either, the duty being tied to the auditor's own knowledge and not to the company's approval timetable. The decisive fact is the day her reason to believe crystallised, which also fixes the later 15-day computation once the Board's or Audit Committee's reply arrives.

questions.category: Section 143(12) - Manner and Form of Report
questions.question:
The report forwarded to the Central Government under the duty to report frauds must contain or satisfy which of the following?
1. The postal address of the auditor.
2. The e-mail address of the auditor.
3. The mobile number of the auditor.
4. The signature of the auditor along with his seal and Membership Number.
5. The company's written acknowledgement of the fraud in its Board report.
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1, 2, 3 and 4 only
2, 3, 4 and 5 only
questions.explanation: The report shall be on the letter-head of the auditor containing his postal address, e-mail address and mobile number, shall be signed by the auditor with his seal and Membership Number, and shall be in Form ADT-4, sent in a sealed cover to the Secretary, MCA by Registered Post with Acknowledgement Due or by Speed Post followed by e-mail. Items 1 to 4 are therefore requirements of the report itself, while item 5 is not: disclosure of fraud details in the Board report is the consequence prescribed for frauds involving less than ₹1 crore and is the company's act, not a condition or content of the auditor's report to the Central Government. The option that omits the mobile number understates the letter-head content, and the option that reads every listed item as mandatory confuses the two routes. The auditor's Membership Number and seal are identification requirements of the filing and not part of the company's disclosure.

questions.question: In two separate audits the same firm fails to forward the report on a fraud of ₹2 crore, committed in each company by its officers or employees, to the Central Government. In the first engagement the company is a listed entity; in the second the company is a private company which is a subsidiary of a public company and is not listed. The firm contends that a single penalty must apply to both because the amount of fraud and its own conduct are identical. Which is the correct evaluation?
options: The contention is correct, the penalty being graded by the amount of the fraud and not by the class of the company
The penalty is ₹5 lacs for the listed company and ₹1 lac for the company which is not a listed company, so the amount of the fraud does not govern the rate
Both attract ₹5 lacs, a private company which is a subsidiary of a public company being treated as a listed company for this purpose
The penalty is ₹1 lac for the listed company and ₹5 lacs for the company which is not a listed company, the listed rate being the lower one
questions.explanation: Non-compliance with section 143(12) exposes the auditor to a penalty of ₹5 lacs in the case of a listed company and ₹1 lac in the case of any other company, so the rate is graded by the listing status of the audited company. The first engagement attracts ₹5 lacs and the second ₹1 lac, and the identity of the fraud amount across the two cases is beside the point, which is why the firm's contention fails. Reading a private company that is a subsidiary of a public company as a listed company for this purpose imports a classification the provision does not use, and reversing the two figures misstates which class carries the higher exposure. The decisive fact in each case is whether the company audited is a listed company.

questions.question: An auditor has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving ₹5.4 crore has been committed in the company by its officers or employees. He reports the matter to the Board on the day after his knowledge, seeking its reply within 45 days, and the Board replies after 30 days. What must he send to the Central Government, and when?
options: Only his own report, since the Board's reply remains the company's internal record
Only the Board's reply, his own report having already been given to the Board
His report together with the reply of the Board, within 15 days from receipt of that reply
His report together with the reply of the Board, but only after the financial statements are signed
questions.explanation: The second step of the chain requires the auditor, on receipt of the reply, to forward his report and the reply of the Board or Audit Committee to the Central Government within 15 days from receipt of such reply. Both documents travel together, so sending only his own report or only the Board's reply is incomplete, and the timing is anchored to receipt of the reply rather than to the auditor's first report or to the date of his knowledge. Nothing in the requirement defers the filing to the signing of the financial statements, and the Board's reply having arrived after 30 days does not shorten or extend the 15 days. The report must be in Form ADT-4 on the auditor's letter-head with his postal address, e-mail address and mobile number, signed with his seal and Membership Number, and sent in a sealed cover to the Secretary, MCA by Registered Post with Acknowledgement Due or by Speed Post followed by e-mail.

questions.question:
M/s Heera & Co. audit four companies for FY 2024-25 and in each case obtains reason to believe that an offence of fraud has been committed in the company by its officers or employees, as follows:
(i) Arjun Metals Ltd., a listed company - ₹1.05 crore by the works manager and an accounts clerk.
(ii) Padma Textiles Ltd., an unlisted public company - ₹95 lakh by the head of sales.
(iii) Chirag Developers (P) Ltd., an unlisted company - ₹1 crore exactly by two directors and an employee.
(iv) Veda Chemicals Ltd., a listed company - ₹60 lakh by an accounts assistant.
For which companies must the matter be carried to the Central Government through the two-stage process, and for which does the duty rest with a report to the Audit Committee or Board?
options: (i), (ii) and (iii) to the Central Government, since each of these amounts is material for the company concerned; (iv) to the Audit Committee or Board only
All four to the Central Government, because every fraud of which the auditor obtains reason to believe in the course of audit must reach the Government in Form ADT-4
(i) and (iii) to the Audit Committee or Board only, the Board being competent to deal with matters arising in its own company; (ii) and (iv) to the Central Government
(i) and (iii) to the Central Government through the two-stage process; (ii) and (iv) to the Audit Committee or Board, with the company disclosing details of such frauds in the Board report
questions.explanation: The threshold is a fraud involving ₹1 crore or above, so (i) at ₹1.05 crore and (iii) at exactly ₹1 crore fall on the Central Government side of the line, while (ii) at ₹95 lakh and (iv) at ₹60 lakh fall on the Audit Committee or Board side, the auditor specifying the nature of fraud with description, the amount involved and the parties involved and the company disclosing the details in its Board report. Listing is not the criterion for choosing the route, which is why Veda Chemicals Ltd. being listed does not push a ₹60 lakh fraud into Form ADT-4, nor does Chirag Developers being an unlisted private company keep a ₹1 crore fraud out. The decisive facts are the amounts, with (iii) testing that the threshold is inclusive of ₹1 crore. For (i) and (iii) the full two-stage chain applies, namely report to the Board or Audit Committee within 2 days of knowledge seeking a reply within 45 days, then forwarding the report and reply to the Central Government within 15 days of receipt of the reply.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): An auditor who has reported a fraud of ₹1 crore or above to the Audit Committee within 2 days of his knowledge cannot treat his duty as discharged merely because the Audit Committee has internally taken action.
Reason (R): On receipt of the reply of the Board or Audit Committee, the auditor shall forward his report and that reply to the Central Government within 15 days from receipt of such reply, and where he fails to get any reply he shall forward his report along with a note that he has not received any reply.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
questions.explanation: The reporting to the Board or Audit Committee is only the first step, and the auditor's duty is completed by forwarding his report and that body's reply to the Central Government within 15 days from receipt of the reply, with the fallback of forwarding the report along with a note of non-receipt where no reply comes. Reason (R) states exactly this and therefore explains why the Committee's own corrective action cannot close the auditor's obligation, since the addressee of the final report is the Central Government and not the company. The decisive point is that the duty to report is a duty to report to the Central Government, the Board stage being procedural. It is not the case that R fails to explain A, nor that A is correct while R is not, nor that A is not correct while R is correct. Both statements being correct and R being the true reason for A, the view that both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A is the right one.

questions.question: An auditor dealing with frauds and other reporting matters for FY 2024-25 does three things: (1) he files a report in Form ADT-4 with the Central Government on a ₹1.30 crore fraud committed by the company's cashier and a store keeper, after reporting it to the Board within 2 days of his knowledge; (2) he includes in his audit report the statement on the matters specified in CARO 2020; (3) he reports a ₹40 lakh fraud to the Audit Committee within 2 days of his knowledge, after which the company discloses the details in its Board report. A director objects that everything the auditor knows about fraud should have been placed in the auditor's report itself, and nothing sent outside it. Evaluate.
options: The director is right, since all matters arising in the course of audit, including every fraud of which the auditor has knowledge, must be placed in the auditor's report and dealt with there, and nothing is to be sent outside it

The auditor's handling is consistent with the reporting structure, the ₹1 crore and above fraud going to the Central Government in Form ADT-4 through the Board stage, the sub-₹1 crore fraud going to the Audit Committee or Board within 2 days with the company disclosing it in the Board report, and the CARO 2020 statement forming part of the auditor's report under section 143(11)

The auditor should have reported the ₹40 lakh matter to the Central Government in Form ADT-4 and left the ₹1.30 crore matter with the Board alone, the smaller fraud being the one that requires the Government's attention

The auditor's report cannot carry a statement on CARO 2020, which must instead be filed as a separate letter with the Registrar of Companies, so that part of his handling is wrong whatever the view on the frauds
questions.explanation: Three different duties operate here and each is discharged in its own manner: section 143(11) requires the auditor's report to include a statement on the matters specified in CARO 2020, issued by the Central Government after consultation with the National Financial Reporting Authority; section 143(12) requires a fraud of ₹1 crore or above committed in the company by its officers or employees to reach the Central Government in Form ADT-4 through the Board or Audit Committee stage; and a fraud below ₹1 crore is reported to the Audit Committee or Board within 2 days of knowledge, the company then disclosing details of such frauds in the Board report. The handling that keeps these three channels apart is therefore consistent with the reporting structure. The director's objection, that every fraud of which the auditor has knowledge must be placed in the auditor's report with nothing sent outside it, collapses these three channels into one and would destroy the statutory scheme, in which the fraud reports are addressed outside the audit report while CARO matters are addressed within it. The reading that the ₹40 lakh matter should have gone to the Central Government in Form ADT-4 and the ₹1.30 crore matter left with the Board alone reverses the thresholds. The view that the auditor's report cannot carry a statement on CARO 2020, which must instead be filed as a separate letter with the Registrar of Companies, wrongly removes CARO reporting from the auditor's report. The decisive fact is the amount of each fraud, which selects the route, alongside the separate duty to report specified matters in the report itself.

questions.question: Ms. Ila has reason to believe that a fraud of ₹45 lakh has been committed in the company by an employee. She proposes to wait for the outcome of management's inquiry and to report to the Audit Committee only if the amount is finally shown to exceed ₹1 crore, noting in her working papers that the 45-day reply period gives her time. Which of the following is the most appropriate criticism of her proposal?
options: She must report to the Audit Committee or Board within 2 days of her knowledge irrespective of the outcome of management's inquiry, and the sub-₹1 crore route contains no 45-day reply stage at all
She must report to the Central Government within 2 days of her knowledge, the 2-day rule applying to every fraud noticed in audit
Her proposal is correct, the reporting duty arising only once the amount of the fraud is finally quantified above ₹1 crore
She must seek the Audit Committee's reply within 45 days even for a sub-₹1 crore fraud, that stage applying to all fraud reporting
questions.explanation: Where the fraud involves less than ₹1 crore the auditor shall report the matter to the Audit Committee or Board within 2 days of his knowledge of the fraud, specifying the nature of fraud with description, the amount involved and the parties involved, and the company shall disclose details of such frauds in the Board report. Ms. Ila's amount of ₹45 lakh keeps the matter on this route, so a period that runs from her knowledge cannot be deferred pending management's inquiry, and the 45-day reply period belongs only to the ₹1 crore or above chain that passes to the Central Government. The view that she must report to the Central Government within 2 days wrongly sends a sub-threshold fraud to the Central Government; the view that the duty arises only once the amount is finally quantified above ₹1 crore makes it depend on a completed quantification when her reason to believe already exists; and the view that she must seek the Audit Committee’s reply within 45 days imports the reply stage into a route that does not have it. The decisive facts are the amount and the date of her knowledge.

questions.question:
CASE: Priya Synthetics Private Limited is a private company; it is neither a subsidiary of, nor a holding company of, any public company; it is neither a one person company nor a small company. As on 31 March 2025 its paid-up share capital was ₹55 lakh and its reserves and surplus were ₹40 lakh. It had working-capital and term borrowings from banks; these stood at ₹90 lakh on 31 March 2025, but to bridge a temporary liquidity gap the aggregate bank borrowings had touched ₹1.05 crore on 15 August 2024 before falling back. Revenue for FY 2024-25 as per the financial statements was ₹8 crore, which includes ₹0.5 crore from a discontinued operation. During the year the company revalued one class of plant and machinery on the basis of a registered valuer's report, the aggregate change being 12% of the net carrying value of that class.
Is CARO 2020 applicable to Priya Synthetics, and what is the decisive reason?
options: CARO does not apply; capital plus reserves (₹95 lakh) and revenue (₹8 crore) are both within the exemption limits.
CARO applies; the private-company exemption fails because aggregate bank borrowings exceeded ₹1 crore at a point during the year.
CARO does not apply; it is a private company and the revaluation is only a clause (i) matter, not an applicability matter.
CARO applies; every private company is covered irrespective of its size.
questions.explanation: A private company enjoys the CARO exemption only if all three monetary conditions are satisfied together. Paid-up capital plus reserves and surplus are measured as on the balance sheet date (₹55 lakh + ₹40 lakh = ₹95 lakh, within ₹1 crore), and revenue is measured during the year as per the financial statements including discontinued operations (₹8 crore, within ₹10 crore), so those two conditions pass. The borrowings condition, however, is measured at any time during the year, and the ₹1.05 crore drawn on 15 August 2024 exceeds ₹1 crore, so this condition fails, and because the three conditions read conjunctively the exemption is lost and CARO applies. The conclusion that capital plus reserves (₹95 lakh) and revenue (₹8 crore) being both within the exemption limits means CARO does not apply ignores the 'at any time during the year' timing for borrowings. The conclusion that it is a private company and the revaluation is only a clause (i) matter, not an applicability matter, confuses a clause-level report with the threshold test for applicability. The conclusion that every private company is covered irrespective of its size misstates the rule, since a qualifying private company can be exempt.

questions.question: A private company (not a subsidiary or holding of a public company) has, for FY 2024-25, paid-up capital ₹55 lakh and reserves ₹40 lakh as on 31 March 2025, revenue ₹8 crore as per the financial statements (including ₹0.5 crore from a discontinued operation), and bank borrowings that never exceeded ₹1 crore at any time during the year. On these facts CARO does not apply. Which additional fact, standing alone, would make CARO applicable?
options: It became a subsidiary of a public company on 1 April 2024.
The company reported a loss rather than a profit for the year.
Its revenue figure included the ₹0.5 crore from the discontinued operation.
Its reserves and surplus were ₹40 lakh rather than ₹45 lakh.
questions.explanation: With borrowings within ₹1 crore, capital plus reserves of ₹95 lakh within ₹1 crore, and revenue of ₹8 crore within ₹10 crore, all three conjunctive conditions are met, so the only remaining bar is the status requirement. The size exemption is available solely to a private company that is not a subsidiary of, or a holding company of, a public company; becoming a subsidiary of a public company destroys the exemption regardless of size. A loss for the year is not one of the exemption conditions, so it changes nothing. Including discontinued-operation revenue is already required and ₹10 crore is not exceeded, so that is neutral. Lower reserves only move the first condition further inside the limit. The decisive fact is the subsidiary-of-a-public-company relationship.

questions.question:
Consider the three monetary conditions for the private-company exemption under CARO 2020:
1. Paid-up capital plus reserves and surplus are measured as on the balance sheet date.
2. Borrowings from a bank or financial institution are measured as on the balance sheet date only.
3. Revenue is measured during the year as per the financial statements and includes revenue from discontinued operations.
4. The three conditions are applied disjunctively, so satisfying any one of them is enough for the exemption.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: the capital-plus-reserves test is measured as on the balance sheet date. Statement 3 is correct: the revenue test is measured during the year as per the financial statements and expressly includes revenue from discontinued operations. Statement 2 is incorrect because the borrowings test is measured at any time during the year, not merely at year end. Statement 4 is incorrect because the three conditions are read conjunctively: the exemption requires all of them to be satisfied simultaneously, not just one. The decisive distinctions are the differing measurement bases of each condition and the conjunctive (not disjunctive) reading.

questions.question:
CASE: Four entities approach their auditors for FY 2024-25. (P) A wholly-owned subsidiary of a listed public company with paid-up capital ₹10 lakh, reserves ₹5 lakh, no borrowings and revenue ₹2 crore. (Q) A company licensed to operate under section 8 of the Companies Act (a non-profit) with revenue ₹40 crore. (R) A foreign company within the meaning of the Companies Act having a place of business in India. (S) A one person company with revenue ₹60 crore.
Statements:
1. P is exempt from CARO because its financial size is within the private-company limits.
2. Q is exempt from CARO.
3. R is covered by CARO.
4. S is covered by CARO.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: P cannot claim the size exemption: that exemption is available only to a private company that is not a subsidiary of, or holding of, a public company, so being a wholly-owned subsidiary of a listed public company defeats it despite tiny figures; statement 1 is wrong. Q, a section 8 (non-profit) company, is on the exempt list without any size condition, so statement 2 is correct. R, a foreign company, is expressly covered because CARO applies to every company including a foreign company and no exemption reaches it, so statement 3 is correct. S, a one person company, is exempt regardless of revenue, so statement 4 is wrong. The decisive points are the subsidiary disqualifier and the fact that the section 8 and OPC exemptions carry no size condition.

questions.question:
Match each entity in Column I with whether CARO 2020 is Exempt or Covered for it in Column II.
Column I:
A. Banking company
B. Insurance company
C. Private company (not a subsidiary or holding of a public company) with paid-up capital plus reserves ₹90 lakh, bank borrowings ₹80 lakh at all times during the year, and revenue ₹5 crore
D. Public company with revenue ₹3 crore
options: A-Exempt, B-Covered, C-Exempt, D-Covered
A-Covered, B-Exempt, C-Covered, D-Exempt
A-Exempt, B-Exempt, C-Exempt, D-Covered
A-Exempt, B-Exempt, C-Covered, D-Covered
questions.explanation: Banking and insurance companies appear directly on the CARO exempt list, so A and B are exempt. C is a private company that is not a subsidiary or holding of a public company and satisfies all three monetary conditions together (₹90 lakh capital plus reserves within ₹1 crore, borrowings never above ₹1 crore, and ₹5 crore revenue within ₹10 crore), so it is exempt. D is a public company: the size exemption is available only to a qualifying private company, so a public company is covered irrespective of how small its revenue is. The decisive rule is that the monetary exemption cannot be used by a public company.

questions.question:
CASE: Vayu Logistics Private Limited is a subsidiary of a public company. For FY 2024-25 its paid-up capital is ₹20 lakh, reserves ₹10 lakh, borrowings nil and revenue ₹4 crore. During the year it revalued its intangible assets (one class of computer software) without any registered valuer's valuation; the aggregate change was 6% of the net carrying value of that class.
Assuming the auditor must complete CARO reporting, which of the following is correct?
options: CARO does not apply; all the monetary size limits are within the exemption.
CARO applies; the auditor must specify the amount of change because a revaluation was carried out during the year.
CARO applies but nothing is reportable under clause (i) because 6% is below the 10% threshold.
CARO applies; the auditor must report that the revaluation was not based on a registered valuer's valuation, though the 6% change need not be quantified.
questions.explanation: Because Vayu is a subsidiary of a public company, the private-company size exemption is unavailable no matter how small its figures are, so CARO applies. Clause (i)(d) has two independent limbs: the auditor must state whether the revaluation was based on a registered valuer's valuation, and must specify the amount of change only if the aggregate change is 10% or more of the net carrying value of each class. Here the revaluation was done without a registered valuer, so that negative fact must be reported, while the 6% change falls below the 10% quantification threshold and need not be spelt out, which is the reporting result stated as right here. The conclusion that CARO does not apply because all the monetary size limits are within the exemption overlooks the subsidiary disqualifier. The conclusion that nothing is reportable under clause (i) because 6% is below the 10% threshold wrongly reads the 10% test as switching off the whole clause. The conclusion that the auditor must specify the amount of change because a revaluation was carried out during the year wrongly quantifies a sub-threshold change.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): CARO 2020 applies to a foreign company.
Reason (R): CARO applies to every company, and none of the enumerated exemptions (banking, insurance, section 8, one person company, small company, or the qualifying private company) reaches a foreign company.
In the light of the above, choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: The general rule is that CARO applies to every company including a foreign company, so the assertion is true. The listed exemptions are exhaustive, and a foreign company does not fit any of them: it is not a banking or insurance company, not a section 8 company, not a one person or small company, and the private-company size exemption requires it to be a private company, which a foreign company is not. The reason is therefore true and it correctly explains why the foreign company is caught, because the assertion rests precisely on the combination of the wide coverage rule and the closed exemption list. No separate ground is needed to explain A.

questions.question:
CASE: An auditor is appointed by a private company for FY 2024-25 and must decide whether CARO applies before drafting the report. The management claims the exemption. Which of the following steps should the auditor take?
1. Verify paid-up capital plus reserves and surplus as on the balance sheet date against ₹1 crore.
2. Verify whether bank or financial-institution borrowings exceeded ₹1 crore at any point during the year, not merely at year end.
3. Confirm that revenue as per the financial statements does not exceed ₹10 crore, including revenue from discontinued operations.
4. Ignore the holding/subsidiary relationship with any public company if the size limits are met, since size alone governs the exemption.
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Steps 1, 2 and 3 correctly capture the three monetary conditions together with their respective measurement bases: capital plus reserves at the balance sheet date, borrowings at any time during the year, and revenue as per the financial statements including discontinued operations. Step 4 is wrong because the size exemption is available only to a private company that is not a subsidiary of, or a holding company of, a public company; the relationship must always be checked even when every monetary limit is satisfied. The decisive point is that satisfying the size conditions is necessary but not sufficient — the status condition must also hold. Hence only actions 1, 2 and 3 are correct.

questions.question:
CASE: A private company, not a subsidiary or holding of a public company and neither a one person company nor a small company, has paid-up capital ₹30 lakh, reserves ₹20 lakh and bank borrowings ₹50 lakh throughout FY 2024-25, all within limits. Its revenue from continuing operations is ₹9.4 crore and from a discontinued operation is ₹0.8 crore.
What is the auditor's most appropriate conclusion on CARO applicability?
options: CARO does not apply; continuing-operations revenue of ₹9.4 crore is within the ₹10 crore limit.
CARO does not apply; the ₹10 crore limit refers to turnover excluding any discontinued operation.
CARO applies; total revenue of ₹10.2 crore (including the discontinued operation) exceeds the ₹10 crore limit.
CARO applies; any private company with revenue above ₹9 crore is covered.
questions.explanation: The revenue condition is measured as per the financial statements and expressly includes revenue from discontinued operations. Adding ₹9.4 crore of continuing revenue to ₹0.8 crore of discontinued revenue gives ₹10.2 crore, which exceeds the ₹10 crore ceiling, so this single condition fails even though capital plus reserves and borrowings are within limits, and because the three conditions are conjunctive the exemption is lost and CARO applies, which is the conclusion stated as right here. The view that continuing-operations revenue of ₹9.4 crore is within the ₹10 crore limit, and the view that the ₹10 crore limit refers to turnover excluding any discontinued operation, both wrongly exclude discontinued-operation revenue from the ₹10 crore test. The view that any private company with revenue above ₹9 crore is covered invents a non-existent ₹9 crore trigger. The decisive fact is the inclusion of discontinued-operation revenue in the ₹10 crore limit.

questions.question:
Statements about CARO 2020 exemptions:
1. An insurance company is exempt from CARO irrespective of its size.
2. A company licensed to operate under section 8 of the Companies Act (a non-profit) is exempt from CARO irrespective of its size.
3. A one person company is exempt from CARO irrespective of its size.
4. A public company is exempt from CARO if its revenue is small enough.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1 and 2 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
questions.explanation: The exempt list includes banking companies, insurance companies, section 8 (non-profit) companies, one person companies and small companies, and each of these is exempt without any size condition, so statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is wrong because the only size-based exemption is available to a qualifying private company; a public company cannot rely on any revenue, capital or borrowing limit to escape CARO and is covered regardless of how small it is. The decisive distinction is between the unconditional exemptions (which list specific company types) and the conditional exemption that belongs only to a private company meeting all three monetary tests.

questions.question:
CASE: In auditing Mountain View Estates Limited (to which CARO applies), the auditor notes:
(1) the company maintains proper records showing full particulars including quantitative details and situation of its PPE, and full particulars of its intangible assets;
(2) management physically verified PPE twice during the year at reasonable intervals, but a material discrepancy in one asset noticed on verification was not properly dealt with in the books;
(3) the title deed of a freehold land disclosed in the financial statements is held in the name of a director, not the company;
(4) no proceeding has been initiated or is pending against the company under the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988.
Statements:
1. Clause (i)(a) requires an adverse remark because the records are complete.
2. Clause (i)(b) requires the auditor to report that a material discrepancy noticed on verification was not properly dealt with in the books.
3. Clause (i)(c) requires details of the land whose title deed is held in the director's name in the prescribed format.
4. Clause (i)(e) requires a statement on whether any benami proceeding is initiated or pending and, if so, whether details are disclosed in the financial statements.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is wrong because clause (i)(a) is satisfied when proper records with quantitative details and situation (for PPE) and full particulars (for intangibles) exist; the facts say the records are adequate, so no adverse remark arises. Statement 2 is correct because clause (i)(b) requires the auditor to report whether material discrepancies noticed on verification were properly dealt with in the books, and here one was not. Statement 3 is correct because clause (i)(c) requires disclosure, in the fixed format, of immovable property whose title deed is not held in the company's name — a director holding it is one of the enumerated categories. Statement 4 correctly reproduces clause (i)(e). The decisive point is separating the satisfied limb (records) from the breached limbs (dealing with discrepancies, title deeds).

questions.question:
Match each CARO clause (i) sub-clause in Column I with the content the auditor must report on it in Column II.
Column I:
(a) Clause (i)(a)
(b) Clause (i)(c)
(c) Clause (i)(d)
(d) Clause (i)(e)
Column II:
p. Gross carrying value, name of holder (promoter/director/relative/employee), period held and reason for the title deed not being in the company's name
q. Whether proper records showing full particulars, including quantitative details and situation of PPE, and full particulars of intangible assets, are maintained
r. Whether a benami proceeding is initiated or pending and whether the company disclosed the details in the financial statements
s. Whether a revaluation is based on a registered valuer's valuation and the amount of change if it is 10% or more of net carrying value of each class
options: a-q, b-p, c-s, d-r
a-q, b-s, c-p, d-r
a-p, b-q, c-s, d-r
a-q, b-p, c-r, d-s
questions.explanation: Clause (i)(a) is the records sub-clause, so it pairs with q (proper records with quantitative details and situation for PPE, full particulars for intangibles). Clause (i)(c) is the title-deed sub-clause, and its prescribed format — gross carrying value, holder category, period held and reason — matches p. Clause (i)(d) is the revaluation sub-clause, matching s (registered valuer and the 10% of net carrying value per class quantification). Clause (i)(e) is the benami sub-clause, matching r. The decisive distinctions are the gross carrying value in the title-deed format versus the net carrying value in the revaluation test, and the benami link to the 1988 Act.

questions.question: Under CARO clause (i)(c), where a title deed of an immovable property disclosed in the financial statements is not held in the name of the company, which option correctly lists the columns of details that must be furnished?
options: Description of property; net book value; held by whom; date of acquisition.
Description of property; fair value; promoter's name; encumbrance details.
Description of property; gross carrying value; held in name of (promoter, director, their relative or employee); period held (indicate range); reason for not being held in the company's name.
Class of asset; gross carrying value; registered valuer's name; period of revaluation.
questions.explanation: The clause (i)(c) format prescribes exactly five columns: description of property, gross carrying value, held in name of (whether promoter, director or their relative or employee), period held (indicated as a range), and reason for not being held in the name of the company. The set of columns that reads description of property, net book value, held by whom and date of acquisition does not follow the format, since net book value and date of acquisition are not the prescribed columns. The set that uses description of property, fair value, the promoter's name and encumbrance details relies on items which belong to no CARO format here. The set that lists class of asset, gross carrying value, the registered valuer's name and period of revaluation borrows the registered-valuer idea from clause (i)(d), which is not part of the title-deed format. The decisive point is that the title-deed format uses gross carrying value, whereas the revaluation test in clause (i)(d) uses net carrying value, and it is the format giving description of property, gross carrying value, held in name of promoter, director, their relative or employee, period held as a range, and reason for not being held in the company's name that is right.

questions.question:
CASE: Aarav Textiles Limited (to which CARO applies) revalued two classes of PPE during FY 2024-25. For class A (plant), the revaluation was done on a registered valuer's report and the aggregate change was 11% of that class's net carrying value. For class B (furniture), the revaluation was done on management's own estimate with no registered valuer and the aggregate change was 4% of that class's net carrying value.
Statements:
1. For class A, the auditor must report that the revaluation was based on a registered valuer's valuation and must specify the amount of change because 11% is at least 10%.
2. For class B, the auditor must report that the revaluation was not based on a registered valuer's valuation.
3. For class B, the auditor must specify the amount of change because a revaluation was carried out during the year.
4. The 10% test is applied by combining the changes of class A and class B together.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
1 and 2 only
questions.explanation: Clause (i)(d) contains two independent limbs. The first limb asks, for every revaluation done during the year, whether it was based on a registered valuer's valuation — so the auditor reports 'yes' for class A and must positively report the absence of a registered valuer for class B, making statements 1 and 2 correct. The second limb requires quantification of the change only where the aggregate change is 10% or more of the net carrying value of each class; class A's 11% qualifies but class B's 4% does not, so statement 3 is wrong. Statement 4 is wrong because the threshold is applied to each class separately, not to a combined total of all classes. The decisive points are the per-class measurement and the two-limb structure of the clause.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Even where management physically verifies PPE at reasonable intervals, the auditor must still make a CARO clause (i)(b) remark if a material discrepancy noticed on verification is not properly dealt with in the books.
Reason (R): Clause (i)(b) is a composite requirement covering both whether PPE were physically verified at reasonable intervals and whether material discrepancies noticed were properly dealt with in the books.
In the light of the above, choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Clause (i)(b) requires the auditor to report two distinct things: that PPE were physically verified at reasonable intervals, and that any material discrepancies noticed on such verification were properly dealt with in the books. Performing the verification satisfies only the first limb; if a material discrepancy is left unadjusted in the books, the second limb fails and a remark is required. The assertion is therefore true, the reason accurately states the two limbs of the clause, and the reason explains the assertion because it identifies the second limb that triggers reporting. Decisive point: reasonable-interval verification does not, by itself, discharge clause (i)(b).

questions.question:
Statements comparing CARO clause (i)(b) (PPE physical verification) with clause (ii)(a) (inventory physical verification):
1. Clause (i)(b) uses the expression 'material discrepancies' with no fixed percentage threshold.
2. Clause (ii)(a) fixes the discrepancy reporting trigger at 10% or more in aggregate for each class of inventory.
3. Clause (ii)(a) expressly expects physical verification of inventory at least once in a year, whereas clause (i)(b) contains no such stated minimum frequency.
4. Both clauses require quantification of discrepancies at the same '10% in aggregate' level.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: clause (i)(b) refers to 'material discrepancies' and deliberately sets no numeric percentage. Statement 2 is correct: clause (ii)(a) triggers reporting only for discrepancies of 10% or more in aggregate for each class of inventory. Statement 3 is correct: clause (ii)(a) carries the parenthetical 'at least once in a year' gloss while clause (i)(b) speaks only of 'reasonable intervals' with no stated minimum. Statement 4 is wrong because clause (i)(b) has no 10% figure at all; only the inventory clause uses the 10% test. The decisive drafting differences are the presence of a numeric threshold and a minimum frequency in clause (ii)(a) but not in clause (i)(b).

questions.question:
CASE: Indus Holdings Limited (to which CARO applies) faces a proceeding initiated under the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 in respect of a property it holds, and the company has made no disclosure of this proceeding in its financial statements.
Under CARO clause (i)(e), what is the auditor's most appropriate reporting?
options: State only whether a proceeding is initiated or pending, without reference to the company's disclosure.
Report nothing, because the proceeding is pending and its outcome is unknown.
Report that a proceeding is initiated or pending and that the company has not appropriately disclosed the details in its financial statements.
Report the matter instead under clause (ix) on loan repayment.
questions.explanation: Clause (i)(e) asks two linked questions: whether any proceeding has been initiated or is pending against the company for holding benami property under the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988, and, if so, whether the company has appropriately disclosed the details in its financial statements. Both limbs are engaged on these facts - a proceeding exists and no disclosure has been made - so the auditor must state both, which is the report described as right here. The view that one states only whether a proceeding is initiated or pending, without reference to the company's disclosure, drops the disclosure limb. The view that nothing is reported because the proceeding is pending and its outcome is unknown wrongly treats a pending proceeding as non-reportable when the clause expressly covers 'initiated or pending'. The view that the matter is reported instead under clause (ix) on loan repayment misplaces it in a different clause. The decisive point is the two-limb structure of clause (i)(e).

questions.question: Under CARO clause (i)(a), which option correctly captures the difference in the records on which the auditor reports for PPE as compared with intangible assets?
options: Both PPE and intangible assets require records showing quantitative details and situation.
Intangible assets require situation; PPE require only full particulars.
Neither requires full particulars; the auditor checks only that some record of assets exists.
PPE require proper records showing full particulars including quantitative details and situation; intangible assets require proper records showing full particulars.
questions.explanation: Clause (i)(a) describes the records asymmetrically: for PPE (which include right-of-use assets under the clause heading) the auditor reports whether proper records showing full particulars, including quantitative details and situation, are maintained, whereas for intangible assets the auditor reports whether proper records showing full particulars are maintained, without the 'quantitative details and situation' overlay. The statement that both PPE and intangible assets require records showing quantitative details and situation wrongly extends the PPE description to intangibles. The view that intangible assets require situation while PPE require only full particulars reverses the two descriptions. The suggestion that neither requires full particulars, the auditor checking only that some record of assets exists, understates the requirement, as full particulars are expressly required. The decisive point is that 'quantitative details and situation' is attached only to PPE, not to intangible assets.

questions.question:
CASE: Sunrise Pharma Limited (to which CARO applies) discloses three immovable properties in its financial statements. Property X's title deed is in the company's name; Property Y's title deed stands in the name of an employee; Property Z's title deed stands in the name of a promoter's relative.
Under CARO clause (i)(c), which properties must be reported with details in the prescribed format, and with which 'held in name of' entry?
options: Only Y, reported as held by an employee.
Y and Z, reported as held by an 'employee' and by 'their relative' (a promoter's relative) respectively.
X, Y and Z, because all immovable properties disclosed must be reported.
Only Z, because a promoter's relative is the only category listed in the format.
questions.explanation: Clause (i)(c) requires details, in the fixed format, of immovable property whose title deed is not held in the name of the company; the 'held in name of' column allows the holder to be a promoter, a director, their relative, or an employee. Property Y (employee) and Property Z (promoter's relative) are both outside the company's name and both fall within the enumerated holder categories, so each must be reported with the appropriate entry. Property X is held in the company's own name and therefore needs no remark. The reporting of only Y as held by an employee omits the promoter's relative; the inclusion of X, Y and Z, because all immovable properties disclosed must be reported, over-reports the compliant property X; and the reporting of only Z, on the footing that a promoter's relative is the only category listed in the format, wrongly treats the employee category as inapplicable. The decisive test is whether the deed is in the company's name and, if not, which listed category applies.

questions.question:
CASE: Deccan Traders Private Limited (to which CARO applies) manufactures goods with two classes of inventory — raw material and finished goods. Management physically verified inventory once during the year (in February 2025), covering the raw-material class at all locations but the finished-goods class at only one of the four locations where it was held, so that the coverage and procedure of that verification were not appropriate. A discrepancy equal to 12% in aggregate was noticed in the finished-goods class at the location that was verified, and that discrepancy was not dealt with in the books. The company was sanctioned aggregate working-capital limits of ₹7 crore from a consortium of banks during the year, on the security of its current assets; the quarterly returns/statements filed with the banks were in agreement with the company's books in all respects except one quarter where the stock statement overstated finished goods by ₹40 lakh.
Under clause (ii)(a), which statement is most appropriate?
options: The auditor must report that the coverage and procedure of verification were not appropriate (the finished-goods class was counted at only one of its four locations) and that the 12% aggregate discrepancy in the finished-goods class was not dealt with in the books.
No remark is needed on verification because inventory was verified once during the year, satisfying the at-least-once-in-a-year expectation.
The auditor need only report the discrepancy if it is material, applying the 'material discrepancy' wording of clause (i)(b).
The auditor must report nothing on discrepancies because the quarterly returns agreed with the books.
questions.explanation: Clause (ii)(a) requires the auditor to report on the reasonableness of verification intervals, on whether the coverage and procedure of verification are appropriate, and on discrepancies of 10% or more in aggregate for each class of inventory together with whether they were dealt with in the books. Here the finished-goods class was counted at only one of the four locations holding it, so the coverage-and-procedure limb fails, and that class carries a 12% (i.e. at least 10%) discrepancy not dealt with in the books, which must be reported. The plea that no remark is needed because inventory was verified once during the year, satisfying the at-least-once-in-a-year expectation, is wrong because one verification that omits three of the four finished-goods locations does not cure the coverage failure. The view that the auditor need only report the discrepancy if it is material wrongly imports clause (i)(b)'s 'material discrepancy' wording in place of the 10% per-class test. The statement that nothing at all should be reported on discrepancies because the quarterly returns agreed with the books confuses clause (ii)(a) with clause (ii)(b). The decisive points are the per-class 10% trigger and the separate coverage-and-procedure requirement.

questions.question:
Statements about CARO clause (ii)(b), which concerns working-capital limits:
1. The reporting trigger is aggregate working-capital limits in excess of ₹5 crores sanctioned at any time during the year.
2. The limits must be sanctioned from banks or financial institutions on the security of current assets.
3. The auditor must report whether the quarterly returns or statements filed by the company are in agreement with the company's books, giving details if they are not.
4. The ₹5 crore limit is tested only as on the last day of the financial year.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Clause (ii)(b) is engaged where, at any time during the year, aggregate working-capital limits in excess of ₹5 crores have been sanctioned by banks or financial institutions on the security of current assets, so statements 1 and 2 are correct. It then requires the auditor to report whether the quarterly returns or statements filed by the company agree with its books, giving details of any disagreement, so statement 3 is correct. Statement 4 is wrong because the ₹5 crore test is applied 'at any time during the year', not only at the year-end date. The decisive features are the 'at any time during the year' timing, the 'in excess of ₹5 crores' threshold, and the 'on the security of current assets' condition.

questions.question:
CASE: Deccan Traders Private Limited (to which CARO applies) manufactures goods with two classes of inventory — raw material and finished goods. Management physically verified inventory once during the year (in February 2025), covering the raw-material class at all locations but the finished-goods class at only one of the four locations where it was held, so that the coverage and procedure of that verification were not appropriate. A discrepancy equal to 12% in aggregate was noticed in the finished-goods class at the location that was verified, and that discrepancy was not dealt with in the books. The company was sanctioned aggregate working-capital limits of ₹7 crore from a consortium of banks during the year, on the security of its current assets; the quarterly returns/statements filed with the banks were in agreement with the company's books in all respects except one quarter where the stock statement overstated finished goods by ₹40 lakh.
Under CARO clause (ii)(b), which of the following actions are correct for the auditor?
1. Because aggregate working-capital limits of ₹7 crore exceeded ₹5 crore at a time during the year, report on the agreement of the quarterly returns/statements with the books.
2. Give details of the quarter in which the stock statement overstated finished goods by ₹40 lakh as a disagreement with the books.
3. Omit the discrepant quarter and report full agreement because the other three quarters agreed.
4. Skip clause (ii)(b) altogether because the company also had a clause (i) revaluation matter.
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
1 and 2 only
questions.explanation: Clause (ii)(b) is engaged because the sanctioned working-capital limits of ₹7 crore exceeded ₹5 crore during the year on the security of current assets, so the auditor must report on the agreement of quarterly returns/statements with the books, making action 1 correct. Where one quarter's stock statement overstated finished goods by ₹40 lakh, that is a disagreement which must be detailed, making action 2 correct. Action 3 is wrong because the clause requires details of any non-agreement; the auditor cannot suppress the one discrepant quarter. Action 4 is wrong because each CARO clause operates independently, so a clause (i) matter does not displace clause (ii). The decisive points are the engagement of the ₹5 crore trigger and the duty to detail every quarterly-return disagreement.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on CARO clause (ii)(a) (inventory):
1. Physical verification of inventory is expected to be conducted at reasonable intervals, at least once in a year.
2. The reporting trigger for inventory discrepancies is any material discrepancy, with no percentage threshold.
3. The 10% discrepancy test applies to total inventory across all classes combined.
4. The auditor must comment on whether the coverage and procedure of such verification are appropriate.
Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
options: 1 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Clause (ii)(a) expressly expects verification at reasonable intervals, at least once in a year, so statement 1 is correct and is not a target of this 'NOT correct' question. Statement 2 is incorrect because the inventory trigger is a fixed 10% or more in aggregate for each class, not the open-ended 'material discrepancy' standard used in clause (i)(b). Statement 3 is incorrect because the 10% test is applied per class of inventory, not to the combined total across all classes. Statement 4 is correct because coverage and procedure appropriateness is expressly part of clause (ii)(a). The question asks for the NOT-correct statements, which are 2 and 3 only. The decisive drafting point is the 10%-in-aggregate-per-class trigger.

questions.question:
CASE: Nandi Infra Limited is a public company. For FY 2024-25, aggregate working-capital limits sanctioned by banks on the security of current assets were ₹5 crore exactly throughout the year and were never in excess of ₹5 crore. Management verified inventory at reasonable intervals with appropriate coverage and procedure, and no discrepancies of 10% or more in aggregate in any class were noticed.
What is the correct CARO clause (ii) outcome for Nandi Infra?
options: Clause (ii)(b) is not triggered because the limits were not in excess of ₹5 crores; clause (ii)(a) still requires a positive statement that verification had appropriate coverage and procedure with no qualifying 10% discrepancy.
Clause (ii)(b) reporting is triggered because the sanctioned limit equals ₹5 crore.
Both clause (ii)(a) and clause (ii)(b) require adverse remarks.
Clause (ii)(a) does not apply to a public company.
questions.explanation: The clause (ii)(b) trigger is 'aggregate working-capital limits in excess of ₹5 crores'; a limit of exactly ₹5 crore is not in excess of ₹5 crore, so clause (ii)(b) is not engaged and there is nothing to report under it. Clause (ii)(a), which has no monetary trigger and applies to every company covered by CARO including a public company, is satisfied on the facts — verification at reasonable intervals with appropriate coverage and procedure and no 10%-per-class discrepancy — so it produces a clean positive statement. The conclusion that clause (ii)(b) reporting is triggered because the sanctioned limit equals ₹5 crore misreads 'in excess of' as 'equal to'. The assertion that both clause (ii)(a) and clause (ii)(b) require adverse remarks wrongly converts compliant facts into adverse remarks. The contention that clause (ii)(a) does not apply to a public company is wrong because clause (ii)(a) is not limited to any company type. The decisive point is the strict 'in excess of ₹5 crores' wording of clause (ii)(b).

questions.question:
Statements about the two different 10% tests in CARO 2020:
1. The revaluation test in clause (i)(d) is 10% or more of the net carrying value of each class of PPE or intangible assets.
2. The inventory test in clause (ii)(a) is 10% or more in aggregate for each class of inventory.
3. The revaluation test measures the change against the gross carrying value of each class.
4. Both tests are applied to the total of all classes combined.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
1 and 2 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: clause (i)(d) quantifies the change only where the aggregate change is 10% or more of the net carrying value of each class of PPE or intangible assets. Statement 2 is correct: clause (ii)(a) reports discrepancies of 10% or more in aggregate for each class of inventory. Statement 3 is wrong because the revaluation test uses net carrying value, not gross carrying value (gross carrying value appears only in the clause (i)(c) title-deed format). Statement 4 is wrong because both tests are applied to each class separately, never to a combined total across classes. The decisive distinctions are net versus gross carrying value and per-class versus combined application.

questions.question:
CASE: Deccan Traders Private Limited (to which CARO applies) manufactures goods with two classes of inventory — raw material and finished goods. Management physically verified inventory once during the year (in February 2025), covering the raw-material class at all locations but the finished-goods class at only one of the four locations where it was held, so that the coverage and procedure of that verification were not appropriate. A discrepancy equal to 12% in aggregate was noticed in the finished-goods class at the location that was verified, and that discrepancy was not dealt with in the books. The company was sanctioned aggregate working-capital limits of ₹7 crore from a consortium of banks during the year, on the security of its current assets; the quarterly returns/statements filed with the banks were in agreement with the company's books in all respects except one quarter where the stock statement overstated finished goods by ₹40 lakh.
Considering clause (ii) as a whole, which of the following remarks is NOT required for Deccan Traders?
options: A remark that the coverage and procedure of inventory verification were not appropriate.
A remark giving details of the quarterly stock statement that disagreed with the books.
A remark on the 12% aggregate discrepancy in the finished-goods class not being dealt with in the books.
A remark that inventory was not verified even once during the year.
questions.explanation: Management did physically verify inventory once during the year, in February 2025, so a statement that inventory was never verified would be factually false and is not the required remark; this is the option NOT required. The coverage-and-procedure remark is required because the finished-goods class was counted at only one of its four locations. The 12% aggregate discrepancy in the finished-goods class, being at least the 10% per-class threshold and not dealt with in the books, must be reported under clause (ii)(a). The disagreeing quarterly stock statement must be detailed under clause (ii)(b). The decisive point is to distinguish the frequency limb (satisfied by a single verification) from the coverage-and-procedure limb (failed), which is where the actual reporting obligation arises.

questions.question:
CARO 2020 clause (iii) on loans, investments, guarantees and securities opens with an introductory condition which must be satisfied before any of its sub-clauses is answered. Consider the following situations of an unlisted public company for FY 2024-25:
1. The company subscribed to debentures issued by a private limited company during the year.
2. The company furnished a bank guarantee on behalf of its wholly owned subsidiary during the year.
3. The company granted an interest-free advance to a limited liability partnership, to be returned at the LLP's convenience.
4. The company paid an instalment to a supplier towards the price of machinery to be delivered, the amount being adjustable against the purchase price.
Which of these situations engage the introductory condition of clause (iii)?
options: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: The introductory words of clause (iii) cover a company which has, during the year, made investments, provided any guarantee or security, or granted any loans or advances in the nature of secured or unsecured loans, to companies, firms, LLP or any other parties. Subscription to debentures is an investment, the bank guarantee is a guarantee provided for another entity, and an interest-free advance repayable at the borrower's convenience is an advance in the nature of a loan granted to an LLP, so situations 1, 2 and 3 each open the gate to sub-clauses (a) to (f). The decisive point is the character of the outflow rather than its size: an instalment paid towards the price of machinery and adjustable against that price is a trading advance and not a loan or an advance in the nature of a loan, so situation 4 does not engage the clause. Note also that the introductory words are not confined to companies, since firms, LLPs and any other parties are expressly included.

questions.question:
Match the sub-clauses of CARO clause (iii) in Column I with the quantification or disclosure which that sub-clause requires, shown in Column II.
Column I
(i) Sub-clause (a)
(ii) Sub-clause (c)
(iii) Sub-clause (d)
(iv) Sub-clause (e)
(v) Sub-clause (f)
Column II
(A) Aggregate amount, percentage to total loans granted, and aggregate amount of loans granted to promoters and to related parties as defined in the Companies Act, 2013
(B) Whether a schedule of principal repayment and of payment of interest has been stipulated, and whether repayments are regular
(C) Aggregate amount and balance outstanding at the balance sheet date, separately for subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates and for other parties
(D) Total amount overdue for more than 90 days, and whether reasonable steps have been taken by the company for recovery
(E) Aggregate amount of dues renewed, extended or settled by fresh loans, and the percentage of that aggregate to total loans or advances
Which of the following pairings is correct?
questions.explanation: Sub-clause (a) is the quantum sub-clause: it asks whether the company has provided loans or advances in the nature of loans, or stood guarantee, or provided security to any other entity, and where it has, requires the aggregate amount and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date to be indicated first for subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates and then for other parties, so (i) pairs with (C). Sub-clause (c) tests stipulation of a schedule of principal repayment and of payment of interest together with regularity of repayment, sub-clause (d) the amount overdue for more than 90 days and the recovery steps, sub-clause (e) the renewal or extension or settlement by fresh loans of dues which fell during the year with its percentage, and sub-clause (f) demand loans and loans granted without specified terms, alone with the promoter and related-party amounts. The pair most often interchanged is (e) with (f): (e) takes its percentage against total loans or advances, whereas (f) takes it against total loans granted and is the only limb which calls for the promoter and related-party figures.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on the sub-clauses of CARO clause (iii):
1. Sub-clause (b) requires the auditor to consider whether the investments made, the guarantees provided and the terms and conditions of the grant of all loans and advances are not prejudicial to the company's interest.
2. Sub-clause (c) is fully discharged once it is established that a schedule of principal repayment has been stipulated, payment of interest being outside its scope.
3. Sub-clause (d) requires the total amount overdue for more than 90 days to be stated, along with whether reasonable steps have been taken by the company for recovery.
4. Sub-clause (e) is confined to loans and advances which had fallen due during the year and which were thereafter renewed or extended or settled by fresh loans.
5. Sub-clause (f) is attracted only where a loan is expressly made repayable on demand, a loan granted without any specified period of repayment falling outside it.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 5 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 3, 4 and 5 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 3 and 4 correctly state sub-clauses (b), (d) and (e). Statement 2 fails because sub-clause (c) makes a double requirement, namely whether a schedule of principal repayment and of payment of interest has been stipulated and whether repayments are regular, so a principal-only schedule leaves the sub-clause unfulfilled. Statement 5 fails because sub-clause (f) is expressed disjunctively and covers loans or advances 'either repayable on demand or without specifying any terms or period of repayment', so the absence of a stated period of repayment attracts it as much as an express demand term does. The distinction which decides this question is that (b) judges the bargain, (c) the stipulation and conduct of repayment, (d) the arrears beyond 90 days, (e) the recycling of matured dues and (f) the loans whose repayment terms are indeterminate.

questions.category: CARO - Clause (iii) Loans and Advances - Case
questions.question:
Vandana Holdings Limited ('VHL'), an unlisted public company engaged in manufacture, has no business of lending. For FY 2024-25 the aggregate of loans and advances granted by VHL during the year was ₹80 crore. The remaining lending of the company was to unrelated trade customers on customary terms, with stipulated repayment schedules which had been regularly honoured. The auditor noted the following:
Fact 1 - VHL granted ₹20 crore of loans repayable on demand with no period of repayment and no interest schedule, namely ₹9 crore to a trade customer, ₹6 crore to its promoter and ₹5 crore to relatives of its directors who are related parties under the Companies Act, 2013.
Fact 2 - A loan of ₹12 crore granted to VHL's joint venture fell due on 30 November 2024. On 5 December 2024 VHL sanctioned a fresh loan of ₹12 crore to the joint venture, which applied it towards discharging the loan that had fallen due.
Fact 3 - A loan of ₹9 crore granted in FY 2022-23 to a dealer became repayable in full on 20 January 2025. Of this, ₹4.2 crore was still unpaid on the date of the auditor's report, 120 days after the due date, the balance having been received. VHL had issued two demand letters but had started no recovery proceedings.
Fact 4 - VHL stood as guarantor for a term facility availed by its wholly owned subsidiary to the extent of ₹6 crore.
Fact 5 - VHL gave an unsecured advance of ₹2.5 crore to a partnership firm, no schedule of principal repayment or of payment of interest having been stipulated.
Fact 6 - VHL granted a loan of ₹3 crore to a director; the company's law officer recorded that section 185 of the Companies Act, 2013 had not been complied with. That loan has a stipulated schedule and has been serviced regularly.
Which one of the following correctly maps Facts 1 to 5, in that order, to the sub-clause of clause (iii) which each fact directly engages?
options: Fact 1 - (e); Fact 2 - (f); Fact 3 - (d); Fact 4 - (b); Fact 5 - (c)
Fact 1 - (f); Fact 2 - (e); Fact 3 - (d); Fact 4 - (a); Fact 5 - (c)
Fact 1 - (f); Fact 2 - (e); Fact 3 - (b); Fact 4 - (a); Fact 5 - (d)
Fact 1 - (a); Fact 2 - (d); Fact 3 - (e); Fact 4 - (b); Fact 5 - (c)
Fact 1 - (f); Fact 2 - (c); Fact 3 - (d); Fact 4 - (a); Fact 5 - (e)
questions.explanation: Fact 1 is a loan repayable on demand with no period of repayment specified, which is the exact subject matter of sub-clause (f). Fact 2 is a loan which fell due during the year and was settled by a fresh loan to the same borrower, engaging sub-clause (e) with its aggregate and percentage. Fact 3 concerns ₹4.2 crore overdue for more than 90 days and the absence of recovery proceedings, which is sub-clause (d) and not sub-clause (b), because sub-clause (b) judges the terms on which the loan was granted rather than what happened after the due date passed. Fact 4 is a guarantee given for a subsidiary, and sub-clause (a) alone requires the aggregate amount and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date to be classified under subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates. Fact 5 is an advance to a firm for which neither a principal nor an interest repayment schedule was stipulated, the province of sub-clause (c); the tempting reading is to treat an overdue amount as a renewal and a renewal as arrears, which is what the combination 'Fact 1 - (a); Fact 2 - (d); Fact 3 - (e); Fact 4 - (b); Fact 5 - (c)' does.

questions.category: CARO - Clause (iii) Loans and Advances - Case
questions.question:
Vandana Holdings Limited ('VHL'), an unlisted public company engaged in manufacture, has no business of lending. For FY 2024-25 the aggregate of loans and advances granted by VHL during the year was ₹80 crore. The remaining lending of the company was to unrelated trade customers on customary terms, with stipulated repayment schedules which had been regularly honoured. The auditor noted the following:
Fact 1 - VHL granted ₹20 crore of loans repayable on demand with no period of repayment and no interest schedule, namely ₹9 crore to a trade customer, ₹6 crore to its promoter and ₹5 crore to relatives of its directors who are related parties under the Companies Act, 2013.
Fact 2 - A loan of ₹12 crore granted to VHL's joint venture fell due on 30 November 2024. On 5 December 2024 VHL sanctioned a fresh loan of ₹12 crore to the joint venture, which applied it towards discharging the loan that had fallen due.
Fact 3 - A loan of ₹9 crore granted in FY 2022-23 to a dealer became repayable in full on 20 January 2025. Of this, ₹4.2 crore was still unpaid on the date of the auditor's report, 120 days after the due date, the balance having been received. VHL had issued two demand letters but had started no recovery proceedings.
Fact 4 - VHL stood as guarantor for a term facility availed by its wholly owned subsidiary to the extent of ₹6 crore.
Fact 5 - VHL gave an unsecured advance of ₹2.5 crore to a partnership firm, no schedule of principal repayment or of payment of interest having been stipulated.
Fact 6 - VHL granted a loan of ₹3 crore to a director; the company's law officer recorded that section 185 of the Companies Act, 2013 had not been complied with. That loan has a stipulated schedule and has been serviced regularly.
Based on the above case, which of the following statements about the auditor's statement on clause (iii) are correct?
1. Under sub-clause (f) the auditor must disclose ₹20 crore as the aggregate amount of loans repayable on demand, 25 per cent as the percentage to total loans granted, and the ₹6 crore granted to the promoter and ₹5 crore granted to related parties.
2. The ₹12 crore settled by the fresh loan is reportable under sub-clause (e), with the aggregate amount of such dues and the percentage of that aggregate to total loans or advances.
3. Sub-clause (d) requires the auditor to state ₹4.2 crore as the amount overdue for more than 90 days and to state whether reasonable steps have been taken by VHL for recovery.
4. Sub-clause (c) is satisfied for the ₹2.5 crore advance to the partnership firm, because that sub-clause applies only to secured loans and the advance was unsecured.
5. Clause (iv) is not attracted by Fact 6, because a loan to a director is already covered by clause (iii).
options: 1, 2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2, 3 and 5 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
1, 3, 4 and 5 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 follow from the arithmetic and from the wording of sub-clauses (f), (e) and (d): ₹20 crore is 25 per cent of the ₹80 crore of loans granted during the year, ₹12 crore of fallen-due dues settled by a fresh loan is 15 per cent of total loans or advances, and ₹4.2 crore alone had been overdue for 120 days, the ₹4.8 crore received being no longer overdue. Statement 4 is wrong because the introductory words of clause (iii) expressly extend to loans and advances in the nature of secured or unsecured loans, and sub-clause (c) qualifies them by nothing except the requirement of a stipulated schedule of principal and interest repayment and of regular repayment. Statement 5 is wrong because clause (iv) operates independently in respect of loans, investments, guarantees and security and asks a different question, namely compliance with sections 185 and 186, so the same loan of ₹3 crore is reported under both clauses.

questions.category: CARO - Clause (iii) Loans and Advances - Case
questions.question:
Vandana Holdings Limited ('VHL'), an unlisted public company engaged in manufacture, has no business of lending. For FY 2024-25 the aggregate of loans and advances granted by VHL during the year was ₹80 crore. The remaining lending of the company was to unrelated trade customers on customary terms, with stipulated repayment schedules which had been regularly honoured. The auditor noted the following:
Fact 1 - VHL granted ₹20 crore of loans repayable on demand with no period of repayment and no interest schedule, namely ₹9 crore to a trade customer, ₹6 crore to its promoter and ₹5 crore to relatives of its directors who are related parties under the Companies Act, 2013.
Fact 2 - A loan of ₹12 crore granted to VHL's joint venture fell due on 30 November 2024. On 5 December 2024 VHL sanctioned a fresh loan of ₹12 crore to the joint venture, which applied it towards discharging the loan that had fallen due.
Fact 3 - A loan of ₹9 crore granted in FY 2022-23 to a dealer became repayable in full on 20 January 2025. Of this, ₹4.2 crore was still unpaid on the date of the auditor's report, 120 days after the due date, the balance having been received. VHL had issued two demand letters but had started no recovery proceedings.
Fact 4 - VHL stood as guarantor for a term facility availed by its wholly owned subsidiary to the extent of ₹6 crore.
Fact 5 - VHL gave an unsecured advance of ₹2.5 crore to a partnership firm, no schedule of principal repayment or of payment of interest having been stipulated.
Fact 6 - VHL granted a loan of ₹3 crore to a director; the company's law officer recorded that section 185 of the Companies Act, 2013 had not been complied with. That loan has a stipulated schedule and has been serviced regularly.
Which of the following actions should the auditor of VHL take in framing the statement on clause (iii)?
