1. Classify the loans, advances, guarantee and security between subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates on one side and other parties on the other, and give the aggregate amount and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date for each.
2. Form a conclusion under sub-clause (b) on whether the terms of the ₹20 crore of demand loans and the guarantee for the subsidiary's facility are not prejudicial to VHL's interest.
3. Report the entire ₹9 crore of the dealer's loan as overdue under sub-clause (d), that loan having become repayable during the year.
4. State under sub-clause (e) that no disclosure arises, because the fresh ₹12 crore loan was sanctioned only after the earlier loan had fallen due.
5. Establish, for loans and advances, whether schedules of principal repayment and of payment of interest were stipulated and whether repayments were regular.
options: 1, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 5 only
2, 3 and 5 only
1, 2, 3 and 5 only
1, 2, 4 and 5 only
questions.explanation: Sub-clause (d) requires the total amount overdue for more than 90 days, which on these facts is ₹4.2 crore and not the ₹9 crore which became repayable during the year, since ₹4.8 crore was in fact received; action 3 is therefore wrong. Sub-clause (e) is attracted precisely because the loan had fallen due during the year and was then settled by a fresh loan, and the very fact that the fresh loan was sanctioned after the due date is what brings it within the sub-clause, so action 4 is wrong. Actions 1, 2 and 5 are the steps the clause calls for: sub-clause (a) prescribes the two-fold classification of recipients and both the aggregate and the closing outstanding, sub-clause (b) requires a judgment on the terms on which loans were granted and on guarantees provided, and sub-clause (c) requires both stipulation and regularity of repayment to be tested for loans and advances.

questions.question:
Vandana Holdings Limited ('VHL'), an unlisted public company engaged in manufacture, has no business of lending. For FY 2024-25 the aggregate of loans and advances granted by VHL during the year was ₹80 crore. The remaining lending of the company was to unrelated trade customers on customary terms, with stipulated repayment schedules which had been regularly honoured. The auditor noted the following:
Fact 1 - VHL granted ₹20 crore of loans repayable on demand with no period of repayment and no interest schedule, namely ₹9 crore to a trade customer, ₹6 crore to its promoter and ₹5 crore to relatives of its directors who are related parties under the Companies Act, 2013.
Fact 2 - A loan of ₹12 crore granted to VHL's joint venture fell due on 30 November 2024. On 5 December 2024 VHL sanctioned a fresh loan of ₹12 crore to the joint venture, which applied it towards discharging the loan that had fallen due.
Fact 3 - A loan of ₹9 crore granted in FY 2022-23 to a dealer became repayable in full on 20 January 2025. Of this, ₹4.2 crore was still unpaid on the date of the auditor's report, 120 days after the due date, the balance having been received. VHL had issued two demand letters but had started no recovery proceedings.
Fact 4 - VHL stood as guarantor for a term facility availed by its wholly owned subsidiary to the extent of ₹6 crore.
Fact 5 - VHL gave an unsecured advance of ₹2.5 crore to a partnership firm, no schedule of principal repayment or of payment of interest having been stipulated.
Fact 6 - VHL granted a loan of ₹3 crore to a director; the company's law officer recorded that section 185 of the Companies Act, 2013 had not been complied with. That loan has a stipulated schedule and has been serviced regularly.
With reference to Facts 2 and 4, what does sub-clause (a) of clause (iii) require the auditor to indicate?
options: Only the aggregate amount of loans, advances, guarantees and security given during the year, the outstanding balance being relevant solely to sub-clause (d)
The aggregate amount and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date, in each case separately for subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates and for other parties
The aggregate amount for subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates only, a guarantee given for a subsidiary being outside sub-clause (a)
The balance outstanding at the balance sheet date alone, the aggregate being reported under clause (iv)
Only such information as the auditor considers material, sub-clause (a) being directory and not prescriptive
questions.explanation: Sub-clause (a) asks whether the company has provided loans or advances in the nature of loans, or stood guarantee, or provided security to any other entity, and where it has, requires the aggregate amount and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date to be indicated, once for subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates and once again for other parties. On these facts the ₹12 crore joint venture loan and the ₹6 crore guarantee for the wholly owned subsidiary fall in the subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates column, so both the aggregate and the closing outstanding must be shown for that column, while the amounts advanced to the promoter, the related parties, the trade customer, the dealer and the partnership firm fall in the column for other parties. The readings that only the aggregate amount of loans, advances, guarantees and security given during the year is wanted, the outstanding balance being relevant solely to sub-clause (d), and that only the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date is wanted, the aggregate being reported under clause (iv), each drop one of the two prescribed figures. The limitation of the aggregate to subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates only, on the footing that a guarantee given for a subsidiary is outside sub-clause (a), wrongly excludes guarantees, which sub-clause (a) names expressly along with security.

questions.question: Reena Ceramics Limited granted a loan of ₹5 crore to a customer, repayable in full on 10 January 2025. As on the date of the auditor's report ₹1.5 crore remained unpaid, the default having continued for 75 days, and the company had issued one reminder without starting any recovery proceedings. Suppose instead that the same ₹1.5 crore had been overdue for 100 days on the date of the report, every other fact remaining unchanged. What difference does this make to the statement on CARO clause (iii)?
options: None; sub-clause (d) is attracted as soon as any part of a loan becomes overdue, irrespective of the number of days.
The amount becomes reportable under sub-clause (d) only if the auditor also concludes under sub-clause (b) that the terms of the loan were prejudicial to the company's interest.

At 100 days the auditor states ₹1.5 crore as the total amount overdue for more than 90 days and reports whether reasonable steps have been taken by the company for recovery; at 75 days that limb is not yet attracted.
The change affects only sub-clause (c), because a stipulated schedule of repayment ceases to have any content once the due date has passed.
At 100 days the amount becomes reportable under sub-clause (e) as a loan which has fallen due and remains unpaid.
questions.explanation: Sub-clause (d) is expressly keyed to an amount overdue for more than 90 days and then requires two things, the total amount so overdue and whether reasonable steps have been taken by the company for recovery. Crossing the 90-day line therefore creates the disclosure, while a 75-day default does not attract that limb, even though the single reminder without recovery proceedings would become the relevant material once the threshold is crossed. The remaining limbs are independent of the day-count, so sub-clause (b) still judges the terms on which the loan was granted and sub-clause (c) whether a schedule of principal and interest repayment was stipulated and repayment regular, and neither is a precondition of sub-clause (d). Sub-clause (e) is not engaged at all, because no loan has been renewed, extended or settled by a fresh loan.

questions.category: CARO - Clause (iii) Sub-clause (e) - Renewal of Fallen Due Loans
questions.question: Dhwani Metals Limited granted loans and advances aggregating ₹30 crore during FY 2024-25. On 20 February 2025 it extended the due date of a ₹6 crore loan which was not yet due, without charging any additional interest. Suppose instead that the ₹6 crore loan had already fallen due on 31 January 2025 and had been extended on 20 February 2025, every other fact remaining the same. What difference would this make?
options: None, since sub-clause (e) reaches every renewal or extension of a loan or advance made during the year, whether or not the loan had become repayable before the extension was granted.

Sub-clause (e) would not apply to the extension as originally framed, because it reaches only a loan or advance which has fallen due during the year; the extension of a loan not yet due would instead fall to be examined under sub-clause (b) on whether the terms are not prejudicial.
Sub-clause (e) would apply in both cases, but the percentage would be computed on the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date rather than on total loans or advances.
The modified fact would shift the reporting from sub-clause (e) to sub-clause (f), an extension being treated as a loan repayable on demand.
The modified fact would attract sub-clause (d) alone, an extended fallen-due loan being an amount overdue for more than 90 days.
questions.explanation: The words of sub-clause (e) reach any loan or advance which has fallen due during the year and which has been renewed or extended or settled by fresh loans, so the falling due of the loan during the year is the condition which separates a reportable renewal from an ordinary rescheduling granted in advance. On the modified fact ₹6 crore of fallen-due dues would have been extended and both the aggregate and its percentage of total loans or advances would be disclosed. On the original fact sub-clause (e) is not engaged, yet the loan is not immune from clause (iii), because sub-clause (b) still asks whether the terms and conditions of the grant of all loans and advances, including a concession of time without additional interest, are not prejudicial to the company's interest. Nothing in the facts makes the loan repayable on demand or an amount overdue beyond 90 days, so the readings that the modified fact would shift the reporting from sub-clause (e) to sub-clause (f) as a loan repayable on demand, and that it would attract sub-clause (d) alone as an amount overdue for more than 90 days, misapply those limbs.

questions.category: CARO - Clause (iii) Sub-clause (a) - Classification of Recipients
questions.question: Nishtha Infra Limited, a public company, granted during FY 2024-25 an unsecured loan of ₹8 crore to another company in which it holds 2 per cent of the equity, which is accordingly neither its subsidiary, joint venture nor associate. The loan carries a stipulated schedule of principal repayment and of payment of interest and has been regularly serviced, and the auditor reports it in the 'other parties' column of sub-clause (a). Suppose that Nishtha in fact held 45 per cent of the borrowing company so that it became an associate, nothing else changing. What would alter in the statement on clause (iii)?
options: The loan would cease to be reported under sub-clause (a), loans to associates being dealt with exclusively by clause (iv), which alone speaks of the class of recipient.
The loan would move columns, and sub-clause (c) would no longer be asked of it, repayment by an associate being presumed regular.
Nothing would alter, because sub-clause (a) prescribes a single combined figure for all classes of recipient and the identity of the borrower is not relevant.

The loan would move to the subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates column, with the aggregate amount and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date being indicated for that column, while sub-clauses (b) to (f) continue to apply to it in the same way.
The loan would move columns and would additionally have to be reported as a loan repayable on demand, dealings with associates being treated as lacking fixed terms.
questions.explanation: Sub-clause (a) requires the aggregate amount and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date to be indicated twice over, once for loans, advances, guarantees or security given to subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates and once for those given to other parties, so a change in the identity of the recipient changes only the column in which the ₹8 crore appears. The other sub-clauses are not keyed to the class of recipient: sub-clause (b) speaks of the terms and conditions of the grant of all loans and advances, sub-clause (c) of loans and advances generally, sub-clause (d) of amounts overdue and sub-clause (f) of demand loans together with the amounts to promoters and related parties, so the stipulated schedule and the regular servicing would continue to be tested exactly as before. The contentions that the loan would cease to be reported under sub-clause (a) because clause (iv) alone speaks of the class of recipient, that sub-clause (c) would no longer be asked of it because repayment by an associate is presumed regular, and that it must additionally be reported as a loan repayable on demand because dealings with associates lack fixed terms, wrongly allow the recipient's identity to displace a sub-clause; and the position that nothing would alter, because sub-clause (a) prescribes a single combined figure for all classes of recipient, ignores the prescribed two-fold classification.

questions.category: CARO - Clause (iii) Sub-clause (e) - Assertion and Reason
questions.question:
Assertion (A): CARO clause (iii)(e) requires the auditor to specify the aggregate amount of loans or advances which, having fallen due during the year, have been renewed or extended or settled by fresh loans, and also the percentage of that aggregate to total loans or advances.
Reason (R): A loan discharged out of a fresh loan leaves the company's total exposure to that borrower unchanged while making the earlier loan appear to have been repaid, so the quantum of such recycling and its relative size in the company's lending are matters members need in order to judge the quality of the loans appearing on the books.
Which of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
R is true but A is false.
Both A and R are false.
questions.explanation: Assertion A states sub-clause (e) accurately, since the order demands not merely a yes or no answer but the aggregate amount of the dues so renewed, extended or settled by fresh loans and the percentage of that aggregate to total loans or advances. Reason R supplies the rationale for that otherwise unusual demand for quantification: a fresh loan applied to the matured dues extinguishes the record of a repayment without any cash actually coming in, so the apparent regularity of recovery is defeated unless both the amount and the proportion are laid before the members. R therefore explains why the sub-clause prescribes a quantum and a ratio and is not merely a true statement standing beside A, which rules out the conclusion that both are true but R is not the correct explanation of A. Any suggestion that A overstates the clause is unfounded, since the percentage is expressly required, so the conclusions that A is true but R is false, and that R is true but A is false, both fail.

questions.category: CARO - Clause (iii) Sub-clause (f) - Assertion and Reason
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Where a company has granted loans or advances either repayable on demand or without specifying any terms or period of repayment, CARO clause (iii)(f) requires the auditor to state the aggregate amount of such loans, their percentage to total loans granted, and the aggregate amount of loans granted to promoters and to related parties as defined in the Companies Act, 2013.
Reason (R): Sub-clause (f) is confined to unsecured loans granted to parties other than promoters, since loans to promoters and to subsidiaries are reported only under sub-clause (a).
Which of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
R is true but A is false.
Both A and R are false.
questions.explanation: Assertion A reproduces the three disclosures which sub-clause (f) demands where the loan is repayable on demand or is granted without any specified terms or period of repayment, and it is immaterial for this purpose whether the loan is secured or unsecured or who the borrower is. Reason R is false, because sub-clause (f) itself requires the aggregate amount of loans granted to promoters and to related parties as defined in the Companies Act, 2013 to be specified, so promoters and related parties are inside the sub-clause rather than excluded from it. Sub-clause (a) does classify amounts by recipient, but it does so for the aggregate amount and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date under the heads of subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates and of other parties, and not in substitution for the demand-loan disclosure.

questions.category: CARO - Clause (iii) Sub-clause (d) - Direction of Flow
questions.question: Suryan Textiles Limited has missed two quarterly instalments on its ₹40 crore term loan from a consortium of banks, and interest for the quarter ended 31 January 2025 is also unpaid. Separately, a customer to whom Suryan lent ₹6 crore has not paid ₹3 crore for 150 days after the due date fixed for repayment. The auditor is preparing the statement on CARO clause (iii)(d). Which of the following is the correct treatment?
options: Both amounts are reported, since sub-clause (d) covers every overdue amount appearing in the company's books.
The ₹40 crore alone is reported, sub-clause (d) concerning the repayment obligations of the auditee company itself.

The ₹3 crore overdue from the customer is reported, with the total amount overdue for more than 90 days and whether reasonable steps have been taken by Suryan for its recovery; the default to the banking consortium is outside clause (iii), which deals with loans and advances granted by the company.
Neither amount is reported, sub-clause (d) operating only where the borrower is a subsidiary, joint venture or associate of the company.
Both amounts are reported, but the bank default is quantified at the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date and the customer default at the amount overdue.
questions.explanation: Clause (iii) is directed at the company in the capacity of lender: its introductory words ask whether the company has granted loans or advances or provided guarantees or security, and sub-clause (d) then asks for the amount overdue for more than 90 days and whether reasonable steps have been taken by the company for recovery, language capable only of recovery from a borrower. The ₹3 crore which the customer has kept unpaid for 150 days therefore falls squarely within sub-clause (d), while the company's own failure to pay its banks is a default in repayment by the company and cannot be squeezed into a clause about loans given by it. The two positions which report both amounts — one on the footing that sub-clause (d) covers every overdue amount appearing in the company's books, the other quantifying the bank default at the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date and the customer default at the amount overdue — blur that direction of flow. Reporting the ₹40 crore alone, on the footing that sub-clause (d) concerns the repayment obligations of the auditee company itself, reverses it. Reporting neither amount, because sub-clause (d) is said to operate only where the borrower is a subsidiary, joint venture or associate of the company, invents a class-of-borrower restriction the sub-clause does not contain.

questions.question: The auditor of Ajay & Kumar Engineering Limited finds that a loan of ₹7 crore granted to a customer in FY 2023-24 carries interest at 4 per cent per annum against a market rate of 11 per cent, that repayment of principal stands deferred for five years, and that no security has been taken; the borrower has nevertheless paid every instalment as it fell due. Under which limb of CARO clause (iii) does this arrangement call for comment, and why?
options: Sub-clause (c), because the deferral of principal for five years means that no schedule of repayment has in truth been stipulated.

Sub-clause (b), because that sub-clause asks whether the terms and conditions of the grant of all loans and advances are not prejudicial to the company's interest, and a below-market rate with long deferral and no security goes to those terms.
Sub-clause (d), because a loan whose principal is deferred is an amount overdue for more than 90 days.
Sub-clause (f), because a loan whose principal is deferred for five years is a loan granted without any specified period of repayment.
Sub-clause (a), because a loan without security is reportable only in the 'other parties' column.
questions.explanation: Sub-clause (b) is the limb which looks at the bargain itself rather than at conduct after the due date, and it reaches investments made, guarantees provided and the terms and conditions of the grant of all loans and advances. On these facts a schedule was stipulated and has been honoured, so sub-clause (c) is answered affirmatively and the rate, the deferral and the absence of security are not its concern; nothing is overdue, so sub-clause (d) is not reached; and sub-clause (f) speaks of loans repayable on demand or granted without any specified terms or period of repayment, whereas here a five-year period has been specified, however commercially unattractive it may be. The decisive fact is that the complaint is about the terms on which the money was lent, which is the question sub-clause (b) puts.

questions.question:
Match each situation in Column I with the sub-clause of CARO clause (iii) which it principally engages, shown in Column II.
Column I
(i) A loan granted to a limited liability partnership which is repayable at the lender's call and for which no due date has been fixed
(ii) A loan which became repayable in October is replaced in November by a new loan to the same borrower
(iii) A borrower has paid nothing for four months despite two legal notices
(iv) The company has furnished a guarantee for money borrowed by its associate
(v) The company has advanced money to a partnership firm with no interest and no date fixed for the return of principal
Column II
(A) Sub-clause (a) - aggregate amount and balance outstanding at the balance sheet date, for subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates
(B) Sub-clause (c) - no schedule of principal repayment and of payment of interest stipulated
(C) Sub-clause (d) - total amount overdue for more than 90 days and whether reasonable steps have been taken for recovery
(D) Sub-clause (e) - aggregate amount of dues renewed or extended or settled by fresh loans and its percentage to total loans or advances
(E) Sub-clause (f) - loans repayable on demand, with aggregate amount, percentage to total loans granted and amounts granted to promoters and related parties
Which of the following pairings is correct?
questions.explanation: Situation (i) is a loan repayable on demand and so attracts sub-clause (f) with its three disclosures, while situation (v) is an advance to a firm for which neither a principal repayment schedule nor an interest payment schedule has been stipulated, which is the inquiry made by sub-clause (c). Situation (ii) is the classic sub-clause (e) fact, a matured loan being met out of a fresh loan to the same borrower, and situation (iii) is sub-clause (d), four months being more than 90 days and the two legal notices going to whether reasonable steps have been taken for recovery. Situation (iv) is quantified by sub-clause (a), which alone classifies loans, advances, guarantees and security between subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates on one side and other parties on the other. The pairing '(i)-(B), (ii)-(D), (iii)-(C), (iv)-(A), (v)-(E)' exchanges sub-clause (f) with sub-clause (c), and the pairing '(i)-(E), (ii)-(D), (iii)-(B), (iv)-(A), (v)-(C)' likewise loses sub-clause (c) from the advance for which no schedule has been stipulated; both are the likeliest errors, because sub-clause (f) and sub-clause (c) each speak of missing terms but only one of them concerns a loan made repayable on demand.

questions.category: CARO - Clause (iii) and Clause (iv) Integration - Case
questions.question:
Bharat Vallabhh Limited ('BVL'), a public company, has borrowings of ₹120 crore from a consortium of banks. During FY 2024-25 the following facts emerged:
Fact 1 - BVL granted a loan of ₹4 crore to a director for the purchase of a residence; the loan has a stipulated schedule of repayment which the director has been honouring, and the management itself recorded that the conditions subject to which the Companies Act permits such a loan had not been satisfied.
Fact 2 - BVL invested ₹25 crore in debentures issued by an unrelated private limited company; its board note records that the aggregate of investments, loans, guarantees and security exceeded the limits laid down by section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013 and that the necessary approval was not obtained.
Fact 3 - BVL provided security by mortgage of its warehouse for a loan availed by its joint venture, the balance outstanding under that guarantee and security at 31 March 2025 being ₹18 crore.
Fact 4 - BVL accepted ₹10 crore from investors during the year, part of which its compliance register records as having been accepted in contravention of the directives issued by the Reserve Bank of India and of sections 73 to 76 of the Companies Act, 2013. The National Company Law Tribunal has passed an order directing repayment of ₹2 crore and BVL has complied with it.
Fact 5 - BVL is not one of the classes of company for which the Central Government has specified the maintenance of cost records under section 148 of the Companies Act, 2013.
Which one of the following correctly identifies the reporting consequences of Facts 1 and 2?
options: Fact 1 is reported only under clause (iii), clause (iv) being confined to investments and security; Fact 2 is reported only under clause (iv).
Fact 1 attracts clause (iii) alone, while Fact 2 attracts clause (iii)(b) alone, section 186 having no place in clause (iv).

Both facts are reported once only, under clause (iv), because a statement of the statutory position under sections 185 and 186 leaves nothing further to be said about the same transactions under clause (iii).

Facts 1 and 2 are reported under clause (iv), and because the loan and the investment also fall within the introductory condition of clause (iii), the sub-clauses of clause (iii) have to be worked out for them.
Neither fact is reported under clause (iv), that clause operating only where the loan or investment is made in the name of a subsidiary or associate.
questions.explanation: Clause (iv) asks, in respect of loans, investments, guarantees and security, whether the provisions of sections 185 and 186 have been complied with, and where they have not, requires details to be provided; on these facts the company's own records establish non-compliance for both the director's loan and the debenture investment, so both must be detailed. Clause (iii) is not displaced by that report, because its introductory condition is satisfied the moment the company has during the year granted a loan or made an investment, so sub-clauses (a) to (f) still apply to the ₹4 crore and the ₹25 crore so far as each is relevant. The two clauses ask different questions, one about statutory limits and one about prejudice, terms, schedules, arrears, renewals and demand loans, and the alternatives all fail by supposing that answering one of them disposes of the other.

questions.question:
Bharat Vallabhh Limited ('BVL'), a public company, has borrowings of ₹120 crore from a consortium of banks. During FY 2024-25 the following facts emerged:
Fact 1 - BVL granted a loan of ₹4 crore to a director for the purchase of a residence; the loan has a stipulated schedule of repayment which the director has been honouring, and the management itself recorded that the conditions subject to which the Companies Act permits such a loan had not been satisfied.
Fact 2 - BVL invested ₹25 crore in debentures issued by an unrelated private limited company; its board note records that the aggregate of investments, loans, guarantees and security exceeded the limits laid down by section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013 and that the necessary approval was not obtained.
Fact 3 - BVL provided security by mortgage of its warehouse for a loan availed by its joint venture, the balance outstanding under that guarantee and security at 31 March 2025 being ₹18 crore.
Fact 4 - BVL accepted ₹10 crore from investors during the year, part of which its compliance register records as having been accepted in contravention of the directives issued by the Reserve Bank of India and of sections 73 to 76 of the Companies Act, 2013. The National Company Law Tribunal has passed an order directing repayment of ₹2 crore and BVL has complied with it.
Fact 5 - BVL is not one of the classes of company for which the Central Government has specified the maintenance of cost records under section 148 of the Companies Act, 2013.
Based on the above case, which of the following statements are correct?
1. Clause (iv) requires the auditor to state whether sections 185 and 186 have been complied with in respect of loans, investments, guarantees and security, and to give details where they have not.
2. The mortgage given for the joint venture in Fact 3 must be quantified under clause (iii)(a) both as an aggregate amount and as a balance outstanding at the balance sheet date, under the head of subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates.
3. Clause (v) requires the nature of the contraventions relating to deposits and amounts deemed to be deposits to be stated and, separately, whether the order of the Tribunal has been complied with.
4. Because the director is servicing the loan as scheduled, sub-clause (c) of clause (iii) disposes of Fact 1 and clause (iv) need not be touched.
5. Clause (vi) requires the auditor to report that cost records, though not specified under section 148 for BVL, should nevertheless have been made and maintained.
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
2, 3 and 5 only
1, 3, 4 and 5 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 read correctly from the order: clause (iv) is a compliance clause with details in case of default, sub-clause (a) of clause (iii) prescribes both the aggregate amount and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date and classifies guarantees and security given for a joint venture under that head, and clause (v) contains two independent limbs, the compliance of the RBI directives and sections 73 to 76 with the nature of any contravention stated, and the separate question whether an order of the Company Law Board, the National Company Law Tribunal, the Reserve Bank, any court or other tribunal has been complied with. Statement 4 fails because regular repayment answers sub-clause (c) alone and leaves untouched the section 185 question which clause (iv) puts. Statement 5 fails because clause (vi) asks first whether maintenance of cost records has been specified by the Central Government under section 148, and where it has not, the second question of records having been so made and maintained does not arise.

questions.question:
Bharat Vallabhh Limited ('BVL'), a public company, has borrowings of ₹120 crore from a consortium of banks. During FY 2024-25 the following facts emerged:
Fact 1 - BVL granted a loan of ₹4 crore to a director for the purchase of a residence; the loan has a stipulated schedule of repayment which the director has been honouring, and the management itself recorded that the conditions subject to which the Companies Act permits such a loan had not been satisfied.
Fact 2 - BVL invested ₹25 crore in debentures issued by an unrelated private limited company; its board note records that the aggregate of investments, loans, guarantees and security exceeded the limits laid down by section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013 and that the necessary approval was not obtained.
Fact 3 - BVL provided security by mortgage of its warehouse for a loan availed by its joint venture, the balance outstanding under that guarantee and security at 31 March 2025 being ₹18 crore.
Fact 4 - BVL accepted ₹10 crore from investors during the year, part of which its compliance register records as having been accepted in contravention of the directives issued by the Reserve Bank of India and of sections 73 to 76 of the Companies Act, 2013. The National Company Law Tribunal has passed an order directing repayment of ₹2 crore and BVL has complied with it.
Fact 5 - BVL is not one of the classes of company for which the Central Government has specified the maintenance of cost records under section 148 of the Companies Act, 2013.
Which of the following actions should the auditor of BVL take?
options: Set out in the report the details of the loan to the director and of the investment in debentures, clause (iv) requiring details where sections 185 and 186 have not been complied with; consider under clause (iii)(b) whether the investment, the security provided for the joint venture and the terms of the director's loan are not prejudicial to BVL's interest; rely on the fact that the Tribunal's order has been complied with and for that reason omit the contraventions relating to the deposits accepted; state under clause (iii)(a) the aggregate amount and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date of the guarantee and security given for the joint venture.

Set out the details required by clause (iv); omit the contraventions relating to deposits because the Tribunal's order has been complied with; and treat the management's own records of non-compliance as irrelevant unless the auditor independently establishes breach of sections 185 and 186.

Consider clause (iii)(b) on prejudice only, report the joint venture security under clause (iii)(a) alone, and leave the deposit position to be dealt with in the Board's report rather than in the auditor's statement.

Set out the details required by clause (iv); consider clause (iii)(b) on the investment, the security and the director's loan; state the aggregate amount and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date of the joint venture security under clause (iii)(a); and report separately, under clause (v), both the nature of the contraventions and the fact that the Tribunal's order has been complied with.

Report the whole of the ₹10 crore as a contravention under clause (v), report the director's loan under clause (iii)(f) as a demand loan, and make no remark under clause (iv) because the loan was serviced regularly.
questions.explanation: Clause (v) keeps its two limbs apart, so compliance with an order passed by the Tribunal does not remove the need to state the nature of the contraventions of the RBI directives and of sections 73 to 76, which makes the omission proposed in the first two alternatives wrong. The management's own board note and compliance register are audit evidence which the auditor must deal with, and clause (iv) requires details of non-compliance to be provided rather than only of non-compliance he has independently discovered. The correct course is therefore to detail the section 185 and 186 position, to test clause (iii)(b) for the investment, the security and the terms of the director's loan, to quantify the joint venture security under clause (iii)(a), and to report under clause (v) both the contraventions and the compliance with the Tribunal's order. The loan to the director carries a stipulated schedule, so clause (iii)(f) is not attracted.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on CARO clause (iv):
1. It applies to loans, investments, guarantees and security.
2. It requires the auditor to state whether the provisions of sections 185 and 186 of the Companies Act, 2013 have been complied with, and to furnish details where they have not.
3. It is discharged by the same conclusion which answers clause (iii)(b), both turning on whether the transaction is prejudicial to the company's interest.
4. It ceases to operate in respect of a loan which has already been reported in detail under clause (iii).
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
1 and 2 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Clause (iv) is short and self-contained: in respect of loans, investments, guarantees and security the auditor states whether sections 185 and 186 have been complied with and, if not, provides details, so statements 1 and 2 are right and statement 4 is wrong, since the clauses operate on different aspects of the same transaction and a loan may appear both in the clause (iii) disclosures and in the clause (iv) details. Statement 3 confuses a compliance question with a commercial one: clause (iii)(b) asks whether the terms and conditions are not prejudicial to the company's interest, so a transaction can be commercially sound yet breach section 185 or 186, and another can be prejudicial while remaining within the statutory limits. The decisive point is that clause (iv) tests legality and clause (iii)(b) tests the bargain, and neither answers the other.

questions.category: CARO - Clause (v) Deposits - Sequence of Inquiry
questions.question:
An auditor is completing the statement on CARO clause (v) for a company which has accepted amounts from investors during the year. Arrange the following steps in the order in which the clause itself structures the inquiry:
P. Determine whether the directives issued by the Reserve Bank of India and the provisions of sections 73 to 76 of the Companies Act, 2013 have been complied with.
Q. Determine whether the amounts are deposits accepted by the company or amounts which are deemed to be deposits.
R. Determine whether an order has been passed by the Company Law Board or the National Company Law Tribunal or the Reserve Bank of India or any court or other tribunal, and whether the same has been complied with.
S. Where there has been no compliance, state the nature of such contraventions.
T. Verify whether a schedule of repayment has been stipulated for the amounts accepted and whether repayments are regular.
Which of the following sequences is correct?
options: P, Q, S, R
Q, P, R, S
T, Q, P, S
Q, P, S, R
Q, T, P, S
questions.explanation: Clause (v) begins by fixing its subject matter, namely deposits accepted by the company or amounts which are deemed to be deposits, so step Q must come first. It then asks whether the RBI directives and the provisions of sections 73 to 76 have been complied with and, where they have not, directs that the nature of such contraventions be stated, so P precedes S. Its closing words add the independent inquiry whether an order passed by the Company Law Board, the National Company Law Tribunal, the Reserve Bank of India, any court or any other tribunal has been complied with, which is step R and follows the contravention limb. Step T belongs to clause (iii), which governs loans and advances granted by the company, and has no place in a sequence about moneys received, so the two options which insert T are ruled out and the remaining option inverts the identification of the amount and the compliance test.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on CARO clause (v):
1. The clause covers deposits accepted by the company as well as amounts which are deemed to be deposits.
2. The auditor must report whether the directives issued by the Reserve Bank of India and the provisions of sections 73 to 76 of the Companies Act, 2013 have been complied with, and state the nature of any contravention.
3. Where an order has been passed by the Company Law Board, the National Company Law Tribunal, the Reserve Bank of India, any court or any other tribunal, the auditor's statement is confined to whether that order has been complied with and the contraventions cease to be reported.
4. The clause is attracted only where the amount received satisfies the definition of deposit, amounts deemed to be deposits being outside it.
Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
options: 3 only
3 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are faithful to the clause, which names both deposits accepted and amounts which are deemed to be deposits, and both the directives issued by the Reserve Bank of India and sections 73 to 76, with the nature of the contravention to be stated. Statement 3 is not correct because the order limb is additive rather than substitutional: the clause asks whether such an order has been complied with or not in addition to the compliance question already put, so compliance with a Tribunal's order cannot erase the reporting of a contravention. Statement 4 is not correct for the mirror reason, since the words 'or amounts which are deemed to be deposits' extend the clause to receipts which the statute treats as deposits even though they would not answer the description on their own, which is precisely why statement 1 is right and statement 4 wrong.

questions.question: Madhur Spinners Limited accepted ₹18 crore during FY 2024-25 from investors, which its board classified as refundable deposits and which the auditor concludes also fall within the amounts which are deemed to be deposits. The company's compliance register shows that the amount raised exceeded the permissible ceiling, that the required charge on the company's assets was not created, and that the relevant directive issued by the Reserve Bank of India was not observed. On 4 March 2025 the National Company Law Tribunal Bench directed the company to refund ₹6 crore within 30 days, and the company refunded ₹6 crore on 20 March 2025. What should the auditor state under CARO clause (v)?
options: Since the Tribunal's order was complied with within time, the auditor reports compliance and does not report the earlier contraventions.

The auditor reports that the directives issued by the Reserve Bank of India and sections 73 to 76 have not been complied with, states the nature of such contraventions, and separately states that the order of the Tribunal has been complied with.
The auditor reports only on the amounts which satisfy the definition of deposit, the amounts deemed to be deposits being outside clause (v).
The auditor reports the contraventions only if the amount involved is ₹1 crore or more.
The auditor reports the breach of the ceiling but not the absence of a charge or the non-observance of the directive, clause (v) being confined to the provisions of the Companies Act.
questions.explanation: Clause (v) has two limbs which operate independently. The first requires a statement whether the directives issued by the Reserve Bank of India and the provisions of sections 73 to 76 have been complied with in respect of deposits accepted or amounts deemed to be deposits, and where they have not, the nature of the contraventions must be stated, so the ceiling breach, the missing charge and the ignored directive each call for description; that the receipts also fall within the description of deemed deposits is no reason to exclude them, since the clause names them expressly. The second limb asks whether an order passed by the Company Law Board, the National Company Law Tribunal, the Reserve Bank, any court or other tribunal has been complied with, and the timely refund of ₹6 crore is properly reported as compliance with it. The report of compliance and nothing further, because the Tribunal's order was complied with within time, collapses the two limbs; the restriction to amounts which satisfy the definition of deposit, those deemed to be deposits being said to be outside clause (v), reads out the deemed-deposit words; the condition that contraventions be reported only if the amount involved is ₹1 crore or more imports a monetary threshold the clause does not contain; and the report of the ceiling breach without the absence of a charge or the non-observance of the directive, treating clause (v) as confined to the provisions of the Companies Act, wrongly narrows the first limb to the Act alone.

questions.category: CARO - Clause (v) Deposits - Compliance with Orders
questions.question: Kolhapur Steels Limited had accepted deposits in breach of the directives issued by the Reserve Bank of India, and the Company Law Board had earlier passed an order directing repayment of ₹5 crore which the company had not implemented, a matter remarked upon in the auditors' report for FY 2023-24. Suppose that in FY 2024-25 the company has complied fully with the RBI directives and with sections 73 to 76, but the order of the Company Law Board for ₹5 crore remains unimplemented and no fresh deposit has been accepted. What does clause (v) require in the current year's report?
options: Nothing, because clause (v) is engaged only where there is a contravention of the Act or of the directives.
A statement of the contravention alone, the order of the Company Law Board being reportable only if it was passed during the year under audit.
A statement that the directives and sections 73 to 76 have been complied with and, separately, a statement that the order passed by the Company Law Board has not been complied with.
A statement only that the order has not been complied with, the two limbs of the clause being alternatives.
A remark that the order has become infructuous, the company having no outstanding deposit liabilities of the relevant kind.
questions.explanation: The first limb of clause (v) is a positive statement which the auditor must make whether the answer is affirmative or negative, so the year's position of full compliance with the RBI directives and with sections 73 to 76 is itself reported. The second limb asks whether an order passed by the Company Law Board, the National Company Law Tribunal, the Reserve Bank, any court or other tribunal has been complied with, and it is not confined to orders passed during the year under audit, an earlier order continuing to be a live matter so long as it stands unsatisfied. The two limbs are cumulative rather than either-or, which disposes of the views that nothing is reported in the absence of a contravention, that the contravention alone is reportable because the order pre-dates the year under audit, and that the order alone is reportable; and the decisive fact is that the order remains unimplemented even though the deposit-taking itself has become regular.

questions.question: Gojal Sugar Limited manufactures sugar, a line of business for which the Central Government has specified under section 148 of the Companies Act, 2013 the maintenance of cost records. The company kept the specified records up to 30 September 2024 and thereafter discontinued them, and its cost auditor has separately reported deficiencies in the records for the earlier period. What is the statutory auditor's reporting under CARO clause (vi)?
options: Clause (vi) is satisfied once the cost audit has been completed and its report received, the cost auditor's report being the vehicle for any adverse remark.
Cost records are maintained for the purposes of cost audit and not for financial audit, so the statutory auditor reports nothing under clause (vi) whatever the position.
Clause (vi) requires the statutory auditor to certify the correctness of the costs compiled, which he cannot do on the material available, so he disclaims on the point.

Clause (vi) asks whether the maintenance of cost records has been specified by the Central Government under section 148 and whether such records have been so made and maintained; the first answer is affirmative and the second is not, so the report must record that the records were not made and maintained for part of the year.
Clause (vi) requires the auditor to state that cost records have been maintained, since the company did maintain them for six months of the year.
questions.explanation: Clause (vi) puts two questions in sequence: whether maintenance of cost records has been specified by the Central Government under section 148, and whether such records have been so made and maintained. Once the specification for sugar manufacturers exists, the second question is squarely raised, so the view that cost records are maintained for the purposes of cost audit and not for financial audit, and that the statutory auditor reports nothing under clause (vi) whatever the position, cannot stand; and discontinuation from 30 September 2024 means that the records were not made and maintained for the whole of the year, which is the remark to be carried. The clause demands nothing more: the contention that it is satisfied once the cost audit has been completed and its report received, that report being the vehicle for any adverse remark, would transfer the cost auditor's findings to the statutory auditor's report, and the demand that the statutory auditor certify the correctness of the costs compiled, disclaiming on the point for want of material, asks for an opinion the clause does not call for, so the existence of the cost auditor's separate report is not the decisive fact. And the statement that cost records have been maintained, since the company did maintain them for six months of the year, is the trap of treating partial compliance as compliance, whereas the second limb is not satisfied by maintenance for part of the year.

questions.question: Tritra Services Limited, a company providing software services, made no investment and gave no guarantee or security during FY 2024-25. It advanced ₹40 lakh to an employee towards the purchase of a house, carrying interest at the rate applicable to staff loans, to be recovered in forty equal monthly instalments of salary, a schedule of principal repayment and of payment of interest having been stipulated and the instalments having been regularly deducted. The Central Government has not specified the maintenance of cost records for the company's activity. How should the auditor deal with clauses (iii) and (vi) of CARO?
options: Clause (iii) is not attracted at all, the company having made no investment and given no guarantee or security, and clause (vi) calls for no remark because cost records have not been specified.

Clause (iii) is attracted and its relevant sub-clauses must be worked out, while clause (vi) requires the auditor to state that cost records ought to have been made and maintained even though the Central Government has not specified them under section 148.

Clause (iii) is attracted because a loan or advance in the nature of a loan was granted during the year, so the classification required by sub-clause (a) and the repayment test under sub-clause (c) have to be reported, and clause (vi) is answered on its first question in the negative, the second question not arising.
Both clauses require a remark of non-compliance, the advance to the employee being a loan granted without a stipulated schedule and cost records having been specified but not maintained.
Clause (iii) is attracted only if the advance is repaid by the employee in cash rather than by deduction from salary, and clause (vi) is not attracted.
questions.explanation: The introductory condition of clause (iii) is satisfied by any one of three things, an investment made, a guarantee or security provided, or a loan or advance in the nature of a loan granted, the last being capable of being granted to companies, firms, LLP or any other parties, and a housing advance recovered in fixed monthly instalments with a stipulated schedule is an advance in the nature of a loan. Once the gate is open the relevant sub-clauses operate, sub-clause (a) calling for the aggregate amount and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date and sub-clause (c) calling for a statement whether a schedule of principal repayment and of payment of interest has been stipulated and whether repayments are regular, both of which are satisfied on these facts. Clause (vi) is structured as two questions and where the Central Government has not specified maintenance of cost records under section 148 the second question does not arise. The statements that clause (vi) requires a remark that cost records ought to have been made and maintained even though the Central Government has not specified them under section 148, and that both clauses require a remark of non-compliance because cost records were specified but not maintained, misstate clause (vi); while the contentions that clause (iii) is not attracted at all because no investment was made and no guarantee or security given, and that it is attracted only if the advance is repaid by the employee in cash rather than by deduction from salary, misstate clause (iii).

options: Sub-clause (e): ₹12 crore and 12.6 per cent; sub-clause (f): ₹15 crore and 25 per cent.
Sub-clause (e): ₹12 crore and 20 per cent; sub-clause (f): ₹21 crore, 35 per cent of total loans granted, with ₹4 crore granted to promoters and ₹2 crore to related parties.
Sub-clause (e): ₹9 crore and 15 per cent; sub-clause (f): ₹21 crore and 22.1 per cent.
Sub-clause (e): ₹12 crore and 20 per cent; sub-clause (f): ₹21 crore and 35 per cent, the amounts granted to promoters and related parties being required only where the loan is secured.
Sub-clause (e): ₹3 crore and 5 per cent; sub-clause (f): ₹6 crore and 10 per cent, extensions not being renewals within the meaning of the clause.
questions.explanation: Sub-clause (e) takes in every loan or advance which has fallen due during the year and has been renewed or extended or settled by fresh loans, so the ₹9 crore extended and the ₹3 crore settled by fresh loans aggregate ₹12 crore, being 20 per cent of the ₹60 crore of total loans or advances. Sub-clause (f) covers loans and advances repayable on demand or granted without specifying any terms or period of repayment, so the ₹15 crore and the ₹6 crore aggregate ₹21 crore, being 35 per cent of total loans granted, and the clause then separately requires the ₹4 crore granted to promoters and the ₹2 crore granted to related parties. The figures of ₹12 crore and 12.6 per cent for sub-clause (e) with ₹15 crore and 25 per cent for sub-clause (f) measure the 12.6 per cent against the ₹95 crore outstanding balance and narrow sub-clause (f) to demand loans; those of ₹9 crore and 15 per cent for sub-clause (e) with ₹21 crore and 22.1 per cent for sub-clause (f) both restrict sub-clause (e) to settled loans and use the closing balance as the denominator. The report of sub-clause (f) at ₹21 crore and 35 per cent which requires the promoter and related-party amounts only where the loan is secured invents a secured-loan restriction, and the sub-clause (e) figure of ₹3 crore and 5 per cent with sub-clause (f) at ₹6 crore and 10 per cent wrongly supposes that an extension is outside sub-clause (e), the clause naming renewal, extension and settlement by fresh loans together.

questions.question:
Varun Chemicals Limited granted loans and advances aggregating ₹60 crore during FY 2024-25 and had loan and advance balances of ₹95 crore outstanding at 31 March 2025. During the year:
(a) loans of ₹9 crore which had fallen due were extended by six months, and loans of ₹3 crore which had fallen due were settled by fresh loans to the same borrowers;
(b) loans and advances of ₹15 crore were granted repayable on demand;
(c) loans and advances of ₹6 crore were granted without specifying any terms or period of repayment, of which ₹4 crore was granted to promoters and ₹2 crore to related parties as defined in the Companies Act, 2013.
The amounts in (a), (b) and (c) are included in the ₹60 crore granted during the year, and no amount was overdue for more than 90 days on the date of the auditor's report.
Based on the above case, which of the following statements are correct?
1. Sub-clause (a) calls for the aggregate amount as well as the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date of loans or advances and of guarantees or security, classified between subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates on one side and other parties on the other.
2. The ₹95 crore outstanding at 31 March 2025 is the figure prescribed by sub-clause (f) as the denominator for the percentage of demand loans.
3. Sub-clause (e) reaches both the extension of a loan which had fallen due and the settlement of such a loan by a fresh loan.
4. Sub-clause (f) requires the aggregate amount of loans granted to promoters and to related parties as defined in the Companies Act, 2013 to be specified.
options: 1 and 2 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2 and 4 only
3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Sub-clause (a) prescribes two figures, the aggregate amount and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date, together with a two-fold classification of recipients, which is statement 1. Sub-clause (f) expresses its percentage with reference to total loans granted, which on these facts is the ₹60 crore advanced during the year and not the ₹95 crore carried at the year end, so statement 2 misstates the denominator. Statement 3 is right because the words of sub-clause (e) are renewed or extended or settled by fresh loans, so the ₹9 crore of extensions is as reportable as the ₹3 crore met out of fresh loans. Statement 4 is the further disclosure which sub-clause (f) requires once demand loans or loans without specified terms exist, and it is the element most often omitted in practice.

questions.question:
The auditor of Kamdhenu Traders Limited examines four loans and advances for FY 2024-25 for the purposes of CARO clause (iii)(c):
Loan W - a schedule of principal repayment was stipulated but no schedule of payment of interest, and the principal instalments have been received as they fell due.
Loan X - schedules of principal repayment and of payment of interest were stipulated, but two interest instalments have not been paid.
Loan Y - a complete schedule of principal repayment and of payment of interest was stipulated and every instalment has been paid on or before its due date.
Loan Z - no schedule was stipulated at all and the amount is repayable on demand.
Which of the following identifies the loans which are NOT in conformity with sub-clause (c)?
options: X and Z only
W, X, Y and Z
X and Y only
Y and Z only
W, X and Z only
questions.explanation: Sub-clause (c) makes a double requirement, namely whether a schedule of principal repayment and of payment of interest has been stipulated and whether repayments are regular. Loan W fails the first half, because interest has been left out of the schedule however regularly principal has been paid; Loan X fails the second half, because two interest instalments remain unpaid in spite of a complete schedule; Loan Z fails because nothing at all was stipulated, and the fact that it is also a demand loan reported under sub-clause (f) does not excuse sub-clause (c). Loan Y alone satisfies both halves, so each of 'W, X, Y and Z', 'X and Y only' and 'Y and Z only', which includes Y, is wrong. And 'X and Z only' falls into the trap of reading sub-clause (c) as concerned only with actual default, which is the subject of sub-clause (d), and of ignoring the requirement that a schedule be stipulated at all.

questions.category: CARO - Clause (iii) Sub-clause (d) - Scope of the Auditor's Duty
questions.question: Sudama Polymers Limited lent ₹6 crore to a customer, and ₹3 crore of that amount has been outstanding for 200 days beyond the due date. The company issued a demand notice and filed one suit for recovery, and the auditor is satisfied that these are reasonable steps; he is not, however, satisfied that the balance is recoverable, and no provision has been made against it. Management proposes that the CARO statement should say merely that reasonable steps have been taken. Which of the following is the most appropriate view?
options: The auditor must go further and certify that the steps taken will result in recovery, and must qualify the financial statements for the absence of a provision.

The auditor states the total amount overdue for more than 90 days, namely ₹3 crore, and reports whether reasonable steps have been taken by the company for recovery, the clause not requiring him to opine on the success of those steps or on the adequacy of any provision.
The auditor reports only the amount overdue, the question of recovery steps being one for the Board's report and not for the auditor.
Sub-clause (d) is attracted only where the overdue borrower is a company, firm or LLP, and not where the borrower is a customer of the company.
The auditor accepts management's proposal, since sub-clause (d) requires only an assessment of the recovery steps and not the quantification of the overdue amount.
questions.explanation: Sub-clause (d) asks for two matters and no more: the total amount overdue for more than 90 days, and whether reasonable steps have been taken by the company for recovery. ₹3 crore has been overdue for 200 days and is therefore the amount to be stated, and since the demand notice and the suit are reasonable steps the auditor reports that they have been taken, without warranting that they will succeed or extending the clause to realisability and provisioning on which the sub-clause asks nothing. Management's proposal is defective for a different reason, because it drops the primary requirement, namely the quantification of ₹3 crore. The clause is not restricted by the class of borrower, the introductory words of clause (iii) covering loans and advances granted to companies, firms, LLP or any other parties, which disposes of the view that sub-clause (d) is attracted only where the overdue borrower is a company, firm or LLP and not where the borrower is a customer of the company. The demand that the auditor certify that the steps taken will result in recovery and qualify the financial statements for the absence of a provision, the report of the amount overdue alone with recovery steps left to the Board's report, and the acceptance of management's proposal on the footing that only an assessment of the recovery steps and not the quantification of the overdue amount is required, each either adds a duty the clause does not impose or removes one it does.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about clause (vii) of CARO, 2020:
1. The auditor has to report whether the company is regular in depositing undisputed statutory dues, including GST, provident fund, employees' state insurance, income-tax, sales-tax, service tax, customs duty, excise duty, VAT, cess and any other statutory dues, with the appropriate authorities.
2. Where the company is not so regular, the arrears to be indicated are the statutory dues outstanding as on the first day of the financial year for more than six months from the date on which the demand was raised.
3. Because clause (vii)(a) names the dues, a statutory due not appearing in that list is outside the clause unless separately notified.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
questions.explanation: Statement 1 reproduces the requirement of clause (vii)(a) correctly, including the reference to undisputed dues and to deposit with the appropriate authorities. Statement 2 is wrong twice over: the arrears are those outstanding as on the last day of the financial year concerned, and the period of more than six months runs from the due date of the dues, not from the date of the demand. Statement 3 misreads the enumeration, which is introduced by the word 'including' and closed by the words 'and any other statutory dues', so it is illustrative and residual rather than exhaustive. Only statement 1 survives, and the answer is therefore '1 only'.

questions.question:
A customs duty demand of ₹ 1.10 crore against Rane Bearings Ltd became payable by 10.08.2023 and was wholly unpaid on 31.03.2024, the last day of the financial year under audit. The company had filed only an unacknowledged informal written representation with the range officer, without any appeal and without any stay.
What changes if, instead of that representation, the company had preferred a statutory first appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) and obtained a stay of the demand, so that no deposit was called for?
options: In the first situation the amount is indicated as arrears of undisputed dues under clause (vii)(a); in the second it moves out of that clause and is reported under clause (vii)(b) with the amount involved and the forum where the dispute is pending.

In both situations the amount goes to clause (vii)(b) with the forum named, because the company has contested the demand before the department in one form or another, and clause (vii)(a) is confined to dues which have actually been deposited.

Under the second situation nothing is reportable at all, because a demand which stands stayed is neither an arrear nor an undisputed due outstanding on the last day of the financial year, and no forum arises for disclosure.

Nothing changes in either situation, because in each the dues have remained unpaid for well beyond six months from the due date as on the last day of the financial year, so the whole ₹ 1.10 crore is indicated as arrears under clause (vii)(a).
questions.explanation: Clause (vii)(a) requires arrears of outstanding statutory dues, being undisputed dues unpaid as on the last day of the financial year for more than six months from the due date, to be indicated; the customs demand was unpaid for about seven and a half months at 31.03.2024 and therefore satisfies both conditions. A mere representation to the concerned department is expressly not to be treated as a dispute, so the informal representation leaves the amount in the undisputed stream under clause (vii)(a). A first appeal with stay makes the non-deposit one 'because of a dispute', so the amount moves to clause (vii)(b), where the amounts involved and the forum where the dispute is pending have to be mentioned. Clause (vii)(a) is not confined to dues already deposited, and a disputed but unpaid amount is still reportable, so the remaining options fail.

questions.question:
Case study: Vidula Steels Ltd., for FY 2023-24, is a company to which CARO, 2020 applies. The auditor ascertained the following:
(1) Provident fund contributions of ₹ 42 lakh for the quarter ended 30.06.2023, due on 15.07.2023, were deposited only on 26.09.2023, and ₹ 38 lakh for the quarter ended 30.09.2023, due on 15.10.2023, remained unpaid on 31.03.2024.
(2) GST of ₹ 1.90 crore for September 2023, due on 20.10.2023, was paid on 28.02.2024, without any demand or dispute.
(3) An undisputed customs duty demand of ₹ 1.10 crore, payable by 10.08.2023, was still unpaid on 31.03.2024. The company had filed only an informal written representation with the range officer, which was neither acknowledged as an appeal nor supported by any stay.
(4) An income-tax demand of ₹ 5.60 crore arising from an assessment completed in FY 2021-22 is pending in first appeal before the Commissioner (Income-tax) (Appeals), and is not deposited.
(5) TDS of ₹ 26 lakh, deductible in October 2023 and payable by 31.10.2023, was deposited on 05.11.2023.
Management contends that nothing requires to be reported, because every amount was either deposited before the audit report is signed or is covered by a representation or an appeal.
Which of the following amounts must be indicated as arrears of outstanding statutory dues under clause (vii)(a) of CARO, 2020?
options: ₹ 38 lakh (provident fund) and ₹ 1.10 crore (customs duty) only
₹ 1.10 crore (customs duty) only
₹ 1.10 crore (customs duty), ₹ 38 lakh (provident fund) and ₹ 1.90 crore (GST)
₹ 1.10 crore (customs duty) and ₹ 5.60 crore (income-tax)
questions.explanation: Arrears are indicated only where the amount was outstanding as on the last day of the financial year and had been outstanding for more than six months from the due date. The customs duty of ₹ 1.10 crore, unpaid since 10.08.2023, meets both conditions and, an informal representation not being a dispute, remains undisputed and therefore falls in clause (vii)(a). The ₹ 38 lakh of provident fund due on 15.10.2023 was outstanding at 31.03.2024 for barely five and a half months, so it fails the six-month condition even though the company was unquestionably irregular about it. The GST of ₹ 1.90 crore was paid on 28.02.2024 and was not outstanding on the last day of the year at all, and the ₹ 5.60 crore income-tax demand is disputed and belongs to clause (vii)(b) with the forum named.

questions.question:
Case study: Vidula Steels Ltd., for FY 2023-24, is a company to which CARO, 2020 applies. The auditor ascertained the following:
(1) Provident fund contributions of ₹ 42 lakh for the quarter ended 30.06.2023, due on 15.07.2023, were deposited only on 26.09.2023, and ₹ 38 lakh for the quarter ended 30.09.2023, due on 15.10.2023, remained unpaid on 31.03.2024.
(2) GST of ₹ 1.90 crore for September 2023, due on 20.10.2023, was paid on 28.02.2024, without any demand or dispute.
(3) An undisputed customs duty demand of ₹ 1.10 crore, payable by 10.08.2023, was still unpaid on 31.03.2024. The company had filed only an informal written representation with the range officer, which was neither acknowledged as an appeal nor supported by any stay.
(4) An income-tax demand of ₹ 5.60 crore arising from an assessment completed in FY 2021-22 is pending in first appeal before the Commissioner (Income-tax) (Appeals), and is not deposited.
(5) TDS of ₹ 26 lakh, deductible in October 2023 and payable by 31.10.2023, was deposited on 05.11.2023.
Management contends that nothing requires to be reported, because every amount was either deposited before the audit report is signed or is covered by a representation or an appeal.
Which of the following statements are correct regarding the auditor's reporting under clause (vii)?
1. The answer to the first limb of clause (vii)(a) is that the company is not regular in depositing provident fund, GST and TDS, even though no arrears arise from GST and TDS.
2. The income-tax demand of ₹ 5.60 crore is reported under clause (vii)(b) with the amount involved and the forum where the appeal is pending.
3. The customs duty of ₹ 1.10 crore is reported under clause (vii)(b), because the company has made a written representation to the department.
4. The ₹ 38 lakh provident fund arrear is indicated under clause (vii)(a), because it was unpaid on the last day of the financial year.
options: 2 and 4 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
questions.explanation: Regularity in depositing is a finding about conduct during the whole year, so the 73-day delay in the June quarter provident fund, the four-month delay in GST and the five-day delay in TDS each negative the first limb even where no arrear survives at the year-end. The income-tax demand is genuinely in dispute before the Commissioner (Appeals), so clause (vii)(b) applies and the amount and the forum must be mentioned. Statement 3 fails because a mere representation to the concerned department shall not be treated as a dispute; the customs duty is undisputed and is dealt with under clause (vii)(a). Statement 4 fails because it ignores the second condition, that the arrear must have been outstanding for more than six months from the due date, and only about five and a half months had run by 31.03.2024.

questions.question:
Case study: Vidula Steels Ltd., for FY 2023-24, is a company to which CARO, 2020 applies. The auditor ascertained the following:
(1) Provident fund contributions of ₹ 42 lakh for the quarter ended 30.06.2023, due on 15.07.2023, were deposited only on 26.09.2023, and ₹ 38 lakh for the quarter ended 30.09.2023, due on 15.10.2023, remained unpaid on 31.03.2024.
(2) GST of ₹ 1.90 crore for September 2023, due on 20.10.2023, was paid on 28.02.2024, without any demand or dispute.
(3) An undisputed customs duty demand of ₹ 1.10 crore, payable by 10.08.2023, was still unpaid on 31.03.2024. The company had filed only an informal written representation with the range officer, which was neither acknowledged as an appeal nor supported by any stay.
(4) An income-tax demand of ₹ 5.60 crore arising from an assessment completed in FY 2021-22 is pending in first appeal before the Commissioner (Income-tax) (Appeals), and is not deposited.
(5) TDS of ₹ 26 lakh, deductible in October 2023 and payable by 31.10.2023, was deposited on 05.11.2023.
Management contends that nothing requires to be reported, because every amount was either deposited before the audit report is signed or is covered by a representation or an appeal.
Management's contention is to be evaluated by the auditor. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: Accept it, because clause (vii)(a) requires arrears to be reported only if they continue to remain unpaid on the date of the auditor's report.

Reject it, but confine the arrear disclosure to the provident fund, because every other amount was either deposited before the report was signed or is covered by management's written confirmation and the auditor may rely on it.
Reject it: the arrear position is fixed as on the last day of the financial year and regularity is tested across the year, so a later deposit does not neutralise either disclosure.
Accept it in part, because amounts deposited before the audit report is signed cease to be 'undisputed' dues for the purpose of the clause.
questions.explanation: The clause strikes the arrear position as on the last day of the financial year concerned and measures the qualifying period from the due date, so the customs duty and the provident fund position were frozen at 31.03.2024 and the ₹ 1.10 crore crosses both conditions irrespective of any payment made later. Regularity in depositing is a finding about the year's conduct, which the late provident fund deposits, the GST paid four months after the due date and the delayed TDS each establish in the negative. A deposit made after the year-end does not convert undisputed dues into something else, and the disputed income-tax demand must still be disclosed with the forum under clause (vii)(b). The remaining options either move the measurement date, or wrongly discard the customs and income-tax disclosures.

questions.question:
Case study: Vidula Steels Ltd., for FY 2023-24, is a company to which CARO, 2020 applies. The auditor ascertained the following:
(1) Provident fund contributions of ₹ 42 lakh for the quarter ended 30.06.2023, due on 15.07.2023, were deposited only on 26.09.2023, and ₹ 38 lakh for the quarter ended 30.09.2023, due on 15.10.2023, remained unpaid on 31.03.2024.
(2) GST of ₹ 1.90 crore for September 2023, due on 20.10.2023, was paid on 28.02.2024, without any demand or dispute.
(3) An undisputed customs duty demand of ₹ 1.10 crore, payable by 10.08.2023, was still unpaid on 31.03.2024. The company had filed only an informal written representation with the range officer, which was neither acknowledged as an appeal nor supported by any stay.
(4) An income-tax demand of ₹ 5.60 crore arising from an assessment completed in FY 2021-22 is pending in first appeal before the Commissioner (Income-tax) (Appeals), and is not deposited.
(5) TDS of ₹ 26 lakh, deductible in October 2023 and payable by 31.10.2023, was deposited on 05.11.2023.
Management contends that nothing requires to be reported, because every amount was either deposited before the audit report is signed or is covered by a representation or an appeal.
Which of the following actions should the auditor take in finalising the statement on clause (vii)?
options: Fix the outstanding position as on the date of the audit report, drop the customs duty because it is under representation, and report only the provident fund amounts as arrears.

Measure the six-month period from the due date, fix the outstanding position as on 31.03.2024, exclude the income-tax demand from the arrear figure because it is disputed, and record the forum where that dispute is pending.

Measure the six-month period from the date on which each demand was raised, include the income-tax demand up to ₹ 5.60 crore in the arrear figure, and describe the customs representation as a dispute pending before the range officer so that it too moves to clause (vii)(b).
Report only such dues as are named in clause (vii)(a), treating GST and TDS as outside the clause because they are indirect and withholding amounts, and rely on the remittance register for the rest.
questions.explanation: Clause (vii)(a) fixes two reference points which the auditor must apply together: the qualifying period of more than six months runs from the due date, and the outstanding amount is measured as on the last day of the financial year. Disputed dues are carved out of clause (vii)(a) and are separately reported under clause (vii)(b) with the amounts involved and the forum where the dispute is pending, so the income-tax demand must be kept out of the arrear figure without being dropped from the report. The enumeration of dues is inclusive, so GST and TDS are not outside the clause; the period is not measured from the date of the demand or from the report date; and a representation is not a dispute.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding clause (vii)(b) of CARO, 2020:
1. Where statutory dues have not been deposited because of any dispute, the amounts involved are to be mentioned.
2. The forum where the dispute is pending has also to be disclosed.
3. A representation made to the concerned department is sufficient to bring an unpaid statutory due within clause (vii)(b).
4. Clause (vii)(b) is confined to dues which stand quantified by an order of the appropriate authority, and cannot cover a disputed amount computed by the company itself.
Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
options: 1, 2 and 4 only
1 and 2 only
2, 3 and 4 only
3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are precisely the two disclosures the clause requires for dues not deposited because of a dispute, and both are correct. Statement 3 is contrary to the express exclusion in clause (vii)(b) that a mere representation to the concerned department shall not be treated as a dispute, so an unpaid due supported only by a representation remains arrears under clause (vii)(a). Statement 4 imports a limitation the clause does not contain: the test is whether the non-deposit is because of a dispute, not whether an authority has already quantified the demand by order. The pair which is NOT correct is therefore 3 and 4 only.

questions.question:
An auditor applies the following steps to a statutory due while reporting under clause (vii) of CARO, 2020:
P. Ascertain whether the company has been regular in depositing its undisputed statutory dues with the appropriate authorities during the year.
Q. Ascertain whether the due is disputed, that is, whether there is a dispute other than a mere representation to the department.
R. Fix the amount, if any, which remained outstanding as on the last day of the financial year.
S. Test whether that outstanding amount had been outstanding for more than six months from the due date.
T. For amounts not deposited because of a dispute, record the amount and the forum where the dispute is pending.
Which of the following represents the correct order of application?
options: P, Q, R, S, T
Q, P, S, R, T
Q, R, S, P, T
