Assume, in place of fact 2, that the ₹ 15 crore sanctioned was a term loan for warehouse construction, that ₹ 12 crore was in fact spent on that warehouse, and that the remaining ₹ 3 crore was applied to fund the working capital cycle. Which statement correctly describes the change in reporting under clause (ix)?
options: Clause (ix)(d) ceases to apply, because the funds were raised on a long-term basis and mainly used for the sanctioned long-term purpose, but clause (ix)(c) is engaged for the ₹ 3 crore applied to the working capital cycle, the diverted amount and the purpose of its use being reportable.

Neither clause is engaged, because clause (ix) operates only where there has been a default in repayment of principal or interest to a lender, and questions of utilisation of loan proceeds arise under other clauses of the order.

Clause (ix)(c) is engaged for the whole ₹ 15 crore, because the sanction was specific to the warehouse and any departure from it defeats the purpose test for the entire borrowing and not merely for the part misapplied.

Clause (ix)(d) continues to apply, because that sub-clause is drafted to catch every mismatch between the tenure of the funds raised and the tenure of their user, including long-term funds applied to short-term purposes, so the nature and the amount must still be indicated.
questions.explanation: Clause (ix)(d) bites on funds raised on a short-term basis which have been utilised for long-term purposes; where the borrowing is itself a term loan, that condition cannot be satisfied and the sub-clause does not reach the converse movement of long-term funds into short-term uses. Clause (ix)(c) asks whether term loans were applied for the purpose for which they were obtained, so the ₹ 3 crore pushed into the working capital cycle is a departure from the sanctioned purpose, and the source permits the amount of loan so diverted and the purpose for which it is used to be reported. The whole ₹ 15 crore is not shown as diverted, since only ₹ 3 crore left the sanctioned purpose, and clause (ix) is not confined to repayment defaults.

questions.question:
Match the columns of the format prescribed under clause (ix)(a) of CARO, 2020 with what each column is intended to capture:
Columns:
P. Nature of borrowing, including debt securities
Q. Name of lender
R. Amount not paid on due date
S. Whether principal or interest
T. Number of days of delay or unpaid
U. Remarks, if any
Captures:
1. The character of the defaulted amount.
2. The identity of the party to whom the borrowing or the interest was owed.
3. The period of the default.
4. The class of borrowing, so that debentures and other debt securities are covered along with loans.
5. Any further explanation the auditor considers necessary.
6. The quantum which fell due and was not paid.
Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: The format is the mechanism by which the period and the amount of default required by clause (ix)(a) are disclosed. The first column identifies the borrowing and expressly extends to debt securities, which is why debentures and bonds are reported alongside bank and financial institution borrowings; the second identifies the lender, matching the clause's reference to 'any lender'; the third is the quantum which fell due and remained unpaid, not the sanctioned or outstanding principal; the fourth classifies that sum as principal or interest; the fifth states the number of days of delay or unpaid, that is, the period of default; and remarks is the residual explanatory column. Pairings which swap quantum with character, or which read the nature-of-borrowing column as the remarks column, misstate the format.

questions.question:
Base position: Vandana Ceramics Ltd. defaulted in payment of a principal instalment of ₹ 4.50 crore due on 20.06.2024 to a financial institution, and the instalment was cleared only on 17.11.2024, that is, 150 days after the due date. The auditor reported the default in the prescribed format under clause (ix)(a) of CARO, 2020.
What changes if the instalment had instead been cleared on 04.08.2024, that is, after 45 days?
options: The default ceases to be reportable, because a delay of less than 90 days in repayment of a borrowing is not treated as a default for the purposes of the reporting requirements.
The default continues to be reportable, but only by way of a remark, because the format is meant for defaults outstanding for more than six months.
The default continues to be reportable in the same manner, the number of days of delay being stated as 45, because clause (ix)(a) prescribes no minimum period of default.
The default ceases to be reportable, because clause (ix)(a) applies only where the amount remains unpaid on the last day of the financial year, and this instalment was cleared within the year.
questions.explanation: Clause (ix)(a) asks whether the company has defaulted in repayment of loans or other borrowings or in payment of interest to any lender, and requires the period and the amount of default in the format; it contains no threshold of days and no requirement that the sum still be outstanding at the year-end. Shortening the delay from 150 days to 45 days therefore changes only the figure entered in the 'number of days of delay or unpaid' column. Time limits such as 90 days or six months belong to other reporting requirements and cannot be imported here, and the format is not confined to long-outstanding defaults.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on clauses (ix)(c) and (ix)(d) of CARO, 2020:
1. Clause (ix)(c) is confined to term loans, and asks whether they were applied for the purpose for which they were obtained.
2. Where term loans were not so applied, the source language is that the amount of loan so diverted and the purpose for which it is used may be reported.
3. Clause (ix)(d) requires that, where funds raised on a short-term basis have been utilised for long-term purposes, the nature and the amount be indicated.
4. Clause (ix)(d) also covers funds raised for long-term purposes which have been left parked in short-term investments.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 2, 3 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Clause (ix)(c) is drafted only with reference to term loans, so its utilisation test cannot be applied to a working capital or other short-term facility. Its second limb is expressed permissively in the source, the diverted amount and the purpose for which the loan was used being reported, while clause (ix)(d) is expressed in mandatory terms and requires the nature and the amount to be indicated whenever short-term funds are applied to long-term purposes. Statement 4 reverses the direction of the flow which clause (ix)(d) regulates: it is short-term money going into long-term uses that is caught, not long-term money resting in short-term investments.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding clause (ix) of CARO, 2020:
1. Clause (ix)(f) applies to loans raised by the company during the year on the pledge of securities which the company holds in its subsidiaries, joint ventures or associate companies.
2. Clause (ix)(f) requires details of such loans and also requires the auditor to report whether the company has defaulted in the repayment of such loans raised.
3. Because clause (ix)(f) carries its own default requirement, a default in payment of interest on such a loan is disclosed only under clause (ix)(f) and not in the format under clause (ix)(a).
4. Clauses (ix)(a) and (ix)(b) use the same set of counterparties, so a declaration of wilful default made by any lender whatsoever is reportable under clause (ix)(b).
options: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Clause (ix)(f) looks at loans raised by the company on the pledge of securities held by it in its subsidiaries, joint ventures or associates, and imposes a dual disclosure: the details of such loans and whether there has been default in repayment of them. That dual requirement does not displace the general default reporting, since clause (ix)(a) requires the period and amount of any default in repayment of loans or borrowings or in payment of interest to any lender to be set out in the prescribed format, so the same default appears there as well. The two sub-clauses differ in their counterparties: clause (ix)(a) speaks of any lender, whereas clause (ix)(b) confines the wilful-defaulter enquiry to a bank or a financial institution.

questions.question:
Case study: Solapur Textiles Ltd., FY 2024-25. A term loan of ₹ 60 crore was sanctioned in April 2024 for a spinning-mill project at ₹ 40 crore and a warehouse at ₹ 20 crore. By 31.03.2025 the company had applied ₹ 24 crore to the spinning mill, ₹ 6 crore to the warehouse, ₹ 22 crore to purchase raw cotton for its trading stock, and ₹ 8 crore to acquire plant for a business taken over as a going concern. Two interest instalments totalling ₹ 2.10 crore, due on 30.09.2024 and 31.12.2024, were paid on 22.11.2024 and 19.05.2025 respectively.
Which of the following best describes the reporting under clause (ix) of CARO, 2020?
options: Clause (ix)(a) is engaged only for the instalment due on 31.12.2024, because the earlier instalment was regularised within the year and no arrear survives at the year-end, the format being confined to amounts unpaid on the last day of the financial year, whether of principal or of interest.

Clause (ix)(c) is engaged for ₹ 30 crore of the proceeds applied otherwise than for the purposes for which the loan was obtained, and clause (ix)(a) requires both interest defaults to be entered in the format with the amount and the days of delay or unpaid.

Clause (ix)(c) is engaged for ₹ 30 crore and clause (ix)(d) is engaged for the same ₹ 30 crore, because raw cotton held as trading stock and a business taken over as a going concern are both long-term purposes within that sub-clause.

Clause (ix)(d) alone is engaged, because a single term loan applied to mixed purposes is treated as funds raised for one purpose and utilised for another, and clause (ix)(c) cannot apply where part of the loan has been properly utilised.
questions.explanation: Clause (ix)(c) asks whether term loans were applied for the purposes for which they were obtained; ₹ 24 crore on the mill and ₹ 6 crore on the warehouse answer that question in the affirmative, while the ₹ 22 crore of raw cotton and the ₹ 8 crore of plant for the acquired business, aggregating ₹ 30 crore, do not, and the amount so diverted together with the purpose for which it is used is reportable. Clause (ix)(d) is unavailable because it addresses funds raised on a short-term basis used for long-term purposes, and this borrowing is a term loan. Both interest instalments are defaults in payment of interest to the lender and are entered in the format with the days of delay or unpaid, one being 53 days and the other standing unpaid at the year-end and beyond, since clause (ix)(a) prescribes no minimum period and no year-end survival test.

questions.question:
Case study: Kethan Jewellers Ltd., for FY 2024-25, is a company to which CARO, 2020 applies. The auditor observed the following:
(1) Transactions in bullion of ₹ 3.20 crore, which were not recorded in the books of account, were surrendered and disclosed as income of ₹ 84 lakh in the company's return filed under the Income-tax Act, 1961 on 12.11.2024.
(2) No entry for the surrendered income was made in the books of account during FY 2024-25; the management proposes to record it in FY 2025-26 once the assessment attains finality.
(3) In a regular assessment under the Income-tax Act, the assessing officer accepted an item of income of ₹ 40 lakh which had already been recorded in the books of account.
(4) The sales-tax authorities assessed additional turnover of ₹ 1.10 crore which was not recorded in the books, and the company disclosed that amount as income in those sales-tax proceedings.
Which of the above facts call for a report under clause (viii) of CARO, 2020?
options: Facts (2) and (4) only
Facts (1) and (2) together
Facts (1), (2) and (4)
questions.explanation: Clause (viii) has two limbs which must both be worked through: whether any transactions not recorded in the books have been surrendered or disclosed as income in the tax assessments under the Income-tax Act, 1961, and if so, whether such previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded in the books during the year. Facts (1) and (2) are the two halves of one such event and both limbs are answered, the second in the negative because nothing was recorded during FY 2024-25. Fact (3) does not involve previously unrecorded income at all, the item having already been booked. Fact (4) arises in sales-tax proceedings, whereas the clause is expressed by reference to tax assessments under the Income-tax Act, 1961.

questions.question:
Case study: Kethan Jewellers Ltd., for FY 2024-25, is a company to which CARO, 2020 applies. The auditor observed the following:
(1) Transactions in bullion of ₹ 3.20 crore, which were not recorded in the books of account, were surrendered and disclosed as income of ₹ 84 lakh in the company's return filed under the Income-tax Act, 1961 on 12.11.2024.
(2) No entry for the surrendered income was made in the books of account during FY 2024-25; the management proposes to record it in FY 2025-26 once the assessment attains finality.
(3) In a regular assessment under the Income-tax Act, the assessing officer accepted an item of income of ₹ 40 lakh which had already been recorded in the books of account.
(4) The sales-tax authorities assessed additional turnover of ₹ 1.10 crore which was not recorded in the books, and the company disclosed that amount as income in those sales-tax proceedings.
Assertion (A): The auditor's answer on the second limb of clause (viii) in respect of facts (1) and (2) is in the negative, and the report must state that the previously unrecorded income has not been properly recorded in the books during the year.
Reason (R): Surrendering transactions not recorded in the books and offering the resulting income to tax in an assessment under the Income-tax Act, 1961 is itself the breach which clause (viii) requires the auditor to report adversely.
Which of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is correct but R is incorrect.
A is incorrect but R is correct.
questions.explanation: The assertion is correct: the first limb of clause (viii) is satisfied by the surrender of unrecorded bullion transactions, and the second limb then calls for a statement whether that previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded in the books during the year, which it has not, the entry being postponed to FY 2025-26. The reason misstates the clause. The surrender or disclosure itself is not the mischief clause (viii) is directed at; the reporting turns on the failure to bring the previously unrecorded income into the books within the year. Once the reason is rejected as an inaccurate statement of the rule, what stands is that A is correct but R is incorrect, and the assertion cannot be treated as wrong merely because the reason is.

questions.question:
Case study: Kethan Jewellers Ltd., for FY 2024-25, is a company to which CARO, 2020 applies. The auditor observed the following:
(1) Transactions in bullion of ₹ 3.20 crore, which were not recorded in the books of account, were surrendered and disclosed as income of ₹ 84 lakh in the company's return filed under the Income-tax Act, 1961 on 12.11.2024.
(2) No entry for the surrendered income was made in the books of account during FY 2024-25; the management proposes to record it in FY 2025-26 once the assessment attains finality.
(3) In a regular assessment under the Income-tax Act, the assessing officer accepted an item of income of ₹ 40 lakh which had already been recorded in the books of account.
(4) The sales-tax authorities assessed additional turnover of ₹ 1.10 crore which was not recorded in the books, and the company disclosed that amount as income in those sales-tax proceedings.
Which of the following statements are correct?
1. Clause (viii) is opened by income being either surrendered or disclosed in the tax assessments, so either event triggers the enquiry into the books.
2. If the company had passed the entry for ₹ 84 lakh in its books of account on 28.03.2025, the second limb of clause (viii) would have been satisfied.
3. Fact (3) would have to be reported under clause (viii) if the assessing officer had accepted a larger amount of income than the company had recorded.
4. Clause (viii) is attracted only if the transactions surrendered relate to the financial year under audit itself.
options: 1, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: The clause uses the disjunction 'surrendered or disclosed', so either event opens the enquiry into the state of the books. Recording the surrendered income before the year-end is exactly what the second limb asks for, so statement 2 is correct on the altered facts. Fact (3) concerns income which had already been recorded, and the clause is directed at transactions not recorded in the books, so the size of the officer's acceptance does not make it a reportable item. Statement 4 is unsupported: the clause asks whether transactions not recorded in the books have been surrendered or disclosed and whether the previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded in the books during the year, and a surrender made in the year in respect of earlier transactions is squarely within it.

questions.question:
Match each situation with the clause of CARO, 2020 under which it is reported:
Situations:
P. A service tax demand which the company has not paid because it is in appeal before the Tribunal.
Q. Undisputed cess which remained unpaid for eight months from its due date as on 31st March of the year.
R. Income surrendered in an assessment under the Income-tax Act which had not been recorded in the books of account.
S. Proceeds of a term loan used to repay a working capital overdraft.
Clauses:
1. (vii)(a)   2. (vii)(b)   3. (viii)   4. (ix)(c)   5. (ix)(d)
Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Statutory dues not deposited because of a dispute are reported with the amounts involved and the forum where the dispute is pending under clause (vii)(b), so P pairs with 2. Undisputed cess outstanding at the year-end for eight months from the due date is arrears under clause (vii)(a), so Q pairs with 1. Income surrendered in an Income-tax assessment which was not recorded in the books is the subject matter of clause (viii), so R pairs with 3. Term loan proceeds applied otherwise than for the purpose for which the loan was obtained fall in clause (ix)(c); clause (ix)(d) regulates the opposite movement, of short-term funds into long-term uses, and cannot host S.

questions.question:
Case study: Bhima Coins Ltd., FY 2023-24, a company to which CARO, 2020 applies. (i) Excise duty of ₹ 92 lakh for January 2024, due on 10.02.2024, was unpaid on 31.03.2024. (ii) VAT of ₹ 1.40 crore for April 2023, due on 20.05.2023, was paid on 04.01.2024 after the department raised a demand with interest, which the company did not contest. (iii) An employees' state insurance demand of ₹ 28 lakh is disputed before the Employees' Provident Fund Appellate Tribunal and stands undeposited. (iv) A hire purchase instalment of principal of ₹ 19 lakh, due on 05.01.2024 to a financial institution, was paid on 30.04.2024.
Which of the following is correct as the auditor completes clauses (vii) and (ix)?
options: Arrears of ₹ 92 lakh only are indicated under clause (vii)(a); the employees' state insurance amount is also shown there because an appeal is not a dispute; and the hire purchase delay is not reported because hire purchase is not a loan.

Arrears of ₹ 2.32 crore are indicated under clause (vii)(a); the employees' state insurance amount is reported under clause (vii)(b); and both the hire purchase and the VAT delays are defaults reportable under clause (ix)(a).

Nothing is reported under clause (vii), because the VAT demand was settled; the employees' state insurance amount is reported under clause (vii)(a); and the hire purchase delay is reported under clause (ix)(c).

No arrears are indicated under clause (vii)(a); the employees' state insurance amount is reported under clause (vii)(b) with the forum; and the hire purchase delay is reported under clause (ix)(a) with the number of days of delay.
questions.explanation: Arrears under clause (vii)(a) must be outstanding as on the last day of the financial year and for more than six months from the due date. The ₹ 92 lakh of excise fails the second condition, having fallen due only on 10.02.2024, and the ₹ 1.40 crore of VAT fails the first, having been paid on 04.01.2024, although both delays negative the answer on regularity. The employees' state insurance demand is undeposited because it is in dispute before an appellate forum, so it is disclosed under clause (vii)(b) with the amount and the forum. The hire purchase instalment is a borrowing from a financial institution which fell due and was paid 115 days late, so it is a default reportable in the clause (ix)(a) format, which covers loans or other borrowings and is not confined to loans; clause (ix)(c) deals with application of term loans, not with repayment.

questions.question:
Case study: Thoothukudi Spin Mills Ltd., for FY 2024-25, is a company to which CARO, 2020 applies. The auditor noted the following:
(1) On 02.07.2024 the company borrowed ₹ 25 crore for a tenure of four years from Shencotta Finance Ltd, a non-banking financial company, against pledge of equity shares which the company held in its subsidiary Tuticorin Yarns Pvt Ltd. The sanction letter recorded the purpose of the loan as general corporate purposes. Quarterly interest of ₹ 1.05 crore was payable on 30.09.2024, 31.12.2024 and 31.03.2025.
(2) The interest instalment due on 30.09.2024 was paid on 28.10.2024, and the instalment due on 31.12.2024 was still unpaid on 31.03.2025.
(3) In January 2025 the company received ₹ 4 crore from a partnership firm in which its directors are partners, and applied it to discharge a statutory liability of its associate Koranji Spinning Mills Ltd.
(4) ₹ 20 crore of the ₹ 25 crore borrowing was applied to construct a dyeing unit.
(5) In November 2024 the company factored trade receivables of ₹ 12 crore on a recourse basis and spent ₹ 9 crore of the proceeds on civil works for the same dyeing unit.
Which of the following correctly identifies the sub-clauses of clause (ix) engaged by these facts?
options: Clause (ix)(d) by facts (4) and (5); clause (ix)(f) by fact (1); and clause (ix)(b) by fact (2), because interest remained unpaid at the year-end.
Clause (ix)(a) by facts (1) and (2); clause (ix)(c) by fact (3), because funds were received from a related party; and clause (ix)(d) by fact (4), because a dyeing unit is a long-term purpose.

Clause (ix)(f) alone is engaged by facts (1) and (2), the interest default being fully covered within that sub-clause; clause (ix)(e) by fact (3); clause (ix)(c) by fact (4); and clause (ix)(d) by fact (5), so that no separate entry arises in the format under clause (ix)(a).
Clause (ix)(f) and clause (ix)(a) are both engaged by facts (1) and (2); clause (ix)(e) by fact (3); and clause (ix)(d) by fact (5), while clause (ix)(c) is not engaged by fact (4).
questions.explanation: Fact (1) is a loan raised during the year on the pledge of securities held in a subsidiary, which is clause (ix)(f), and fact (2) is a default in payment of interest to a lender, which clause (ix)(a) requires to be put in the prescribed format; clause (ix)(f) separately asks whether the company defaulted in repayment of such loans, so both disclosures arise from the same borrowing. Fact (3) is funds taken from a person to meet an obligation of an associate and falls in clause (ix)(e). Fact (5) is short-term finance raised by recourse factoring and spent on construction, a long-term purpose, so the nature and the amount go under clause (ix)(d). Clause (ix)(c) is not engaged by fact (4), the sanctioned purpose having been recorded as general corporate purposes, and clause (ix)(b) is not engaged, no bank or financial institution having recorded a wilful default.

questions.question:
Case study: Thoothukudi Spin Mills Ltd., for FY 2024-25, is a company to which CARO, 2020 applies. The auditor noted the following:
(1) On 02.07.2024 the company borrowed ₹ 25 crore for a tenure of four years from Shencotta Finance Ltd, a non-banking financial company, against pledge of equity shares which the company held in its subsidiary Tuticorin Yarns Pvt Ltd. The sanction letter recorded the purpose of the loan as general corporate purposes. Quarterly interest of ₹ 1.05 crore was payable on 30.09.2024, 31.12.2024 and 31.03.2025.
(2) The interest instalment due on 30.09.2024 was paid on 28.10.2024, and the instalment due on 31.12.2024 was still unpaid on 31.03.2025.
(3) In January 2025 the company received ₹ 4 crore from a partnership firm in which its directors are partners, and applied it to discharge a statutory liability of its associate Koranji Spinning Mills Ltd.
(4) ₹ 20 crore of the ₹ 25 crore borrowing was applied to construct a dyeing unit.
(5) In November 2024 the company factored trade receivables of ₹ 12 crore on a recourse basis and spent ₹ 9 crore of the proceeds on civil works for the same dyeing unit.
How should the defaults in fact (2) be entered in the format prescribed under clause (ix)(a)?
options: Two entries: nature of borrowing, debt securities; lender, Shencotta Finance Ltd; amounts not paid on due date, ₹ 1.05 crore and ₹ 25 crore; whether principal or interest, interest and principal; number of days of delay or unpaid, 28 and 90.

Two entries: nature of borrowing, loan against pledge of equity shares held in the subsidiary; lender, Shencotta Finance Ltd; amount not paid on due date, ₹ 1.05 crore in each case; whether principal or interest, interest; days of delay or unpaid, 28 and 90.

One entry: nature of borrowing, a four year loan raised for general corporate purposes; lender, Shencotta Finance Ltd; amount not paid on due date, ₹ 2.10 crore being the aggregate of both instalments; whether principal or interest, interest; number of days of delay, 118.

One entry only, for the instalment which remained unpaid at the year-end, because the instalment cleared on 28.10.2024 ceases to be a default; days of delay, 90; amount not paid on due date, ₹ 1.05 crore; whether principal or interest, interest.
questions.explanation: The format captures each default by borrowing and by due date, stating the amount which was not paid on that date, its character, and the number of days of delay or unpaid. The two instalments are separate defaults of ₹ 1.05 crore of interest each on a borrowing whose nature is that it is secured by the pledge of shares held in the subsidiary; the first was delayed by 28 days and the second stood unpaid for 90 days at the year-end. Aggregating them into one entry destroys the period of each default, entering ₹ 25 crore treats sanctioned principal as unpaid when no principal had fallen due, and dropping the regularised instalment wrongly assumes that a default disappears on payment, clause (ix)(a) having no minimum period and no year-end survival test.

questions.question:
Case study: Thoothukudi Spin Mills Ltd., for FY 2024-25, is a company to which CARO, 2020 applies. The auditor noted the following:
(1) On 02.07.2024 the company borrowed ₹ 25 crore for a tenure of four years from Shencotta Finance Ltd, a non-banking financial company, against pledge of equity shares which the company held in its subsidiary Tuticorin Yarns Pvt Ltd. The sanction letter recorded the purpose of the loan as general corporate purposes. Quarterly interest of ₹ 1.05 crore was payable on 30.09.2024, 31.12.2024 and 31.03.2025.
(2) The interest instalment due on 30.09.2024 was paid on 28.10.2024, and the instalment due on 31.12.2024 was still unpaid on 31.03.2025.
(3) In January 2025 the company received ₹ 4 crore from a partnership firm in which its directors are partners, and applied it to discharge a statutory liability of its associate Koranji Spinning Mills Ltd.
(4) ₹ 20 crore of the ₹ 25 crore borrowing was applied to construct a dyeing unit.
(5) In November 2024 the company factored trade receivables of ₹ 12 crore on a recourse basis and spent ₹ 9 crore of the proceeds on civil works for the same dyeing unit.
What changes if, instead of receiving ₹ 4 crore and applying it to the associate's statutory liability, Thoothukudi had advanced ₹ 4 crore of its own money to that associate, which the associate used to discharge its own liability?
options: Clause (ix)(f) applies, because money moved to an associate company, and clause (ix)(c) also applies, because the company's funds were diverted from its own business, the amount so diverted and the purpose of its use being reportable.

Nothing changes, because clause (ix)(e) covers every movement of funds between the company and its subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures, whether the company receives the funds or parts with them, and the amount in each case has to be given.

Clause (ix)(e) ceases to apply, because it is engaged only where the company takes funds from any entity or person to meet the obligations of its subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures, and an outflow of its own funds to an associate is not reported under clause (ix) at all.

Clause (ix)(e) continues to apply, because the associate's statutory liability was in truth discharged with the company's money, and the clause is to be read on the substance of who ultimately bore the burden of the obligation, together with the nature of the transaction and the amount.
questions.explanation: Clause (ix)(e) is drawn on the inflow side: it asks whether the company has taken any funds from any entity or person to meet the obligations of its subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures, and requires the details, the nature of such transactions and the amount in each case. Where the company parts with its own money to an associate, that condition is not met and the sub-clause falls away. Clause (ix)(f) requires a loan raised on the pledge of securities held in a subsidiary, joint venture or associate, and clause (ix)(c) requires a term loan applied otherwise than for the purpose for which it was obtained, so neither can be stretched to cover the altered fact; reporting of loans and advances granted by the company is dealt with elsewhere in CARO and not in clause (ix).

questions.question:
CASE STUDY: Meridian Synthetics Limited, a listed public company, has a financial year ending 31 March 2025. The following facts were ascertained in the audit:
(1) In May 2024 the company raised ₹300 crore by way of a further public offer. The objects stated in the offer document were: setting up a new manufacturing plant — ₹200 crore; working capital — ₹60 crore; general corporate purposes — ₹40 crore. The plant expenditure of ₹200 crore was incurred and paid by December 2024, and the ₹40 crore for general corporate purposes was fully utilised. The ₹60 crore for working capital lay in a bank account and was deployed only in January 2025, eight months after the date on which the offer document indicated it would be applied; no part of it was used for any other object.
(2) In October 2024 the company made a preferential allotment of equity shares raising ₹80 crore, the stated object of which was capital expenditure on a captive solar facility. The auditor could not obtain evidence that the requirements of section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013 had been complied with, and ₹50 crore of the proceeds was used to repay an existing bank term loan.
(3) In February 2025 the company issued ₹40 crore of wholly convertible debentures by private placement. Evidence of compliance with section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 was complete and the entire ₹40 crore was applied to the stated object of financing a warehouse.

Based on the above case, which of the following statements are correct in relation to CARO 2020 clause (x)?
1. The answer under clause (x)(a) must carry the particulars of the eight month delay in applying the ₹60 crore and of the fact that it was subsequently applied in January 2025.
2. Because the ₹60 crore was ultimately applied to the object for which it was raised, clause (x)(a) is answered in the affirmative without any further particulars.
3. Clause (x)(b) requires the auditor to state whether the requirements of section 42 and of section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013 have been complied with and whether the funds raised have been used for the purposes for which they were raised.
4. Where the answer under clause (x)(b) is in the negative, the auditor has to give the amount involved and the nature of the non-compliance.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Clause (x)(a) asks whether moneys raised by way of an initial public offer or a further public offer were applied for the purposes for which they were raised, and where they were not, directs that details together with delays or default and subsequent rectification, if any, be reported. The ₹60 crore was applied late, and the delay followed by its application in January 2025 is precisely the pair of particulars the clause calls for, so statement 1 is right and statement 2 is wrong because it treats ultimate application as closing the enquiry. Statement 3 reproduces the two limbs of clause (x)(b) as framed for preferential allotment and private placement, and statement 4 states the consequence the clause prescribes for a negative answer. On these facts the plant and general corporate purposes sums were applied, the solar facility object was not, and the section 62 position could not be established.

questions.question:
CASE STUDY: Meridian Synthetics Limited, a listed public company, has a financial year ending 31 March 2025. The following facts were ascertained in the audit:
(1) In May 2024 the company raised ₹300 crore by way of a further public offer. The objects stated in the offer document were: setting up a new manufacturing plant — ₹200 crore; working capital — ₹60 crore; general corporate purposes — ₹40 crore. The plant expenditure of ₹200 crore was incurred and paid by December 2024, and the ₹40 crore for general corporate purposes was fully utilised. The ₹60 crore for working capital lay in a bank account and was deployed only in January 2025, eight months after the date on which the offer document indicated it would be applied; no part of it was used for any other object.
(2) In October 2024 the company made a preferential allotment of equity shares raising ₹80 crore, the stated object of which was capital expenditure on a captive solar facility. The auditor could not obtain evidence that the requirements of section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013 had been complied with, and ₹50 crore of the proceeds was used to repay an existing bank term loan.
(3) In February 2025 the company issued ₹40 crore of wholly convertible debentures by private placement. Evidence of compliance with section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 was complete and the entire ₹40 crore was applied to the stated object of financing a warehouse.

Which of the following actions should the statutory auditor take in framing the answer under CARO clause (x) for the above company?
1. Under clause (x)(a), state that the moneys raised by the further public offer were applied for the purposes for which they were raised, and add the particulars of the eight month delay in applying ₹60 crore and of the application made in January 2025.
2. Under clause (x)(b), report the ₹80 crore preferential allotment, the absence of evidence of compliance with section 62 and the user of ₹50 crore to repay a bank term loan, and state the amount involved and the nature of non-compliance.
3. Treat the ₹40 crore private placement of wholly convertible debentures as outside clause (x)(b) on the ground that the instrument issued is a debenture and not a share.
4. Report the diversion of ₹50 crore from the solar facility object under clause (x)(a), since it is money raised from the public.
Which of the above actions should be taken?
options: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Clause (x)(b) expressly extends to a preferential allotment or private placement of shares or convertible debentures, so the ₹40 crore of wholly convertible debentures issued by private placement is squarely within it and the suggestion that a debenture is outside the clause fails; for that instrument the answer is affirmative on both limbs, section 42 compliance having been established and the whole ₹40 crore having been applied to the warehouse object. The proposal to report the ₹50 crore under clause (x)(a) also fails, because that limb is confined to moneys raised by way of an initial public offer or a further public offer and a preferential allotment reaches the CARO statement only through limb (b). The remaining two actions follow the particulars which each limb separately demands, and the first correctly refuses to convert a delayed application into an unqualified affirmative answer.

questions.question:
CASE STUDY: Meridian Synthetics Limited, a listed public company, has a financial year ending 31 March 2025. The following facts were ascertained in the audit:
(1) In May 2024 the company raised ₹300 crore by way of a further public offer. The objects stated in the offer document were: setting up a new manufacturing plant — ₹200 crore; working capital — ₹60 crore; general corporate purposes — ₹40 crore. The plant expenditure of ₹200 crore was incurred and paid by December 2024, and the ₹40 crore for general corporate purposes was fully utilised. The ₹60 crore for working capital lay in a bank account and was deployed only in January 2025, eight months after the date on which the offer document indicated it would be applied; no part of it was used for any other object.
(2) In October 2024 the company made a preferential allotment of equity shares raising ₹80 crore, the stated object of which was capital expenditure on a captive solar facility. The auditor could not obtain evidence that the requirements of section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013 had been complied with, and ₹50 crore of the proceeds was used to repay an existing bank term loan.
(3) In February 2025 the company issued ₹40 crore of wholly convertible debentures by private placement. Evidence of compliance with section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 was complete and the entire ₹40 crore was applied to the stated object of financing a warehouse.

In the above case the ₹60 crore raised by the further public offer for working capital was deployed in January 2025, eight months late, and no part of it was used for any other object. What changes if, instead, the entire ₹60 crore had been advanced in May 2024 to a company promoted by the chairperson, had remained there for eight months and had been brought back in January 2025 with interest, with no part of it ever applied to working capital?
options: Clause (x)(a) alone is engaged and the auditor confines his answer to the delay in application and the subsequent rectification, because the whole ₹60 crore was ultimately returned with interest before the year end and no part of it was applied to any other stated object of the offer.

Nothing material changes, because the amount came back with interest before the balance sheet date, the offer document did not fix an enforceable date for application, and the temporary user of funds between objects is a matter for the Board rather than for the auditor's CARO statement.

The clause (x)(a) answer becomes adverse and calls for the details of the non-application together with the period of default and the subsequent rectification, and the transaction additionally calls for examination under the clauses on loans and advances and on related parties.

Clause (x)(b) becomes the route through which this is reported, since the money has gone to an entity promoted by the chairperson and limb (b) is the only limb of clause (x) which expressly asks for the amount involved and the nature of the non-compliance.
questions.explanation: On the revised facts money raised by a further public offer has not been applied for the purpose for which it was raised at all, so clause (x)(a) requires the details of that non-application together with the delays or default and the subsequent rectification; restoration with interest in January 2025 meets the last of those particulars but does not efface the first two. The views which rest on the return of the money before the year end, and which treat the delay as cured by the eventual application, both fail for that reason. Clause (x)(b) is not the route, because it is confined to preferential allotment and private placement of shares or convertible debentures and this transaction is neither. The decisive point is that one transaction can simultaneously be unapplied public offer proceeds under clause (x)(a), a loan or advance under the loans clause and a related party transaction under clause (xiii), each of which has to be answered separately.

questions.question:
CASE STUDY: Surya Nidhi Limited is a Nidhi Company constituted under the Companies Act, 2013 and functioning under the Nidhi Rules. Its financial year ends on 31 March 2025. The following facts were ascertained during the audit:
(1) Net Owned Funds as at 31 March 2025 were ₹15 crore and the outstanding deposits were ₹330 crore. The company had borrowed only from its members and had not accepted money from any person who was not a member.
(2) The company held term deposits of ₹36 crore with scheduled banks, of which ₹5 crore stood pledged to a bank against a working capital facility availed during the year.
(3) Interest on cumulative deposits falling due in November 2024 and in December 2024 was paid to members between three and five days after the respective due dates. One member's matured deposit of ₹2.5 lakh was repaid 22 days after the date of maturity. The Audit Committee recorded these facts in its minutes, and no court, tribunal or regulator has passed any order against the company.
(4) The company's Net Owned Funds had been ₹16.5 crore on 30 September 2024, when outstanding deposits stood at ₹330 crore.

Based on the above case, which of the following statements are correct with respect to CARO clause (xii)(a)?
1. The answer is in the negative, because ₹15 crore of Net Owned Funds supports ₹330 crore of deposits whereas a ratio of 1:20 requires Net Owned Funds of at least ₹16.5 crore.
2. The answer is in the affirmative, because the company borrowed only from its members and therefore has no public deposit liability to meet.
3. The ratio contemplated by clause (xii)(a) is the ratio of Net Owned Funds to Deposits of 1:20, and the shortfall has to be carried into the clause (xii) statement.
4. Because the position on 30 September 2024 was exactly at the limit, clause (xii)(a) is answered in the affirmative for the year.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
questions.explanation: Clause (xii)(a) asks whether the Nidhi Company has complied with the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio of 1:20 to meet its liabilities. On ₹330 crore of deposits the required Net Owned Funds are ₹16.5 crore and the company has ₹15 crore, so the answer is in the negative and the shortfall is what the clause requires to be reported, which makes statements 1 and 3 correct. Statement 2 misdirects the test, because clause (xii)(a) is a capital adequacy ratio measured against the deposits the company has to meet and the identity of the depositors forms no part of it. Statement 4 uses a mid-year snapshot to override the year-end position; the 30 September figures show only that the ratio was not breached on that date, which does not cure the non-compliance reported for the year.

questions.question:
CASE STUDY: Surya Nidhi Limited is a Nidhi Company constituted under the Companies Act, 2013 and functioning under the Nidhi Rules. Its financial year ends on 31 March 2025. The following facts were ascertained during the audit:
(1) Net Owned Funds as at 31 March 2025 were ₹15 crore and the outstanding deposits were ₹330 crore. The company had borrowed only from its members and had not accepted money from any person who was not a member.
(2) The company held term deposits of ₹36 crore with scheduled banks, of which ₹5 crore stood pledged to a bank against a working capital facility availed during the year.
(3) Interest on cumulative deposits falling due in November 2024 and in December 2024 was paid to members between three and five days after the respective due dates. One member's matured deposit of ₹2.5 lakh was repaid 22 days after the date of maturity. The Audit Committee recorded these facts in its minutes, and no court, tribunal or regulator has passed any order against the company.
(4) The company's Net Owned Funds had been ₹16.5 crore on 30 September 2024, when outstanding deposits stood at ₹330 crore.

In the above case, what is the correct answer under CARO clause (xii)(b) and why?
options: Affirmative, since the company holds term deposits of ₹36 crore with scheduled banks and that figure exceeds the ₹33 crore which 10% of the outstanding deposits requires.

Negative, since the 10% contemplated by clause (xii)(b) is measured upon the Net Owned Funds of the company rather than upon its deposits, and the ₹5 crore pledge leaves the company short of the amount so measured.
Affirmative, since the ₹5 crore pledge secures a working capital facility which the company uses in the very business of lending to its members out of which the deposit liability arises.
Negative, since only ₹31 crore of the ₹36 crore of term deposits is unencumbered, against a requirement of ₹33 crore being 10% of the outstanding deposits of ₹330 crore.
questions.explanation: Clause (xii)(b) asks whether the Nidhi Company is maintaining 10% unencumbered term deposits as specified in the Nidhi Rules to meet its liabilities, so two conditions have to hold together — the quantum, being 10% of the ₹330 crore of outstanding deposits, that is ₹33 crore, and the unencumbered character of those term deposits. Pledging ₹5 crore destroys that character for that portion and leaves ₹31 crore, a shortfall of ₹2 crore, so the answer must be in the negative. The affirmative answer which counts only the quantum satisfies one condition and ignores the word unencumbered, and the affirmative answer built on the purpose of the pledge states the company's reason for pledging, which is not one of the conditions in the clause. The remaining negative answer reaches the right conclusion on the wrong base, treating the 10% as a fraction of Net Owned Funds and so confusing this limb with the 1:20 ratio of clause (xii)(a).

questions.question:
CASE STUDY: Surya Nidhi Limited is a Nidhi Company constituted under the Companies Act, 2013 and functioning under the Nidhi Rules. Its financial year ends on 31 March 2025. The following facts were ascertained during the audit:
(1) Net Owned Funds as at 31 March 2025 were ₹15 crore and the outstanding deposits were ₹330 crore. The company had borrowed only from its members and had not accepted money from any person who was not a member.
(2) The company held term deposits of ₹36 crore with scheduled banks, of which ₹5 crore stood pledged to a bank against a working capital facility availed during the year.
(3) Interest on cumulative deposits falling due in November 2024 and in December 2024 was paid to members between three and five days after the respective due dates. One member's matured deposit of ₹2.5 lakh was repaid 22 days after the date of maturity. The Audit Committee recorded these facts in its minutes, and no court, tribunal or regulator has passed any order against the company.
(4) The company's Net Owned Funds had been ₹16.5 crore on 30 September 2024, when outstanding deposits stood at ₹330 crore.

With respect to the facts in paragraph (3) of the above case, which of the following is the correct treatment under CARO clause (xii)(c)?
options: No reporting is required, because clause (xii)(c) is confined to a default which continues unsubstituted up to the last day of the financial year, and both the defaults here stood made good before 31 March 2025.

Clause (xii)(c) is engaged only where a court, tribunal, the Registrar of Companies or the Reserve Bank of India has passed an order against the company in respect of the default, and paragraph (3) of the case records that no such order has ever been passed against the company.

Clause (xii)(c) is engaged, since it asks whether there has been any default in payment of interest on deposits or in repayment thereof for any period, and details of the delayed interest and of the ₹2.5 lakh repaid 22 days late have to be given.

No reporting is required, because the delays were of three to five days on interest and of 22 days on a single small repayment, and a clause directed at defaults in the payment of deposits does not reach a default which the company has made good within the same accounting year.
questions.explanation: The clause is framed as 'any default in payment of interest on deposits or in repayment thereof for any period' and directs that, where there has been such default, details thereof be reported. Interest falling due in November and December 2024 and paid three to five days late, and a matured deposit of ₹2.5 lakh paid 22 days after maturity, are each a default for a period, so the third limb is engaged and the particulars must be given. Neither of the two answers which exclude reporting survives, because the clause imposes no materiality floor measured in days and does not require the default to be subsisting at the year end. The answer which waits for an order of a court or tribunal imports a condition clause (xii)(c) does not contain; the absence of any order is a fact which appears relevant in paragraph (3) but is not decisive.

questions.question:
CASE STUDY: Surya Nidhi Limited is a Nidhi Company constituted under the Companies Act, 2013 and functioning under the Nidhi Rules. Its financial year ends on 31 March 2025. The following facts were ascertained during the audit:
(1) Net Owned Funds as at 31 March 2025 were ₹15 crore and the outstanding deposits were ₹330 crore. The company had borrowed only from its members and had not accepted money from any person who was not a member.
(2) The company held term deposits of ₹36 crore with scheduled banks, of which ₹5 crore stood pledged to a bank against a working capital facility availed during the year.
(3) Interest on cumulative deposits falling due in November 2024 and in December 2024 was paid to members between three and five days after the respective due dates. One member's matured deposit of ₹2.5 lakh was repaid 22 days after the date of maturity. The Audit Committee recorded these facts in its minutes, and no court, tribunal or regulator has passed any order against the company.
(4) The company's Net Owned Funds had been ₹16.5 crore on 30 September 2024, when outstanding deposits stood at ₹330 crore.

In the above case, what changes if the company's Net Owned Funds at 31 March 2025 are ₹17 crore instead of ₹15 crore, while the ₹36 crore of term deposits continues to include ₹5 crore pledged against the working capital facility and the November and December interest delays continue to occur?
options: Clause (xii)(a) becomes affirmative and clause (xii)(b) becomes affirmative, but clause (xii)(c) still requires a negative answer with details.
Clause (xii)(a) still remains negative, because the 1:20 ratio is satisfied only if the whole of 10% of the ₹330 crore of deposits is also available as Net Owned Funds.
Clause (xii)(a) becomes affirmative, but the answers required under clauses (xii)(b) and (xii)(c) are unchanged.
All three limbs become affirmative, because the company has restored its capital position above the level required by the 1:20 ratio.
questions.explanation: ₹17 crore of Net Owned Funds against ₹330 crore of deposits satisfies the 1:20 ratio, which requires a minimum of ₹16.5 crore, so clause (xii)(a) turns affirmative. Clause (xii)(b) is an independent test which is unaffected, since unencumbered term deposits of ₹31 crore still fall ₹2 crore short of the ₹33 crore required, and clause (xii)(c) is unaffected because a default in payment of interest for a period has nothing to do with the capital position. The decisive point is that the three limbs of clause (xii) operate independently of one another and curing one does not cure the others, which defeats the answers which sweep all three along with the restored ratio. The remaining answer invents a condition for clause (xii)(a) which the clause does not contain.

questions.category: CARO - NBFC and Core Investment Company
questions.question:
CASE STUDY: Pragathi Capital Holdings Limited is a public company and the holding company of the Pragathi Group, which comprises six companies. Its financial year ends on 31 March 2025. The following facts were ascertained in the audit of this company:
(1) The company holds equity shares, preference shares and debt instruments issued by its Group entities, and is registered with the Reserve Bank of India under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 as a Core Investment Company (CIC) as defined in the regulations of RBI. The auditor verified that it continues to fulfil the criteria of a CIC throughout the year.
(2) Two other companies of the Group, Kaveri Finquest Private Limited and Pragathi Investments Limited, are also CICs, so that the Group has three CICs. Kaveri Finquest Private Limited is an exempted and unregistered CIC — it has not obtained registration under section 45-IA and continues to fulfil the criteria applicable to such a CIC.
(3) Apart from its CIC activity, the company advanced housing loans to two directors of its subsidiary and to three members of the public between April 2024 and January 2025. It obtained a valid Certificate of Registration (CoR) for housing finance from RBI only on 31 January 2025 and has held it since.
(4) Pragathi Forgings Limited, a Group company, is a manufacturer which has neither accepted deposits nor carried on any activity of a financial nature.

Based on the above case, which of the following statements are correct with respect to CARO clause (xvi)?
1. Clause (xvi)(a) is a two part enquiry — whether the company is required to be registered under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and, if so, whether the registration has been obtained.
2. Since a valid Certificate of Registration was obtained on 31 January 2025, clause (xvi)(b) is answered in the affirmative without further particulars.
3. Clause (xvi)(b) is engaged, because the company conducted housing finance activity between April 2024 and January 2025 without a valid Certificate of Registration from RBI.
4. Clause (xvi)(d) requires the auditor to indicate the number of CICs which are part of the Group, being three.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Clause (xvi)(a) tests the requirement of registration under section 45-IA and, where registration is required, the fact of registration, while clause (xvi)(b) is a separate enquiry into whether any non-banking financial or housing finance activity was conducted without a valid Certificate of Registration from RBI. The certificate obtained on 31 January 2025 answers limb (a) but does not efface the ten month period covered by limb (b), which is why the statement treating the later certificate as closing the enquiry is wrong and the statement identifying April 2024 to January 2025 as a breach of limb (b) is correct. Statement 4 follows limb (d), which asks whether the Group has more than one CIC and, if yes, requires the number of CICs which are part of the Group to be indicated; on these facts that number is three, the company itself being one of them.

questions.category: CARO - NBFC and Core Investment Company
questions.question:
CASE STUDY: Pragathi Capital Holdings Limited is a public company and the holding company of the Pragathi Group, which comprises six companies. Its financial year ends on 31 March 2025. The following facts were ascertained in the audit of this company:
(1) The company holds equity shares, preference shares and debt instruments issued by its Group entities, and is registered with the Reserve Bank of India under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 as a Core Investment Company (CIC) as defined in the regulations of RBI. The auditor verified that it continues to fulfil the criteria of a CIC throughout the year.
(2) Two other companies of the Group, Kaveri Finquest Private Limited and Pragathi Investments Limited, are also CICs, so that the Group has three CICs. Kaveri Finquest Private Limited is an exempted and unregistered CIC — it has not obtained registration under section 45-IA and continues to fulfil the criteria applicable to such a CIC.
(3) Apart from its CIC activity, the company advanced housing loans to two directors of its subsidiary and to three members of the public between April 2024 and January 2025. It obtained a valid Certificate of Registration (CoR) for housing finance from RBI only on 31 January 2025 and has held it since.
(4) Pragathi Forgings Limited, a Group company, is a manufacturer which has neither accepted deposits nor carried on any activity of a financial nature.

In the audit of which of the companies described in the above case would the second part of clause (xvi)(c) — whether, in case the company is an exempted or unregistered Core Investment Company, it continues to fulfil such criteria — fall to be answered?
options: Pragathi Capital Holdings Limited alone, since it is the holding company of the Group.
Kaveri Finquest Private Limited, since it is the exempted and unregistered CIC among the companies described.
Pragathi Forgings Limited, since it has neither accepted deposits nor carried on any activity of a financial nature.
Every company of the Pragathi Group, since clause (xvi)(c) is answered at the level of the Group.
questions.explanation: Clause (xvi)(c) operates on the company whose report is being given: its first limb asks whether that company is a CIC as defined in the regulations of RBI and, if so, whether it continues to fulfil the criteria of a CIC, and its second limb covers the company which is an exempted or unregistered CIC and asks whether it continues to fulfil such criteria. Kaveri Finquest Private Limited is the only company in the case described as exempted and unregistered, and it is in its own audit that this limb has to be worked out rather than carried across from the holding company's CARO statement. The answer which spreads the limb across the Group fails because only clause (xvi)(d) looks to the Group, the answer nominating the holding company fails because that company is registered and falls under the first limb, and Pragathi Forgings Limited's facts engage nothing in clause (xvi).

questions.category: CARO - NBFC and Core Investment Company
questions.question:
CASE STUDY: Pragathi Capital Holdings Limited is a public company and the holding company of the Pragathi Group, which comprises six companies. Its financial year ends on 31 March 2025. The following facts were ascertained in the audit of this company:
(1) The company holds equity shares, preference shares and debt instruments issued by its Group entities, and is registered with the Reserve Bank of India under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 as a Core Investment Company (CIC) as defined in the regulations of RBI. The auditor verified that it continues to fulfil the criteria of a CIC throughout the year.
(2) Two other companies of the Group, Kaveri Finquest Private Limited and Pragathi Investments Limited, are also CICs, so that the Group has three CICs. Kaveri Finquest Private Limited is an exempted and unregistered CIC — it has not obtained registration under section 45-IA and continues to fulfil the criteria applicable to such a CIC.
(3) Apart from its CIC activity, the company advanced housing loans to two directors of its subsidiary and to three members of the public between April 2024 and January 2025. It obtained a valid Certificate of Registration (CoR) for housing finance from RBI only on 31 January 2025 and has held it since.
(4) Pragathi Forgings Limited, a Group company, is a manufacturer which has neither accepted deposits nor carried on any activity of a financial nature.

In the above case, what changes if on 1 December 2024 both Kaveri Finquest Private Limited and Pragathi Investments Limited cease to be Core Investment Companies, while Pragathi Capital Holdings Limited continues to fulfil the criteria of a CIC throughout the year and all other facts remain unchanged?
options: Clauses (xvi)(a) and (xvi)(b) become adverse answers, because a company whose Group no longer comprises three CICs can no longer be regarded as validly registered under section 45-IA or as having held a valid Certificate of Registration throughout the year.

Clause (xvi)(c) becomes an adverse answer, because one of the conditions on which the regulations of RBI recognise a Core Investment Company is that the Group of which it forms part should contain at least two other such companies.

The whole of clause (xvi) falls away from the company's CARO statement, since the clause is directed only at Groups which contain more than one Core Investment Company and has nothing to say about a Group with a single such company.
Clause (xvi)(d) is answered that the Group does not have more than one CIC, so no number is to be indicated, while limbs (a), (b) and (c) are unaffected by the change.
questions.explanation: Clause (xvi)(d) is conditioned on the Group having more than one CIC and requires the number to be indicated if it does; with only Pragathi Capital Holdings Limited remaining a CIC the answer to that enquiry is in the negative and no number is reported. The change is confined to limb (d), because registration under section 45-IA, the housing finance activity carried on before 31 January 2025 and the company's own continued fulfilment of the CIC criteria are each tested by reference to the audited company and are untouched by what happens to other Group companies. The answers which turn the entity level limbs into Group level tests, and the answer which drops the clause altogether, both invert this scheme, and the answer which finds a group strength condition in limb (c) states a requirement the clause does not contain.

questions.category: CARO - NBFC and Core Investment Company
questions.question:
CASE STUDY: Pragathi Capital Holdings Limited is a public company and the holding company of the Pragathi Group, which comprises six companies. Its financial year ends on 31 March 2025. The following facts were ascertained in the audit of this company:
(1) The company holds equity shares, preference shares and debt instruments issued by its Group entities, and is registered with the Reserve Bank of India under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 as a Core Investment Company (CIC) as defined in the regulations of RBI. The auditor verified that it continues to fulfil the criteria of a CIC throughout the year.
(2) Two other companies of the Group, Kaveri Finquest Private Limited and Pragathi Investments Limited, are also CICs, so that the Group has three CICs. Kaveri Finquest Private Limited is an exempted and unregistered CIC — it has not obtained registration under section 45-IA and continues to fulfil the criteria applicable to such a CIC.
(3) Apart from its CIC activity, the company advanced housing loans to two directors of its subsidiary and to three members of the public between April 2024 and January 2025. It obtained a valid Certificate of Registration (CoR) for housing finance from RBI only on 31 January 2025 and has held it since.
(4) Pragathi Forgings Limited, a Group company, is a manufacturer which has neither accepted deposits nor carried on any activity of a financial nature.

Which of the following actions should the statutory auditor take in settling the clause (xvi) answers for Pragathi Capital Holdings Limited described in the above case?
1. State that the company is required to be registered under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and that such registration has been obtained.
2. Report that housing finance activity was conducted from April 2024 to January 2025 without a valid Certificate of Registration from RBI, notwithstanding that the Certificate has been held since 31 January 2025.
3. State that the company is a Core Investment Company as defined in the regulations of RBI and continues to fulfil the criteria of a CIC, and indicate that the Group has three CICs.
4. Keep the status of Kaveri Finquest Private Limited as an exempted and unregistered CIC out of this company's clause (xvi) answer, bringing the other Group companies in only through the number of CICs indicated under clause (xvi)(d).
Which of the above actions should be taken?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Actions 1 to 3 trace limbs (a) to (d) of clause (xvi) exactly: registration required and obtained, the period during which housing finance activity was carried on without a valid Certificate of Registration, the company's continued fulfilment of the CIC criteria and the count of three Group CICs. Action 4 is also correct and is the point most often missed — the exempted or unregistered CIC limb of clause (xvi)(c) belongs to that CIC's own CARO statement, and in this company's report the other Group companies enter only through the number required by limb (d). Dropping action 4 would have the auditor opining on another company's continued fulfilment of CIC criteria in a report which is not that company's, while dropping any of actions 1 to 3 would leave a limb which these facts engage unanswered.

questions.question:
CASE STUDY: Falcon Electronics Limited, a listed public company, has a financial year ending 31 March 2025. During the audit the following matters arose:
(1) In July 2024 the company's internal watch detected that a warehouse supervisor had removed inventory costing ₹4.8 crore and sold it to a trader outside the group. The company recovered ₹3.1 crore from the supervisor and his family, settled the balance privately and lodged no complaint with the police.
(2) In January 2025 the directors, in order to satisfy a financial covenant given to a consortium of lenders, caused ₹9.6 crore of export sales which had not taken place to be recorded in the books. The manipulation was reversed in the audited financial statements at the instance of the statutory auditor.
(3) Three complaints were received during the year under the company's vigil mechanism. The Audit Committee inquired into them and recorded in its minutes that two were not substantiated and that one was partly substantiated. The statutory auditor did not read the complaints or the records of inquiry, taking the view that the vigil mechanism is the concern of the Audit Committee.
(4) The statutory auditor filed with the Central Government a report under section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 in Form ADT-4 in respect of the matter described in paragraph (1).

Based on the above case, which of the following statements are correct with respect to CARO clause (xi)(a)?
1. Only the matter in paragraph (2) is within clause (xi)(a), because that clause is confined to fraud by the company.
2. Both paragraphs (1) and (2) are within clause (xi)(a), because the clause covers fraud by the company as well as fraud on the company whenever either has been noticed or reported during the year.
3. The matter in paragraph (1) is outside clause (xi)(a), because the company settled it privately and lodged no police complaint.
4. Where a matter falls within clause (xi)(a), both the nature and the amount involved have to be indicated.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Clause (xi)(a) is drafted on both sides — any fraud by the company and any fraud on the company — and on both modes of coming to knowledge, noticed or reported during the year. The supervisor's removal and sale of inventory costing ₹4.8 crore is a fraud on the company which was noticed during the year, and the private settlement and the absence of a police complaint are not conditions of the clause, so statement 3 is wrong; the directors' recording of ₹9.6 crore of export sales which did not take place is a fraud by the company and is equally within it, so statement 1 is wrong. Statement 4 gives the two particulars the clause requires when the answer is affirmative, namely nature and amount. Neither paragraph is taken outside the clause by the recovery of ₹3.1 crore or by the reversal of the fictitious sales in the audited financial statements.

(4) The statutory auditor filed with the Central Government a report under section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 in Form ADT-4 in respect of the matter described in paragraph (1).

In regard to paragraph (3) of the above case, what does CARO clause (xi)(c) require and is the statutory auditor's position tenable?
options: The clause requires the auditor to report the outcome of the Audit Committee's inquiry into the complaints, which he may properly do by reproducing what its minutes record, the inquiry being a matter delegated to it by the Board.

The clause applies only to a whistle-blower complaint which is ultimately substantiated, so the auditor has to consider one of the three complaints and may treat the two recorded as not substantiated as lying outside the clause.

The clause asks whether the whistle-blower complaints received by the company have been considered by the auditor, and his position is not tenable, the Audit Committee's inquiry being no substitute for that consideration.

The clause is answered in the affirmative once the company is shown to have a vigil mechanism duly established and in operation throughout the year, since the auditor is entitled to rely upon the working of that mechanism.
questions.explanation: Clause (xi)(c) asks whether the auditor has considered the whistle-blower complaints received by the company, which is a question about the auditor's own process. The decisive fact is that he did not read the complaints or the records of inquiry, so the clause cannot be answered cleanly and the deficiency has to be carried into the CARO statement. The answers which rest on the Audit Committee's minutes, and on the existence of a functioning vigil mechanism, are inputs the auditor may use but are not substitutes for consideration, and the answer which admits only substantiated complaints adds a merit filter the clause does not contain, its subject being the complaints received by the company irrespective of their outcome.

The Audit Committee inquired into them and recorded in its minutes that two were not substantiated and that one was partly substantiated. The statutory auditor did not read the complaints or the records of inquiry, taking the view that the vigil mechanism is the concern of the Audit Committee.
(4) The statutory auditor filed with the Central Government a report under section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 in Form ADT-4 in respect of the matter described in paragraph (1).

Paragraph (4) of the above case records that a report in Form ADT-4 under section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 was filed with the Central Government in respect of the matter in paragraph (1). Which of the following correctly states what CARO clause (xi)(b) requires?
options: It requires the auditor to opine whether the filing of a report under section 143(12) was called for in the circumstances of each matter and to explain fully any omission to file such a report.
It requires the auditor to state whether any report under section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 has been filed by the auditors in Form ADT-4 with the Central Government.

It requires the auditor to describe the manner in which the report under section 143(12) was transmitted to the Central Government, the date on which the reply of the Board or Audit Committee was received and the correspondence which passed between them.
It requires the auditor to report only those reports under section 143(12) which remain outstanding against the company at the balance sheet date.
questions.explanation: Clause (xi)(b) is a statement of fact about the existence of a filing — whether any report under section 143(12) has been filed by the auditors in Form ADT-4 with the Central Government — and on these facts the answer records that such a report has been filed. The reading which converts it into an opinion on whether the filing obligation was attracted, and the reading which loads it with the transmission formalities, the addressee and the day counts of section 143(12) itself, each give the clause more than its words will bear, since those matters are requirements of the section and not particulars called for by clause (xi)(b). The reading which confines the clause to filings outstanding at the year end is a restriction the clause does not carry, and a clean answer under clause (xi)(b) in any event does not qualify the answers owed under limbs (a) and (c), each of which is independently framed.

The company recovered ₹3.1 crore from the supervisor and his family, settled the balance privately and lodged no complaint with the police.
