2. Report under clause (x)(b) the ₹70 crore applied to the acquisition of shares of another company instead of the new campus, with the amount involved and the nature of non-compliance, notwithstanding that sections 42 and 62 were complied with.
3. State under clause (xi)(a) the nature and the amount of the diversion by the chief operating officer, and state under clause (xi)(b) that no report in Form ADT-4 under section 143(12) has been filed with the Central Government.
4. Leave the diversion out of clause (xi)(a), because the ₹12 crore was recovered in February 2025 and the committee of inquiry had come to its conclusions.
Which of the above actions should be taken?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Clause (x)(a) extends to moneys raised by way of an initial public offer as well as a further public offer and, where they have not been applied for the purposes for which they were raised, requires the details together with the delay or default, so action 1 is right and the completion of the acquisition out of the remaining ₹40 crore does not cure the ₹20 crore. Action 2 is right because clause (x)(b) requires both compliance with sections 42 and 62 and user of the funds for the purposes for which they were raised, so a clean position on the sections does not answer the user limb and the amount involved and the nature of non-compliance have to be given. Action 3 states limbs (a) and (b) of clause (xi) accurately, the diversion being a fraud on the company by its officer noticed and reported during the year and clause (xi)(b) being a statement of the fact that no Form ADT-4 report has been filed. Action 4 is wrong because recovery of ₹12 crore and the conclusions of the company's own inquiry do not remove a fraud noticed during the year from clause (xi)(a).

questions.question:
CASE STUDY: Amaravati Capital Markets Limited is a listed public company and a member of the Amaravati Group. Its financial year ends on 31 March 2025 and its revenue for the year was ₹14,000 crore. The following facts emerged during the audit:
(1) The company raised ₹450 crore by way of an initial public offer in June 2024 for three objects stated in the offer document. ₹20 crore of the amount earmarked for the acquisition of a data-analytics business was instead used to pay the company's salaries and rent and has not been restored; the acquisition was completed in August 2024 out of the remaining ₹40 crore. The other ₹430 crore was applied to the stated objects during the year.
(2) In September 2024 the company made a preferential allotment of equity shares raising ₹120 crore, the object stated in the notice being capital expenditure on a new campus. The auditor established that the requirements of section 42 and section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013 had been complied with, but ₹70 crore of the proceeds was used to acquire the shares of another company.
(3) In December 2024 the chief operating officer was placed under arrest for having, over the two preceding years, diverted ₹12 crore of the company's funds to entities controlled by him. The company constituted a committee of inquiry and ₹12 crore was recovered from him in February 2025. The statutory auditor did not file any report under section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 in Form ADT-4 with the Central Government in respect of any matter during the year.
(4) The company has no internal audit function, the management being of the view that its processes are automated. The statutory auditor read the reports of the concurrent auditors appointed by the company's two largest lenders, and formed no view on whether the company has an internal audit system commensurate with the size and nature of its business.
(5) The company took a twenty year lease of its head office premises from a trust of which the minor children of its chairperson are the sole beneficiaries. The entire consideration for the lease was satisfied by issuing additional equity shares of the company to the trust, no cash passing either way.
(6) The company purchases software licences annually from a company in which the spouse of its whole-time director holds 60% of the paid-up equity shares. The transactions aggregated ₹35 crore during the year, the approvals required in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Companies Act were obtained, and the transactions are disclosed in the notes to the accounts as required by the applicable accounting standard.
(7) The company is registered under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 as a non-banking financial company and is not a Core Investment Company (CIC). The auditor ascertained that the company has not carried on any non-banking financial or housing finance activity without a valid Certificate of Registration at any time during the year. The Amaravati Group comprises eleven companies, of which four are CICs.

Amaravati Capital Markets Limited in the above case is not a Nidhi Company. Which of the following statements correctly explains the treatment of CARO clause (xii) for this company and the content of that clause?
options: Clause (xii) must be answered for this company so far as its third limb is concerned, because a company which has raised ₹450 crore from the public by an initial public offer plainly has money it has to repay, and that limb speaks of deposits in general terms.

Clause (xii) is answered in the negative for this company, because it holds no term deposits in the manner contemplated by the Nidhi Rules and cannot therefore be said to maintain 10% unencumbered term deposits to meet its liabilities.

Clause (xii) applies to every company which holds deposits of any description, and it is only the 1:20 Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio in limb (a) which is confined in its operation to Nidhi Companies.

Clause (xii) does not call for an answer for this company, because all three of its particulars — the 1:20 ratio, the 10% unencumbered term deposits and any default in payment of interest on deposits or in repayment — are directed at a Nidhi Company.
questions.explanation: Clause (xii) is directed to a Nidhi Company and carries three limbs — compliance with the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio of 1:20 to meet its liabilities, maintenance of 10% unencumbered term deposits as specified in the Nidhi Rules, and any default in payment of interest on deposits or in repayment thereof for any period, with details. Since Amaravati Capital Markets Limited is not a Nidhi Company the clause is not engaged at all, and the money it raised from the public is dealt with under clause (x) instead, which defeats the answers which detach the third limb, or the ratio limb, from the Nidhi context. A company lying outside a clause cannot have an adverse answer under it either, so the answer which returns a negative for limb (b) is doubly wrong; the answers these facts do engage are those under clauses (x), (xi), (xiii), (xiv), (xv) and (xvi).

questions.question:
Which of the following statements regarding CARO 2020 clauses (x) to (xvi) are NOT correct?
1. Clause (x)(a) requires a report on the application of moneys raised by way of an initial public offer or a further public offer, and it is also the clause under which a preferential allotment of shares is reported.
2. Clause (xi)(a) is confined to fraud by the company and does not extend to fraud on the company.
3. Clause (xii)(b) requires a Nidhi Company to maintain unencumbered term deposits equal to 10% of its Net Owned Funds.
4. Clause (xiv)(a) tests the internal audit system against the size of the company's business alone, the nature of the business being dealt with elsewhere.
5. Clause (xvi)(d) requires the auditor to indicate the number of Core Investment Companies which are part of the Group wherever the Group has more than one such company.
Which of the above statements are NOT correct?
options: 1, 2, 3 and 5 only
2, 3, 4 and 5 only
1, 2, 4 and 5 only
1, 2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statement 1 conflates the two limbs of clause (x), because a preferential allotment or private placement of shares or convertible debentures is reported under limb (b) while limb (a) is confined to initial and further public offer proceeds. Statement 2 ignores the words 'any fraud on the company' in clause (xi)(a). Statement 3 puts the 10% on the wrong base, clause (xii)(b) requiring 10% unencumbered term deposits as specified in the Nidhi Rules to meet the company's liabilities, Net Owned Funds being used instead by the 1:20 ratio in clause (xii)(a). Statement 4 drops 'and nature of its business' from clause (xiv)(a), which is measured against both. Statement 5 is the only correct statement and reproduces clause (xvi)(d).

questions.question:
Match the situations in Column I with the CARO 2020 clause under which each is required to be reported, shown in Column II, and select the correct pairing.
Column I
A. Moneys raised by a further public offer have been applied to the stated object only after a delay of eight months
B. An officer of the company has caused export sales which did not take place to be recorded in the books
C. The company has transferred a building to its managing director against shares allotted to him, no cash passing
D. The statutory auditor did not read the reports of the internal auditors before signing his report
E. The company carried on housing finance activity for ten months before obtaining a valid Certificate of Registration from RBI
Column II
1. Clause (x)(a)
2. Clause (xi)(a)
3. Clause (xv)
4. Clause (xiv)(b)
5. Clause (xvi)(b)
6. Clause (xiii)
questions.explanation: Each situation maps to the limb which actually raises it: money raised by a further public offer and applied late falls under clause (x)(a), which calls for the details together with the delay and any subsequent rectification; recording of sales which did not take place by an officer is a fraud by the company within clause (xi)(a); a building transferred to a director against shares is a non-cash transaction with a director attracting clause (xv) and the section 192 enquiry; the auditor's failure to read internal audit reports is clause (xiv)(b); and housing finance activity carried on before a valid Certificate of Registration was obtained is clause (xvi)(b). The pairings which route any of these situations through clause (xiii) misapply it, since clause (xiii) addresses compliance of related party transactions with sections 177 and 188 and their disclosure under the applicable accounting standards, and the pairing which interchanges the internal audit and RBI limbs reverses two unrelated requirements.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A statutory auditor who has established that the audited company employs a well staffed internal audit department covering all its significant processes has thereby satisfied both limbs of CARO clause (xiv) and may answer the clause without further enquiry.
Reason (R): Clause (xiv) poses two distinct questions, namely whether the company has an internal audit system commensurate with the size and nature of its business, and whether the reports of the internal auditors were considered by the statutory auditor.
Which of the following is true?
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is correct but Reason (R) is incorrect.
Assertion (A) is incorrect but Reason (R) is correct.
questions.explanation: Reason (R) reproduces the two limbs of clause (xiv) exactly and is correct. Assertion (A) is incorrect, because establishing the existence, staffing and coverage of the internal audit function goes to limb (a) alone, while limb (b) is framed by reference to the statutory auditor's own act of considering the internal auditors' reports and cannot be answered with evidence about the composition of the department. An auditor who has not obtained and read the internal audit reports has a deficiency to carry into the CARO statement even where limb (a) is fully satisfied. The relationship between the two statements is therefore one of contradiction rather than of explanation, the reason given in R being precisely why A does not follow.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): While reporting under clause (xiv)(a), the auditor cannot conclude that the internal audit system is commensurate merely because the audited company employs as many internal auditors as another company of comparable turnover.
Reason (R): Clause (xiv)(a) measures the internal audit system against the size and the nature of the company's business, so the character of the operations has to be reflected in the system and not only their volume.
Which of the following is true?
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is correct but Reason (R) is incorrect.
Assertion (A) is incorrect but Reason (R) is correct.
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct, because the standard in clause (xiv)(a) is commensuration with the audited company's own size and nature of business and not a peer comparison; two companies of the same revenue can differ entirely in the number of locations, the dispersion of assets, the complexity of products and the concentration of authority. Reason (R) is correct and is the explanation of A, since it is the word 'nature' which brings the character of the operations into the test, so an internal audit function confined to a head office is not commensurate with a widely branched distribution business however many officers it employs. Both statements therefore hold and the second gives the reason why the first holds, which is why the alternatives treating them as merely coincidentally true, or treating either as incorrect, cannot stand.

questions.question:
CARO 2020 prescribes, clause by clause, the particulars to be given in the auditor's statement. Which of the following pairings of sub-clause with the particulars it requires are correct?
1. Clause (x)(a) — details, together with the delays or default in applying moneys raised by an initial or further public offer and the subsequent rectification, if any.
2. Clause (x)(b) — the amount involved and the nature of the non-compliance.
3. Clause (xi)(a) — the nature and the amount involved.
4. Clause (xii)(c) — details of any default in payment of interest on deposits or in repayment thereof for any period.
5. Clause (xvi)(d) — the reasons for which the Group has been constituted together with the number of Core Investment Companies in the Group.
Which of the above pairings are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 5 only
1, 2, 3 and 4 only
2, 3, 4 and 5 only
questions.explanation: The first four pairings reproduce the particulars which the respective limbs expressly call for: clause (x)(a) requires details with the delay or default and any subsequent rectification; clause (x)(b) requires the amount involved and the nature of non-compliance where sections 42 and 62 or the user of the funds are not in order; clause (xi)(a) requires nature and amount where a fraud by or on the company has been noticed or reported; and clause (xii)(c) requires details of any default in payment of interest on deposits or in repayment thereof. The fifth pairing is wrong in its first half, because clause (xvi)(d) asks only whether the Group has more than one CIC and, if yes, requires the number of CICs which are part of the Group to be indicated, and not an explanation of why the Group has been constituted.

questions.question: Vandana Laboratories Limited, an unlisted public company, purchased laboratory equipment for ₹7 crore in November 2024 by an ordinary electronic transfer in favour of an engineering company in which its whole-time director holds no interest, and recorded the purchase as a routine capital expenditure. What changes if, instead of that purchase, the company had taken the same equipment, valued at the same ₹7 crore, from the whole-time director in lieu of the entire consideration for a plot of land standing at ₹7 crore in his books, with no cash passing either way?
options: Nothing changes, because clause (xv) is concerned only with transactions between the company and persons connected with its directors and a director dealing with the company in the ordinary course of its business for cash lies outside it.

The transaction comes within clause (xv), because it is a non-cash transaction with a director, and the auditor then has to state whether the provisions of section 192 of the Companies Act, 2013 have been complied with.

The transaction becomes reportable under clause (x)(b), because the company has taken property from a director against an issue of its own shares otherwise than by an initial or a further public offer.

The transaction is reportable under clause (xv), but the auditor need not examine section 192 of the Companies Act, 2013, since that section deals with loans and quasi-loans given by the company and not with the purchase or transfer of property.
questions.explanation: Clause (xv) is engaged only where the company has entered into a non-cash transaction with directors or persons connected with him, and it then requires the auditor to state whether the provisions of section 192 of the Companies Act, 2013 have been complied with. In the original version the purchase is for cash from an unrelated third party, so the clause is not attracted; on substitution both conditions are present, the counterparty being a director and no cash passing, and the section 192 enquiry follows. The view that a director dealing with the company in the ordinary course lies outside the clause mis-states its scope, since directors are named in it expressly, the view resting on clause (x)(b) mistakes a transfer of property for a preferential allotment or private placement, and the view which admits the clause but excludes section 192 splits a single enquiry into two, section 192 being the very provision the clause directs the auditor to report upon.

questions.question:
Indus Ventures Limited, a listed public company, issued 6 crore new equity shares by way of preferential allotment in November 2024 to the Greenmead Trust, of which the minor children of its whole-time director are the sole beneficiaries. The entire consideration was satisfied by the Trust transferring a software platform to the company and no money was received by the company. The auditor could not establish that the requirements of section 42 and section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013 had been complied with. The allotment is disclosed in the notes to the accounts as a transaction with a related party and the approval of the Audit Committee was obtained. Which of the following statements are correct?
1. Clause (x)(b) is engaged because a preferential allotment of shares has been made, and the auditor must state whether the requirements of section 42 and section 62 have been complied with, giving the amount involved and the nature of the non-compliance so far as they have not been.
2. Clause (xv) is not engaged, because the allottee is a trust and not a director of the company.
3. Clause (xiii) is engaged, and the auditor must report whether the transaction is in compliance with sections 177 and 188 and whether its details have been disclosed in the financial statements as per the applicable accounting standards.
4. Clause (xv) is engaged, because the company has entered into a non-cash transaction with persons connected with a director, and the auditor must state whether section 192 of the Companies Act, 2013 has been complied with.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: A preferential allotment of shares is within clause (x)(b) whatever the mode of consideration, so the failure to establish compliance with sections 42 and 62 requires the amount involved and the nature of non-compliance to be reported; the use of funds limb has nothing to operate upon because no money was raised, which is a distinction the clause permits rather than a reason to drop the transaction from it. The transaction is also non-cash and is with the minor children of a whole-time director, that is, with persons connected with a director, so clause (xv) and the section 192 enquiry are engaged and the statement excluding clause (xv) because a trust rather than a director is the allottee is wrong. Statement 3 is correct because the allotment is a transaction with a related party whose compliance with sections 177 and 188 and whose disclosure in the financial statements under the applicable accounting standards are both tested by clause (xiii), the Audit Committee approval and the note disclosure being evidence for that answer rather than a substitute for it.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about CARO 2020 clause (xvii) (cash losses):
1. It requires reporting whether the company has incurred cash losses during the financial year under audit.
2. It also requires reporting cash losses, if any, in the immediately preceding financial year.
3. Where cash losses are reported, the amount of such cash losses must be stated.
4. It is attracted only when cash losses occur in both the current year and the immediately preceding year taken together.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 2, 3 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3 only
questions.explanation: The source states clause (xvii) as: whether the company has incurred cash losses in the financial year and in the immediately preceding financial year, if so, state the amount of cash losses. Statements 1 and 2 correctly capture that both the current year and the immediately preceding year are examined, and statement 3 correctly captures that the quantum must be stated. Statement 4 is wrong because the clause imposes no conjunctive trigger - a cash loss in either year is reportable with its amount. The correct combination is therefore statements 1, 2 and 3; any combination admitting statement 4 fails.

questions.question: Sunrich Ceramics Ltd is a CARO-applicable company. Its auditor computes cash flows showing a positive operating cash flow for FY 2024-25 but a cash loss of ₹ 1.8 crore for FY 2023-24. Management argues that clause (xvii) is reportable only when the current financial year itself shows a cash loss. Applying clause (xvii), what changes in this argument?
options: Nothing is reported, because only the year under audit is examined and it shows a cash surplus.
A cash loss of ₹ 1.8 crore must be reported for FY 2023-24, the immediately preceding year, with its amount stated.
Nothing is reported, because clause (xvii) is attracted only when the current financial year and the immediately preceding financial year both show cash losses together.
The fact of a loss is reported but the amount need not be stated, because clause (xvii) asks only for a yes/no.
questions.explanation: Clause (xvii) explicitly extends to cash losses 'in the financial year and in the immediately preceding financial year', so a loss confined to the preceding year is still within the reporting net, and the source requires the amount to be stated. The decisive fact is the ₹ 1.8 crore cash loss in FY 2023-24, reportable even though FY 2024-25 is cash-positive. The readings that confine reporting to the current year, or that require losses in both years together, are wrong, as is the reading that drops the mandatory statement of amount.

questions.question: In which one of the following situations is the CARO clause (xviii) disclosure (resignation of the statutory auditor during the year, and whether the auditor took into consideration the issues/objections/concerns raised by the outgoing auditors) squarely attracted?
options: The statutory auditor tenders resignation from the office during the financial year and a new auditor is appointed to complete the term.
The statutory auditor's five-year term expires and a new firm is appointed at the annual general meeting.
The board removes the statutory auditor before term expiry with the requisite Central Government leave.
The statutory auditor ceases to hold office on the amalgamation of the company with another entity, the scheme of amalgamation taking effect on the appointed date.
questions.explanation: Clause (xviii) is triggered specifically by 'resignation of the statutory auditors during the year', and then asks whether the issues, objections or concerns raised by the outgoing auditors have been taken into consideration. Only the resignation situation attracts it. Expiry of term, board removal with Central Government leave and cessation on amalgamation are all cesser of office that are not resignations, so the clause's resignation limb is not engaged.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Under CARO clause (xviii), where there has been a resignation of the statutory auditor during the year, the auditor must state whether the outgoing auditor's issues, objections or concerns have been taken into consideration.
Reason (R): Clause (xviii) is directed at surfacing whether the outgoing auditor left with unresolved concerns or disagreements that the continuing audit work must address.
Which of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is true: on resignation during the year the clause reads whether the auditor has taken into consideration the issues, objections or concerns raised by the outgoing auditors. R is also true and is the logic behind that second limb - a resignation may signal unresolved matters, so the auditor must confirm those concerns were considered. Because R supplies the reason underpinning A, the correct choice is that both are true and R explains A; the 'R not the correct explanation' reading understates the link, and the two 'one limb false' readings deny a limb the source states.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about CARO clause (xix) (going concern):
1. The auditor forms the opinion on the basis of financial ratios, ageing and expected date of realisation of financial assets and payment of financial liabilities.
2. The auditor's knowledge of the management's plans is one input to the clause (xix) assessment.
3. The opinion is that no material uncertainty exists, as on the date of the audit report, that the company is capable of meeting its liabilities existing at the balance sheet date as and when they fall due within one year from the balance sheet date.
4. The one-year window for meeting liabilities runs from the date of the audit report.
Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: The source lists, as the basis for clause (xix), financial ratios, ageing and expected date of realisation of financial assets and payment of financial liabilities, together with the auditor's knowledge of management's plans - so statements 1 and 2 are accurate. The opinion sought is that no material uncertainty exists as on the date of the audit report that the company can meet its balance-sheet liabilities as and when they fall due within one year from the balance sheet date, so statement 3 is accurate. Statement 4 is wrong: the discharge window is one year from the balance sheet date, while the date of the audit report is only the reference date for judging whether a material uncertainty exists.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Clause (xix) uses two different reference points - the date of the audit report to judge whether a material uncertainty exists, and the balance sheet date to measure the one-year window over which recognised liabilities must be payable.
Reason (R): Clause (xix) asks the auditor to opine that no material uncertainty exists, as on the date of the audit report, that the company is capable of meeting its liabilities existing at the balance sheet date as and when they fall due within a period of one year from the balance sheet date.
Which of the following is correct?
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: R restates the clause exactly as the source words it, and that wording is precisely what A analyses: the existence of a material uncertainty is tested 'as on the date of the audit report', while the liabilities and the one-year payment window are anchored to the balance sheet date. Both statements are true and R is the correct explanation of A. The 'R not the correct explanation' reading fails because R is the very text that generates A's two-date distinction; the two 'one limb false' readings contradict the source.

questions.category: CARO xix vs Audit Report - Going Concern Interplay
questions.question: Nitron Motors Ltd is a CARO-applicable company. On the strength of negative working capital, ₹ 46 crore of borrowings falling due within a year and an unsigned plan to sell a stake, the auditor concludes that a material uncertainty exists regarding the company's ability to settle its balance-sheet liabilities as they fall due within one year from 31 March 2025. The financial statements adequately disclose the matter. With reference to clause (xix), which statement is correct?
options: Clause (xix) is discharged simply by adding an Emphasis of Matter paragraph to the audit report, because CARO itself then needs no separate affirmative statement on the company's ability to meet its balance-sheet liabilities within one year.
The presence of a material uncertainty makes CARO inapplicable, so clause (xix) is omitted altogether.
Clause (xix) compels a disclaimer of opinion regardless of whether sufficient appropriate audit evidence was obtained.

The auditor cannot give the affirmative 'no material uncertainty exists' statement contemplated by clause (xix) and must report accordingly, without displacing the separate going-concern treatment in the audit report.
questions.explanation: Clause (xix) seeks an affirmative opinion that no material uncertainty exists (as on the date of the audit report) about meeting balance-sheet liabilities within one year from the balance sheet date. Here the auditor's own conclusion is that a material uncertainty exists, so the affirmative statement contemplated by the clause is unavailable and the true position must be reported through the CARO statement, independently of how the matter is presented in the audit report. Treating CARO as replaced by an Emphasis of Matter, as ceasing to apply, or as compelling a disclaimer, is each wrong.

questions.question:
Match the elements in Column I with the requirements in Column II for CARO clause (xx) (Corporate Social Responsibility):
Column I:
(1) Non-ongoing project - destination of the unspent amount
(2) Non-ongoing project - compliance deadline for transfer
(3) Ongoing project - destination of the unspent amount
(4) Ongoing project - sub-section governing the special-account transfer
Column II:
(P) Fund specified in Schedule VII
(Q) Within 6 months of the expiry of the financial year
(R) Special account
(S) Section 135(6)
Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Clause (xx)(a) covers amounts unspent in respect of projects other than ongoing projects, which must be transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within 6 months of the expiry of the financial year in compliance with section 135(5); clause (xx)(b) covers unspent amounts pursuant to an ongoing project, which must be transferred to a special account in compliance with section 135(6). So (1)-P, (2)-Q, (3)-R and (4)-S. The pairings that place the special account against the non-ongoing head, or attach the 6-month deadline to the ongoing head, misread which limb of clause (xx) governs which case.

questions.question: Kalpa Pharma Ltd (CARO applies) had ₹ 3 crore unspent at 31 March 2025. The amount related to a project classified as an ongoing project under section 135(5) up to 30 September 2025. On 15 October 2025 the project was completed, so the amount became 'other than an ongoing project' and remained unspent. Applying clause (xx)(a), what is the correct consequence of this change of classification?
options: A special account; the clock is one year from the balance sheet date.
A Fund specified in Schedule VII, but with no time limit once the project ceases to be an ongoing project, so the transfer made on 15 October 2025 remains compliant under clause (xx)(a).
A Fund specified in Schedule VII; the deadline is 6 months from the expiry of the financial year, which on these facts had already elapsed.
The same special account; clause (xx)(a) can never apply to an amount that began its life as an ongoing project.
questions.explanation: Once the amount is 'other than an ongoing project', clause (xx)(a) governs it. The unspent amount must therefore go to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within 6 months of the expiry of the financial year, i.e., by 30 September 2025 here, in compliance with section 135(5); that window had already closed on 15 October 2025, so the position is non-compliant. Applying the ongoing-project treatment (special account/section 135(6)) or a one-year clock, saying there is no time limit, or holding (xx)(a) inapplicable to reclassified amounts, are each wrong.

questions.question:
Aurora Holdings Ltd prepares consolidated financial statements consolidating three subsidiaries. In their separate CARO reports: subsidiary S1 carries an adverse remark under clause (vii) on statutory dues; S2's audit report has an Emphasis of Matter paragraph but no qualification or adverse CARO remark; S3 has an observation under clause (iii) but no qualification or adverse CARO remark.
Consider the statements:
1. Clause (xxi) requires covering qualifications or adverse remarks appearing in the CARO reports of companies included in the CFS.
2. S1's adverse clause (vii) remark is within the scope of clause (xxi).
3. S2's Emphasis of Matter paragraph is itself an adverse CARO remark requiring reporting under clause (xxi).
4. For each qualifying matter, clause (xxi) requires details of the companies and the paragraph numbers of the CARO report containing the qualification/adverse remark.
Which are correct?
options: 1, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only
1, 2 and 3 only
questions.explanation: Clause (xxi) captures qualifications or adverse remarks made by the respective auditors in the CARO reports of companies included in the consolidated financial statements, and requires, where such exist, details of the companies and the paragraph numbers of the CARO report containing them. S1's adverse clause (vii) remark is therefore in scope, so statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. An Emphasis of Matter paragraph is not a qualification or an adverse CARO remark, so statement 3 is wrong, which defeats every combination admitting statement 3.

questions.question:
Case: Vidhya Textiles Ltd is a company to which CARO 2020 applies. For FY 2024-25 the following facts emerge: (1) The company incurred cash losses of ₹ 2.5 crore in FY 2024-25 and cash losses of ₹ 1.1 crore in FY 2023-24. (2) Its statutory auditor resigned in November 2024 and a new firm was appointed to complete the term; the new firm says it did not obtain or consider the outgoing auditor's inputs. (3) At 31 March 2025 the company had undisputed GST dues outstanding for 8 months from the due date, and a customs duty demand that is genuinely disputed before the Commissioner. (4) An unspent CSR amount of ₹ 4 crore relates to projects that are NOT ongoing; it was transferred to a Schedule VII fund on 15 January 2026. (5) A subsidiary consolidated in Vidhya's consolidated financial statements has an adverse remark in its CARO report. The audit report itself is unmodified.
Which combination lists the CARO clauses each of which requires a reporting or concern on these facts, without omitting a clearly engaged clause or adding a clause not engaged?
options: (xvii), (xviii), (vii), (xx)(b), (xxi)
(xvii), (xix), (vii), (xx)(a), (xxi)
(xviii), (xvii), (ix), (xx)(a), (xxi)
(xvii), (xviii), (vii), (xx)(a), (xxi)
questions.explanation: Five clauses are engaged on these facts: (xvii) cash losses in both years; (xviii) resignation with the outgoing auditor's concerns not considered; (vii) undisputed GST over 6 months from the due date plus a genuine customs dispute to be reported with the forum; (xx)(a) non-ongoing CSR transferred on 15 January 2026, beyond 6 months of FY expiry; and (xxi) the consolidated subsidiary's adverse CARO remark. The correct set must contain exactly (xvii), (xviii), (vii), (xx)(a) and (xxi). The set with (xx)(b) misapplies the ongoing-project limb to non-ongoing facts, the set with (xix) drops (xviii) and adds a clause no fact establishes as adverse, and the set with (ix) but no (vii) invokes a lender default absent from the case.

questions.category: CARO - Statutory Dues vs CSR (Case Study)
questions.question:
Case: Vidhya Textiles Ltd is a company to which CARO 2020 applies. For FY 2024-25 the following facts emerge: (1) The company incurred cash losses of ₹ 2.5 crore in FY 2024-25 and cash losses of ₹ 1.1 crore in FY 2023-24. (2) Its statutory auditor resigned in November 2024 and a new firm was appointed to complete the term; the new firm says it did not obtain or consider the outgoing auditor's inputs. (3) At 31 March 2025 the company had undisputed GST dues outstanding for 8 months from the due date, and a customs duty demand that is genuinely disputed before the Commissioner. (4) An unspent CSR amount of ₹ 4 crore relates to projects that are NOT ongoing; it was transferred to a Schedule VII fund on 15 January 2026. (5) A subsidiary consolidated in Vidhya's consolidated financial statements has an adverse remark in its CARO report. The audit report itself is unmodified.
Which single option states BOTH the correct statutory-dues conclusion and the correct CSR conclusion?
options: Clause (xx)(a) records non-compliance because the transfer was beyond 6 months of the financial year's expiry (the window ending 30 September 2025); the undisputed GST 8 months past the due date is reported under (vii)(a); and the genuinely disputed customs duty is reported under (vii)(b) with the forum.

The ₹ 4 crore was transferred within the permissible window, so clause (xx)(a) is fully satisfied and needs no adverse comment; and the disputed customs duty, being unpaid on the last day of the financial year, is itself arrears to be reported under clause (vii)(a).
Both dues are reported under (vii)(a) as arrears because both were unpaid on the last day of the financial year; the CSR transfer is compliant.
(vii)(a) applies only to disputed dues, so only the customs duty is reported; the CSR transfer is tested against the same '6 months from the due date' yardstick.
questions.explanation: Two different '6 months' yardsticks apply. Clause (vii)(a) reports undisputed arrears outstanding on the last day of the financial year for more than 6 months from the due date, so the 8-month GST default is reported; clause (vii)(b) reports dues unpaid due to a genuine dispute (a mere representation is not a dispute, but this is a real dispute before the Commissioner). Clause (xx)(a) measures the non-ongoing CSR transfer against 6 months from the expiry of the financial year (by 30 September 2025), so the 15 January 2026 transfer is late. Treating the transfer as timely, reporting the dispute under (vii)(a), or applying (vii)(a) to all unpaid amounts, misstates these tests.

questions.question:
Case: Vidhya Textiles Ltd is a company to which CARO 2020 applies. For FY 2024-25 the following facts emerge: (1) The company incurred cash losses of ₹ 2.5 crore in FY 2024-25 and cash losses of ₹ 1.1 crore in FY 2023-24. (2) Its statutory auditor resigned in November 2024 and a new firm was appointed to complete the term; the new firm says it did not obtain or consider the outgoing auditor's inputs. (3) At 31 March 2025 the company had undisputed GST dues outstanding for 8 months from the due date, and a customs duty demand that is genuinely disputed before the Commissioner. (4) An unspent CSR amount of ₹ 4 crore relates to projects that are NOT ongoing; it was transferred to a Schedule VII fund on 15 January 2026. (5) A subsidiary consolidated in Vidhya's consolidated financial statements has an adverse remark in its CARO report. The audit report itself is unmodified.
With respect to the auditor change in November 2024, what should clause (xviii) record, and why?
options: Nothing, because a resignation followed by appointment to complete the term is not reportable; only removal is.

That the outgoing auditor's concerns stood necessarily considered in law, because a resignation from the office of statutory auditor cannot take place unless those matters had first been documented and placed before the board.
That there was a resignation of the statutory auditor during the year, and that the auditor did not take into consideration the issues, objections or concerns raised by the outgoing auditor.
A clause (xviii) statement only if the resignation is shown to have arisen from a disagreement connected with the financial statements.
questions.explanation: Clause (xviii) triggers on any resignation of the statutory auditor during the year and then asks whether the auditor has taken into consideration the issues, objections or concerns raised by the outgoing auditors. A resignation occurred (November 2024) and the new firm admits it did not consider the outgoing auditor's inputs, so the CARO statement records that this required consideration was not had. Limiting the clause to removal, presuming consideration automatically in law, or requiring a financial-statement-linked reason, each add conditions the source does not impose.

questions.category: CARO - Cash Losses and CFS (Case Study)
questions.question:
Case: Vidhya Textiles Ltd is a company to which CARO 2020 applies. For FY 2024-25 the following facts emerge: (1) The company incurred cash losses of ₹ 2.5 crore in FY 2024-25 and cash losses of ₹ 1.1 crore in FY 2023-24. (2) Its statutory auditor resigned in November 2024 and a new firm was appointed to complete the term; the new firm says it did not obtain or consider the outgoing auditor's inputs. (3) At 31 March 2025 the company had undisputed GST dues outstanding for 8 months from the due date, and a customs duty demand that is genuinely disputed before the Commissioner. (4) An unspent CSR amount of ₹ 4 crore relates to projects that are NOT ongoing; it was transferred to a Schedule VII fund on 15 January 2026. (5) A subsidiary consolidated in Vidhya's consolidated financial statements has an adverse remark in its CARO report. The audit report itself is unmodified.
Two issues: (i) what does clause (xvii) require as to cash losses; and (ii) what does clause (xxi) require as to the consolidated subsidiary's adverse remark?
options: (i) Only the FY 2024-25 cash loss of ₹ 2.5 crore; (ii) the subsidiary's remark need not be mentioned because it is in a separate CARO report.

(i) Cash losses of ₹ 2.5 crore for FY 2024-25 and ₹ 1.1 crore for the immediately preceding FY 2023-24, stated separately; (ii) details of the company concerned and the paragraph number(s) of that CARO report containing the qualification/adverse remark.
(i) The combined ₹ 3.6 crore for both years; (ii) the full text of the adverse remark must be reproduced.
(i) Cash losses need be confirmed qualitatively without amounts; (ii) clause (xxi) covers only qualifications, not adverse remarks.
questions.explanation: Clause (xvii) examines cash losses in the financial year and the immediately preceding financial year and requires the amount to be stated, so both the ₹ 2.5 crore (FY 2024-25) and ₹ 1.1 crore (FY 2023-24) figures are reported separately, not combined. Clause (xxi), where there are qualifications or adverse remarks in the CARO reports of companies included in the CFS, requires details of the companies and the paragraph numbers, and it covers both qualifications and adverse remarks. Dropping the preceding year, netting the two years, omitting amounts, or excluding adverse remarks, is each wrong.

questions.question:
Match each CARO clause in Column I with the exact threshold or period it uses in Column II.
Column I:
(1) Clause (i)(d) - aggregate change triggering reporting, per class of PPE/intangible assets
(2) Clause (ii)(a) - discrepancy level triggering reporting, per class of inventory
(3) Clause (xii)(a) - Nidhi company ratio
(4) Clause (xii)(b) - unencumbered term deposits a Nidhi company must maintain
(5) Clause (iii)(d) - period beyond which overdue loan amounts are reported
(6) Clause (ii)(b) - working-capital-limit threshold
Column II:
(P) 10% or more of net carrying value of each class
(Q) 10% or more in aggregate for each class of inventory
(R) 1:20
(S) 10% unencumbered term deposits
(T) More than 90 days overdue
(U) In excess of ₹ 5 crore
Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Clause (i)(d) reports where the aggregate change is 10% or more of the net carrying value of each class of PPE/intangible assets, and clause (ii)(a) reports discrepancies of 10% or more in aggregate for each class of inventory. Clause (xii)(a) uses the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio of 1:20, while clause (xii)(b) requires 10% unencumbered term deposits under the Nidhi Rules. Clause (iii)(d) reports the total amount overdue for more than 90 days, and clause (ii)(b) engages where aggregate working-capital limits in excess of ₹ 5 crore are sanctioned on the security of current assets. The three '10%' uses are distinguished by their anchor - net carrying value, aggregate inventory, and unencumbered deposits - which is exactly what the shuffled P/Q/S wrong options try to confuse.

questions.category: CARO - Statutory Dues vs CSR Timelines (Integration)
questions.question: Two CARO-applicable companies. Company M has undisputed income-tax dues, payable on a due date of 15 August 2024, still unpaid on 31 March 2025, i.e., about 7 months past the due date on the last day of FY 2024-25. Company N has an unspent CSR amount for FY 2024-25 relating to a non-ongoing project, transferred to a Schedule VII fund on 20 September 2025. Applying the '6 months' yardstick in clause (vii)(a) and clause (xx)(a), which option correctly tests reportability?
options: Both are measured from the due date to the last day of the financial year, so the 20 September 2025 transfer fails clause (xx)(a).

Clause (vii)(a) is breached whenever any undisputed due is unpaid on the last day of the financial year, irrespective of months elapsed; clause (xx)(a) requires transfer within 6 months of the balance sheet date.
Clause (xx)(a)'s 6 months run from the due date of the CSR contribution and clause (vii)(a)'s 6 months run from the expiry of the financial year.

Clause (vii)(a) measures arrears on the last day of the financial year as more than 6 months from the due date (so M's ~7-month arrears are reported), while clause (xx)(a) measures the transfer against 6 months from the expiry of the financial year (so N's 20 September 2025 transfer, within the window ending 30 September 2025, is compliant).
questions.explanation: Clause (vii)(a) reports undisputed statutory dues outstanding, as on the last day of the financial year, for more than 6 months from the due date; M's income-tax dues about 7 months overdue on 31 March 2025 are therefore reportable. Clause (xx)(a) measures a non-ongoing project's unspent CSR transfer against 6 months from the expiry of the financial year (by 30 September 2025), so N's 20 September 2025 transfer is timely. The decisive point is that the two '6 months' run from different reference dates. Applying one common yardstick, dropping the 6-month test in (vii)(a), or reversing the two clauses, is wrong.

questions.question: Arohana Alloys Ltd is a private company and a subsidiary of a listed public company. For FY 2024-25: turnover ₹ 42 crore; aggregate borrowings from banks/financial institutions ₹ 18 crore at all times during the year; paid-up capital plus reserves ₹ 0.8 crore. On these facts, what is the correct position as to (I) applicability of CARO and (II) applicability of point (i) of section 143(3) (adequacy of internal financial controls)?
options: CARO does not apply because the financial figures are small; point (i) of section 143(3) also does not apply.

CARO applies because the private-company exemption is lost as it is a subsidiary of a public company; but point (i) of section 143(3) does not apply because turnover is below ₹ 50 crore and aggregate borrowings are below ₹ 25 crore.
CARO applies; and point (i) of section 143(3) also applies, because the two exemptions are the same.

CARO does not apply because capital-plus-reserves and borrowings are both within ₹ 1 crore, so the company is said to fall wholly outside the order; and point (i) of section 143(3) applies, because the aggregate borrowings figure is said to exceed ₹ 1 crore.
questions.explanation: The CARO private-company exemption is available only to a private company that is not a subsidiary or holding of a public company and that satisfies all three ceilings (capital plus reserves up to ₹ 1 crore, borrowings up to ₹ 1 crore, revenue up to ₹ 10 crore); Arohana is a subsidiary of a public company, so CARO applies despite the small figures. Independently, the carve-out from point (i) of section 143(3) for a private company depends on turnover below ₹ 50 crore plus aggregate borrowings below ₹ 25 crore at any time during the year, which Arohana (₹ 42 crore and ₹ 18 crore) satisfies, so point (i) does not apply. Conflating the two regimes, treating them as identical, or applying the ₹ 1 crore CARO borrowings figure to the section 143(3)(i) test, are each wrong.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on CARO 2020 and section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013:
1. The carve-out from point (i) of section 143(3) for a private company uses turnover below ₹ 50 crore plus aggregate borrowings below ₹ 25 crore at any time during the year, whereas the CARO private-company exemption uses capital-plus-reserves up to ₹ 1 crore, borrowings up to ₹ 1 crore and revenue up to ₹ 10 crore.
2. Section 143(12) reporting to the Central Government is triggered where fraud of ₹ 1 crore or above is involved; the auditor first reports to the Board/Audit Committee within 2 days of knowledge and seeks their reply within 15 days.
3. Non-compliance with section 143(12) attracts a penalty of ₹ 5 lakh for a listed company and ₹ 1 lakh for any other company.
4. Clause (ii)(b) engages where, at any time during the year, aggregate working-capital limits in excess of ₹ 5 crore were sanctioned by banks/financial institutions on the security of current assets.
Which are correct?
options: 1, 2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are faithful to the source: the two exemption tests (statement 1), the ₹ 5 lakh / ₹ 1 lakh penalty split (statement 3) and the ₹ 5 crore working-capital trigger in clause (ii)(b) (statement 4) are all correct. Statement 2 is wrong on the day-count: after reporting to the Board/Audit Committee within 2 days of knowledge, the auditor seeks their reply within 45 days, and the 15-day count runs for forwarding the report and the reply to the Central Government after receipt of the reply, not for seeking the reply. The correct combination therefore excludes statement 2, i.e., statements 1, 3 and 4 only.

questions.category: CARO - Overdue Loans vs Lender Default (Integration)
questions.question: Clause (iii)(d) reports the total amount overdue for more than 90 days on loans and advances given by the company, while clause (ix)(a) reports, in a prescribed format, the 'number of days of delay or unpaid' for the company's own defaults in repayment of borrowings or interest to a lender. A CARO-applicable company reports a ₹ 5 crore loan it gave to a customer, overdue 100 days, and a ₹ 3 crore term-loan instalment it failed to pay to its bank, delayed 40 days. Which pairing is correct?
options: Both are reported under clause (iii)(d) because each involves an amount overdue beyond a period.
The ₹ 3 crore bank default is reported under clause (iii)(d) and the ₹ 5 crore customer loan under clause (ix)(a).
Neither is reportable, because clauses (iii)(d) and (ix)(a) apply only above ₹ 5 crore.

The ₹ 5 crore customer loan (overdue 100 days) is reported under clause (iii)(d) as amount overdue for more than 90 days on loans given; the ₹ 3 crore bank instalment (delayed 40 days) is reported under clause (ix)(a) with the number of days of delay/unpaid, and is not filtered by a 90-day test.
questions.explanation: The decisive distinction is the direction of credit. Clause (iii)(d) deals with money the company has lent and catches amounts overdue for more than 90 days, so the ₹ 5 crore customer loan overdue 100 days is reported. Clause (ix)(a) deals with the company's own defaults to its lenders and reports the number of days of delay or unpaid with no 90-day floor, so the ₹ 3 crore bank instalment delayed 40 days is reported there. Running the lender default through a 90-day filter, reversing the direction, or inventing a monetary floor that neither clause contains, are each wrong.

questions.question:
During the audit of a CARO-applicable company, the auditor obtains reason to believe that an offence of fraud of ₹ 2.5 crore has been committed by employees. Arrange the reporting steps in the order the source prescribes, ending with the CARO linkage:
1. Report the matter to the Board/Audit Committee within 2 days of knowledge, seeking their reply within 45 days.
2. On receipt of the reply, forward the report and the Board/Audit Committee reply to the Central Government within 15 days of receipt of the reply.
3. In the CARO statement on clause (xi), report whether a report under section 143(12) in Form ADT-4 has been filed with the Central Government.
What is the correct sequence?
questions.explanation: Because the fraud is ₹ 2.5 crore, i.e., ₹ 1 crore or above, the section 143(12) route to the Central Government applies: the auditor first reports to the Board/Audit Committee within 2 days of knowledge and seeks their reply within 45 days (step 1), then forwards the report and the reply to the Central Government within 15 days of receipt of the reply (step 2). Only after that mechanism runs is the CARO clause (xi) statement made, recording whether the ADT-4 report under section 143(12) was filed (step 3), which is why step 3 is last. Placing step 2 before step 1, or step 3 before the Central Government report, inverts the statutory order.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements on fraud reporting:
1. Clause (xi)(a) is engaged by any fraud by the company or on the company noticed or reported during the year, and requires the nature and amount involved to be indicated.
2. Section 143(12) reporting to the Central Government is triggered only where the offence of fraud involves ₹ 1 crore or above; a fraud below ₹ 1 crore is reported to the Audit Committee/Board within 2 days.
3. Because clause (xi)(a) refers to frauds of any amount, every fraud disclosed under clause (xi) must also be reported to the Central Government under section 143(12).
4. Clause (xi)(b) links CARO to the section 143(12) mechanism by asking whether a report in Form ADT-4 has been filed with the Central Government.
Which of the above are NOT correct?
options: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Statement 3 is NOT correct: clause (xi)(a) has no monetary floor and reports any fraud noticed or reported during the year, whereas section 143(12) reporting to the Central Government is confined to frauds of ₹ 1 crore or above, so a small fraud disclosed under clause (xi) does not automatically go to the Central Government. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are faithful to the source - clause (xi)(a) requires nature and amount, section 143(12) uses the ₹ 1 crore cut-off with the below-threshold fraud going to the Audit Committee/Board within 2 days, and clause (xi)(b) asks whether the ADT-4 report was filed. Hence only statement 3 is incorrect, and combinations treating 1, 2 or 4 as incorrect are wrong.

questions.question: Two auditors fail to comply with section 143(12). Auditor A audited a listed company and did not report a ₹ 3 crore fraud to the Central Government; Auditor B audited an unlisted company and did not report a ₹ 1.5 crore fraud. A colleague argues that because CARO clause (xi)(a) only requires nature and amount, no monetary penalty can flow from the section 143(12) failure. Which option is correct?
options: A is liable to ₹ 1 lakh and B to ₹ 5 lakh, since the penalty under section 143(12) is said to turn on the size of the fraud rather than on whether the company whose auditor failed to report is listed or unlisted.
Both are liable to ₹ 5 lakh because each fraud exceeds the ₹ 1 crore threshold.
A is liable to ₹ 5 lakh (listed company) and B to ₹ 1 lakh (any other company); CARO clause (xi)'s disclosure of nature and amount does not displace the section 143(12) penalty.
Neither is liable, because section 143(12) applies only to frauds of ₹ 10 crore or above.
questions.explanation: For non-compliance with section 143(12), the source prescribes a penalty of ₹ 5 lakh in the case of a listed company and ₹ 1 lakh in the case of any other company; the duty triggers at fraud of ₹ 1 crore or above, and both frauds here qualify. Auditor A (listed) attracts ₹ 5 lakh and Auditor B (unlisted, hence 'any other company') attracts ₹ 1 lakh. The colleague's argument fails because CARO clause (xi) and section 143(12) are separate obligations. Reversing the listed/unlisted split, charging both at ₹ 5 lakh on fraud size, or importing a ₹ 10 crore trigger, are each wrong.

questions.question: An auditor of a CARO-applicable company concludes that, judged on financial ratios and the ageing of expected realisation of financial assets versus payment of financial liabilities, and considering the management's plans, no material uncertainty exists as on the date of the audit report that the company can meet its liabilities existing at the balance sheet date as and when they fall due within one year from the balance sheet date. Under which CARO clause is this conclusion recorded?
options: Clause (ix) loan repayment, because it deals with liabilities to lenders.
Clause (vii) statutory dues, because liabilities falling due include statutory dues.
Clause (iii) loans and investments, because financial ratios drive the overdue analysis.
Clause (xix) going concern, which frames this as an affirmative capability statement.
questions.explanation: Only clause (xix) requires the auditor to opine, on the basis of financial ratios, ageing of realisation of financial assets and payment of financial liabilities and knowledge of management's plans, that no material uncertainty exists as on the date of the audit report that the company can meet its balance-sheet liabilities within one year from the balance sheet date. Clauses (ix), (vii) and (iii) address transaction-level matters (defaults to lenders, statutory-dues arrears, overdue loans given) and do not call for this holistic capability assessment. The distractors borrow vocabulary from the correct clause (liabilities, ratios, dues) but attach it to clauses whose tested point is different.

questions.category: CARO Statement vs Opinion Modification - Interplay (Integration)
questions.question: Meridian Infra Ltd (CARO applies) cannot produce records evidencing title to its freehold land, and a proceeding is pending against it under the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988. Because sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the land's carrying amount - material and pervasive - could not be obtained, the auditor modifies (disclaims) the opinion. Which statement best captures the relationship between the modified audit report and the CARO statement on clause (i)?
options: The CARO statement on clause (i) (title deeds held in the name of the company; benami proceeding and its disclosure) and the modification of the audit report serve different purposes and are given independently; a modified opinion does not remove the obligation to make the clause (i) statement.
Once the opinion is modified for this matter, CARO reporting is subsumed in the opinion and no clause (i) statement is given.
Clause (i) itself requires the opinion to be qualified, so the CARO statement is optional whenever the report is modified.
The matter is reported only under clause (xix) going concern because land affects the balance sheet.
questions.explanation: CARO reporting is an additional statutory statement over and above the opinion; it is neither displaced by, nor a substitute for, a modification of the audit report. Even where the auditor disclaims the opinion for inability to obtain evidence on the land, clause (i) still requires the auditor to address title deeds held in the company's name and any pending benami proceeding and its disclosure, independently of the report modification. Saying CARO is subsumed in the opinion, treating a CARO clause as dictating the opinion and making CARO optional, or re-attributing the title/benami issue to clause (xix), are each wrong.

questions.question:
Case: For FY 2024-25, Raman Agro Ltd (CARO applies) reports: (a) cash losses of ₹ 0.9 crore in FY 2024-25 and NIL in FY 2023-24; (b) undisputed provident-fund dues outstanding on 31 March 2025 for 5 months from the due date; (c) an unspent CSR amount of ₹ 1.5 crore on a non-ongoing project transferred to a Schedule VII fund on 5 October 2025.
Consider the statements:
1. Clause (xvii) requires reporting the ₹ 0.9 crore cash loss for FY 2024-25; the nil preceding year is examined but yields no amount.
2. Clause (vii)(a) requires reporting the PF arrears because they are more than 6 months past the due date on the last day of the financial year.
3. Clause (xx)(a) records non-compliance because the ₹ 1.5 crore was transferred after 6 months from the expiry of the financial year (i.e., after 30 September 2025).
Which are correct?
options: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: clause (xvii) reports the current-year cash loss of ₹ 0.9 crore and also addresses the immediately preceding year, which being nil yields no amount. Statement 2 is NOT correct: clause (vii)(a) reports undisputed arrears outstanding on the last day of the financial year for more than 6 months from the due date, and here the PF dues are only 5 months past the due date, so the 6-month condition is not crossed. Statement 3 is correct: clause (xx)(a) measures the non-ongoing CSR transfer against 6 months from the expiry of FY 2024-25 (ending 30 September 2025), and 5 October 2025 is late, so non-compliance is recorded. The two different '6 months' windows are decisive; the correct combination is 1 and 3 only.

questions.question:
Case: Indus Steel Ltd (CARO applies) shows a current ratio of 0.7, ₹ 120 crore of financial liabilities falling due within one year from 31 March 2025 against ₹ 70 crore of financial assets expected to realise in that window, a draft management plan to convert a term loan into equity that is not yet approved, and no confirmed buyer for a proposed asset sale. Management's disclosures do not identify any material uncertainty.
Which actions are consistent with clause (xix)?
1. Evaluate the ability to pay balance-sheet liabilities falling due within one year from the balance sheet date using ratios, ageing and expected realisation of financial assets.
2. Weigh the auditor's knowledge of management's plans (equity conversion, asset sale) for whether they are approved or capable of implementation.
3. Because the plan is only a draft, conclude a material uncertainty exists yet affirm in the clause (xix) statement that no material uncertainty exists.
Which of the above should the auditor do?
options: 1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.explanation: Clause (xix) directs the auditor to base the opinion on financial ratios, ageing and expected realisation of financial assets versus payment of financial liabilities (action 1) and on knowledge of management's plans (action 2), including whether those plans are realisable - so the unapproved draft equity conversion and the unconfirmed asset sale must be assessed. Action 3 is internally contradictory: clause (xix) seeks the affirmative 'no material uncertainty exists' statement only where supportable, and on these facts (a ₹ 50 crore shortfall within the window and no committed mitigation) it cannot be truthfully affirmed. Only actions 1 and 2 are consistent.

questions.question:
Case: Greenprint Media Ltd appointed new statutory auditors in July 2024 after the predecessor resigned in May 2024, citing a disagreement over an inventory write-off. For FY 2024-25 there were no cash losses, but the immediately preceding year (FY 2023-24) had a cash loss of ₹ 0.6 crore. The new firm, to save time, did not examine the outgoing auditor's note of objections.
What should the CARO statement report?
options: Cash loss only for FY 2024-25 (nil), so clause (xvii) is silent; no clause (xviii) statement because the resignation pre-dated the new auditors' appointment.
Only clause (xviii), because cash losses are reported only when they occur in the current financial year under audit.
Only clause (xvii), because a resignation is not reportable when the reason relates to an inventory matter.

Under clause (xvii), the ₹ 0.6 crore cash loss for the immediately preceding FY 2023-24; and under clause (xviii), that there was a resignation during the year and that the issues/objections/concerns of the outgoing auditor were not taken into consideration.
questions.explanation: Clause (xvii) looks at the financial year and the immediately preceding financial year, so the ₹ 0.6 crore cash loss in FY 2023-24 must be stated even though FY 2024-25 is cash-positive. Clause (xviii) is triggered by the resignation of the statutory auditor during the year, and the new firm did not take the outgoing auditor's objections into consideration, which must be recorded. The resignation date pre-dating the appointment and the inventory reason are irrelevant to the clause triggers. Confine-to-current-year, resignation-only and cash-loss-only readings each miss one clause or wrongly exclude the resignation.

questions.question: Base: Vistas Retail Pvt Ltd is a private company, not a subsidiary or holding of any public company, with paid-up capital plus reserves ₹ 0.5 crore, no borrowings from banks/financial institutions, and revenue ₹ 6 crore, so it is exempt from CARO. Altered fact: during FY 2024-25 it becomes a subsidiary of a public company, while its capital, borrowings and revenue figures stay unchanged. What changes?
options: It remains exempt, because all three monetary conditions (capital-plus-reserves up to ₹ 1 crore, borrowings up to ₹ 1 crore, revenue up to ₹ 10 crore) are still satisfied.
It ceases to be exempt, because the private-company CARO exemption requires the company not to be a subsidiary or holding of a public company; the CARO clauses, including (xvii)-(xxi), now apply.
It ceases to be exempt, but only clauses (xvii)-(xxi) apply while the remaining clauses stay exempt.
It remains exempt, because the subsidiary condition bites only when revenue exceeds ₹ 10 crore.
questions.explanation: The CARO exemption for a private company is conditioned both on the monetary ceilings and on the company not being a subsidiary or holding of a public company; once Vistas becomes a subsidiary of a public company the relationship condition fails and CARO applies in full, notwithstanding the small figures. The decisive fact is the change of relationship, not any number. Relying on the monetary ceilings alone, inventing a clause-wise partial exemption, or tying the subsidiary condition to revenue, are each wrong; because CARO now applies, all clauses including (xvii)-(xxi) must be addressed.

questions.question:
Case: Zenith Group Ltd consolidates two subsidiaries, both CARO-applicable. In subsidiary A's audit, the auditor - applying clause (xix) - is unable to affirm that no material uncertainty exists about A meeting its balance-sheet liabilities within one year, and A's CARO report records this as a qualification. Subsidiary B's CARO report has only observations, with no qualification or adverse remark.
What must Zenith's clause (xxi) statement indicate?
options: Subsidiary A - details of the company and the paragraph number(s) of A's CARO report containing the qualification/adverse remark; B's mere observations are outside clause (xxi).
Details of both A and B, because all consolidated companies are listed regardless of remarks.
Only subsidiary B, because observations are the reportable item under clause (xxi).
Nothing, because going-concern matters are reported only in the consolidated audit report, never in clause (xxi).
questions.explanation: Clause (xxi) picks up qualifications or adverse remarks made in the CARO reports of companies included in the consolidated financial statements, and requires details of those companies and the paragraph numbers of the CARO report containing such qualification/adverse remark. A's clause (xix) qualification is therefore reported at group level with its details and paragraph numbers, while B's mere observations - being neither a qualification nor an adverse remark - fall outside clause (xxi). Listing all consolidated companies, treating observations as reportable, or saying a going-concern qualification never reaches (xxi), are each wrong.
